Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.08 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)65 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Chest and abdominal radiographyNormal

What is the most likely diagnosis to explain his current admission?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Acute pancreatitis

The diagnosis lies mainly in the symptoms, which are consistent with pancreatitis and one would expect his amylase to be high. Pancreatitis due to medications is an unusual event, but has been reported to be associated with drugs used for inflammatory bowel disease including sulphasalazine, 5- aminosalicylic acid compounds, 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine. The pathogenesis of drug-induced pancreatitis may be due to an idiosyncratic response in some cases (e.g. 6-mercaptopurine, azathioprine).

Drug-induced pancreatitis has no distinguishing clinical features. A high index of suspicion and careful drug history are therefore essential for making the diagnosis. The time course of developing the disorder depends upon the drug involved, and can vary from weeks to months. The prognosis of drug-induced pancreatitis is generally excellent.

D Infective gastroenteritis

Given the history of azathioprine use, coupled with epigastric and left-sided abdominal pain, acute pancreatitis should be ruled out first as the underlying cause of his pain. Abnormal liver function tests would also be unusual in the context of acute gastroenteritis.

A Steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis

Given that this patient’s symptoms have been controlled by reducing doses of corticosteroids, this implies steroid responsiveness. Hence steroid refractory UC is an unlikely diagnosis.

C Cholecystitis

Cholecystitis is more commonly associated with right-sided abdominal and epigastric pain, rather than the left- sided pain reported here.

E Peptic ulcer disease

Peptic ulcer disease is associated with epigastric pain, and not with the abnormal liver function tests and mild hypocalcaemia seen here.

questions.question:
You review a 48-year-old publican who is awaiting discharge from the Gastroenterology Ward after an episode of haematemesis related to oesophageal varices. He received injection sclerotherapy at the time. You review his investigations and decide on medication to reduce further bleeding. He is already on spironolactone.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)115 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.1 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)230 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Hepatic ultrasound scansmall shrunken liver
Liver biopsyadvanced cirrhosis

Which one of the following would be most appropriate strategy to reduce portal blood pressure in this man?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Propranolol

Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker with high hepatic first pass metabolism and in clinical trials has been shown to be the most effective oral agent in long-term therapy for portal hypertension. Porto-systemic shunting is usually reserved for patients who re-bleed and have symptoms of worsening portal hypertension.

D Furosemide

Furosemide can drive symptomatic hyponatraemia and is less effective versus spironolactone in controlling fluid balance in hepatic cirrhosis.

A Atenolol

Atenolol has greater B1 receptor selectivity than propranolol and lower first pass hepatic metabolism, this makes it a less ideal choice for the treatment of portal hypertension.

B Isosorbide dinitrate

Isosorbide dinitrate is less effective in controlling portal hypertension in this situation because of potential difficulties with postural hypotension, and tolerance to the effects of nitrates in the longterm.

E Lactulose

Lactulose and neomycin are usually used to prevent encephalopathy after a large GI bleed by reducing the ammonia load associated with a GI haemorrhage.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman presents with a severe headache, peripheral oedema and indigestion. She is 32 weeks’ pregnant with her first child.

On examination, her BP is 140/90 mmHg and she looks tired; her ankles are swollen.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value

White cell count (WCC)7.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L

International normalised ratio (INR)1.0< 1.1

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome

The combination of severe headache, peripheral oedema, indigestion and proteinuria is very classical for pre- eclampsia. This patient has associated HELLP syndrome. Micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, which accounts for the blood picture seen here, is typical of the situation. Of paramount importance is control of blood pressure and rapid assessment of the pregnancy by the obstetric team. The only way to resolve pre-eclampsia is delivery of the placenta, and hence the neonate.

D Eclampsia

Eclampsia is where seizures are seen on top of the picture of pre-eclampsia described here.

A Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

This is rare, occurring at around week 35 in pregnancy, and is associated with a moderate elevation in transaminases; bilirubin is also raised and clotting is abnormal, although the hypertension seen here is not present.

B Cholestasis of pregnancy

The main symptoms of cholestasis of pregnancy are itching and lethargy, which begin as early as week 25.

E Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP)

ITP is not associated with the other features seen here, including hypertension, proteinuria, renal impairment and abnormal liver function tests.

Urea9.5 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L He is actively resuscitated with fluids and blood products while awaiting urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. During endoscopy, band ligation is performed to control the bleeding. Unfortunately, the bands do

not stem the bleeding and the patient continues to ooze blood.

Which of the following is the next best therapeutic option in controlling this patient’s acute variceal bleed?
options: Continue to perform variceal banding until the bleeding ceases
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)

The combination of banding and terlipressin appears to be most effective in controlling acute variceal bleed, the rebleeding rate and early complications. In the event that banding does not control the bleeding, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance advises considering a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure.

D Variceal sclerotherapy and terlipressin

Variceal banding is preferred to sclerotherapy because it achieves a resolution of large varices in fewer treatment sessions, compared to sclerotherapy.

A Balloon tamponade and terlipressin

Balloon tamponade does not directly target varices and is less effective than banding, although it can be used acutely to control catastrophic haemorrhage.

B Continue to perform variceal banding until the bleeding ceases

If banding fails to control bleeding, an alternative option needs to be sought. In the event that banding does not control bleeding, The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance advises considering a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure.

C Propranolol and variceal sclerotherapy

Although non-selective beta-blockers and nitrates reduce portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding, they are not useful in the acute setting, because of hypotension, as is seen here. Sclerotherapy is also thought to have marginally less good outcomes, compared to banding.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with a 1-month history of dysphagia to solids. He has previously been fit and well and, on direct questioning, denies previous episodes of dysphagia or reflux.

On examination, he appears cachectic, although there are no palpable masses on abdominal examination. An upper endoscopy is performed, which reveals a lower oesophageal mass, not invading the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy of this mass reveals an adenocarcinoma. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the patient’s chest, abdomen and pelvis is completed. After a multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion, the tumour is staged as Tumour (T)3, Node (N)1, Metastasis (M)0.

Which would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
options: External beam radiotherapy and oesophageal stenting
Neoadjuvant cisplatin, paclitaxel and radiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy
Neoadjuvant cisplatin and fluorouracil followed by endoscopic mucosal resection
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Neoadjuvant cisplatin, paclitaxel and radiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy

In T3–4, N1–3, M0 disease, the recommended treatment is neoadjuvant treatment, usually with cisplatin and paclitaxel plus radiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy. This is the standard regime based on the results of the Chemoradiotherapy for Oesophageal Cancer Followed by Surgery Study (CROSS) trial. This approach has been found to improve survival and resection rates, compared with surgery alone, in patients with oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Patients must be assessed for suitability for surgery. If unsuitable for surgery, they may be offered definitive chemoradiotherapy alone. This may be followed by nivolumab in patients who have residual pathological disease following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgery, particularly if there is lymph node involvement due to the high risk of disease recurrence.

E Oesophagectomy

Oesophagectomy alone is recommended for limited disease T1b or low-risk localised T2 disease in patients who are suitable for surgery. In high-risk T2 disease or above, neoadjuvant or definitive chemoradiotherapy is recommended.

A Definitive chemoradiotherapy

Definitive chemoradiotherapy would be an appropriate treatment for this patient if there were any indications that he was not suitable for surgery. Given that we are told he is usually fit and well, with no indication of any past medical history, he is likely to benefit from surgery and, therefore, this is not an appropriate treatment option.

B External beam radiotherapy and oesophageal stenting

External beam radiotherapy and oesophageal stenting may be offered to patients with metastatic disease (M1), in addition to palliative chemoradiotherapy, depending on the degree of dysphagia caused by the oesophageal tumour and its impact on nutrition, quality of life, performance status and prognosis. This treatment may also be considered for recurrent disease.

D Neoadjuvant cisplatin and fluorouracil followed by endoscopic mucosal resection

Endoscopic therapy alone is recommended for patients with localised T1a disease. It is recommended over surgery, as those treated with endoscopic therapy have been shown to have improved cancer-specific survival and decreased morbidity. Endoscopic therapy is not usually recommended in combination with chemotherapy. It may be used as an alternative agent to chemoradiotherapy in T1b disease when patients are not suitable for surgery.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with worsening diarrhoea. She denies vomiting and fever, although she does describe intermittent facial flushing. There is no past medical history of note.

On examination, her blood pressure is 101/58 mmHg and her heart rate is 88 bpm. Her abdomen is soft and only mildly tender, with active bowel sounds. There is facial telangiectasia and evidence of tricuspid regurgitation. Her body mass index is 21 kg/m 2.

Routine bloods undertaken by her General Practitioner reveal:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)108 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea5.5 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)215 U/L7 - 55 U/L

What is the next best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)

Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is used in the diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome presents with facial flushing (75–90% of patients), diarrhoea (> 70%) and intermittent bronchospasm (25%). Associated clinical findings include facial telangiectasia and tricuspid regurgitation. It is caused by the action of serotonin, bradykinin and histamine produced by tumours arising from neuroendocrine cells. Diagnosis is by measuring an increase in the levels of urinary 5-HIAA, a metabolite of serotonin (5-HT). It is likely that this patient’s abnormal alanine aminotransferase level is due to the presence of liver metastases. Pellagra is a nicotinic acid deficiency that can occur as a result of increased requirements for nicotinamide due to the carcinoid tumour. It is an important substrate in the metabolic formation of 5-HT. Deficiency in nicotinic acid can lead to dementia in patients with extensive carcinoid metastases.

E Urinary metanephrines

Urinary metanephrines are used in the investigation of phaeochromocytoma. This is associated with marked hypertension and headaches and may be associated with hypokalaemia. However, it is not associated with significant diarrhoea.

A 0900 cortisol

Cortisol measurement taken at 0900 is used in the diagnosis of Cushing’s disease. This disease is associated with significant weight gain, which does not fit with the diagnosis here.

B Iron-binding studies

Iron deficiency alone is unlikely, given the other symptoms, including facial flushing, diarrhoea and evidence of tricuspid regurgitation— all of which fit better with carcinoid.

C Thyroid receptor antibodies

Thyroid receptor antibodies are used in the diagnosis of autoimmune hyper- or hypothyroidism. Although thyrotoxicosis may be associated with weight loss and diarrhoea, features such as telangiectasia, tricuspid regurgitation and elevated transaminase levels would be unexpected in the context of hyperthyroidism. 72946

questions.question:
A 43-year-old medical secretary with dermatomyositis is referred from the dermatologist with a short history of dysphagia. She has been using the food processor to liquidise her solid food but now find fluids increasingly difficult, too.

She has no previous history of dyspepsia. She is a long-term heavy smoker and drinks socially. Her mother had a gastrectomy for peptic ulcer disease. She now wakes up at night very breathless. She finds eating very distressing and feels that she has lost weight.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)90 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)199 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)95 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)78 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Oesophageal carcinoma

The history of rapid progression from solid to liquid dysphagia is suggestive of a malignant oesophageal lesion, which like bronchial carcinoma is associated with dermatomyositis. In order to confirm the diagnosis of oesophageal malignancy, a histology sample is required. Once diagnosis is confirmed, a computed tomography scan is necessary to assess for disease extent to consider surgical resectability. The following are risk factors for oesophageal carcinoma: male sex, heavy smoking, Barrett’s oesophagus, achalasia, coeliac disease, and tylosis pylori (autosomal dominant, hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles).

D Tracheo-oesophageal fistula

A tracheo-oesophageal fistula presents with recurrent symptoms of aspiration, rather than the picture seen

here.

B Systemic sclerosis

Oesophageal involvement occurs in 90% of those with systemic sclerosis, and symptoms are usually of heartburn or acid regurgitation (due to failure of the gastro-oesophageal physiological sphincter to close).

C Benign peptic stricture

Benign oesophageal stricture is often associated with mixed dysphagia to liquids and solids, and isn’t associated with as much weight loss as a malignant lesion.

E Bronchial carcinoma with oesophageal metastases

In this situation more marked respiratory symptoms would be expected with a bronchial carcinoma than those seen here (which are likely to be associated to muscle weakness).

questions.question:
A 58-year-old Greek woman attended the Emergency Department with a 4-week history of discomfort in the right upper quadrant.

Examination revealed that she was mildly tender in the right upper quadrant and had 4 cm hepatomegaly. She had a previous laparotomy scar, having had a duodenal ulcer oversewn 20 years previously.

The full blood count is normal. Alkaline phosphatase is 1.5 times the upper limit of normal, and the ALT is just above the upper limit of normal. Her abdominal X-ray is shown below:

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Retained foreign body from previous surgery
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Hydatid disease

Hydatid disease is caused by the ingestion of Echinococcus granulosus, a dog tapeworm. It is common in parts of the world associated with raising sheep or cattle, including the Eastern Mediterranean, South America, the Middle East, Australia, and North and East Africa.

The life cycle of E. granulosus includes a stage in pigs, cattle or sheep. It is passed to humans by direct contact with dogs or their faeces. Penetration through the duodenal wall permits the parasite to pass into the liver, from where it can spread to almost any organ. The liver is by far the most common site for hydatid cysts (60%), followed by the lungs (20%). Hydatid cysts can be asymptomatic, but enlarging cysts may cause localised pressure effects, such as pain or jaundice. Up to one-third of affected people have a peripheral eosinophilia.

Complement fixation or haemagglutination tests are often (if not invariably) positive, with assays involving ELISA becoming increasingly prevalent too. About 40% of cysts calcify, and ultrasound or CT imaging frequently shows daughter cysts. Many asymptomatic cysts can be left alone. Pharmacological therapy with Albendazole can shrink cysts, a measure that may be used prior to surgery. Although aspiration was traditionally avoided due to the risk of anaphylaxis, it may now be used therapeutically under chemotherapeutic cover. Complications of untreated hydatid disease include involvement of other organs, secondary infection and cyst rupture.

C Amoebic liver abscess

Amoebic liver abscess is not typically associated with calcification, so cannot explain the radiograph findings. Furthermore, a leukocytosis and abnormal liver enzymes would be expected if this were the diagnosis here.

A Porcelain gallbladder

Firstly, affected people tend to describe a long history of gallstone disease (much longer than the four weeks of symptoms described), and would not be expected to have hepatomegaly. Secondly, radiographs of people with porcelain gallbladder typically show a more irregular pattern of calcification than the smooth, round pattern shown on the radiograph here.

D Pyogenic liver abscess

Pyogenic liver abscess is not typically associated with calcification, so cannot explain the radiograph findings. Furthermore, a leukocytosis and abnormal liver enzymes would be expected if this were the diagnosis here.

E Retained foreign body from previous surgery

It is unlikely that a foreign body would have been retained for twenty years after surgery without complication before now, and there is no surgical equipment that would typically have this appearance on a plain radiograph.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old man with a 20-year history of alcohol misuse is being investigated as an outpatient. He undergoes endoscopy and is found to have three columns of oesophageal varices that occlude the lumen.

On questioning, he denies any previous episodes of melaena or haematemesis. He admits to still drinking 7–10 cans of lager per day. Physical examination reveals moderate ascites. There is no evidence of encephalopathy.

His face is shown below.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)150 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)120 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin45 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)80 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)35 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin30 g/L35–55 g/L
Prothrombin Time (PT)23 s10.6–14.9 s

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment option with respect to reducing portal hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Propranolol

The blood results here are consistent with a diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis. Jaundiced sclera and ascites are signs of chronic liver disease. Portal hypertension is suggested by the low platelet count (due to hypersplenism) and varices at endoscopy. Guidelines published by the British Society of Gastroenterology in 2015 suggest primary prophylaxis with pharmacological treatment with propranolol as the first line, so option E is correct. Non-cardioselective β-blockers such as propranolol cause splanchnic vasoconstriction (via blockade of vasodilatory adrenoreceptors of the splanchnic circulation), reducing portal and collateral blood flow.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jaundice_of_the_sclerotic.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jaundice_of_the_sclerotic.JPG)

C Cyanoacrylate gluing of the varices

This technique is used only to treat gastric varices, not oesphageal varices.

A Trans-jugular intrahepatic porto-systemic shunt (TIPSS)

TIPSS is a shunt created between the portal and hepatic vein in order to reduce portal pressure. A reduction in portal hypertension will reduced the risk of bleeding from varices, but carries a risk of chronic encephalopathy. It is therefore only currently recommended for the treatment of recurrent variceal bleeding.

B Injection sclerotherapy to the varices

The results of trials of sclerotherapy as primary prophylaxis have produced mixed results and it is therefore not recommended.

D Banding ligation of the varices

Pharmacological treatment with propranolol is less invasive and can be as equally as effective in reducing portal hypertension.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old man with a long history of diarrhoea presented with a painful lesion on his leg. He had noticed what he thought was an insect bite some days previously, which rapidly progressed to the lesion depicted below. He had started feeling unwell with the development of the lesion and described general malaise and arthralgia.

His barium enema is shown below:

What is the cause of his diarrhoea?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Ulcerative colitis

The barium enema shows the typical ‘hosepipe’ colonic appearance found in chronic ulcerative colitis. The colonic wall is featureless here, consistent with chronic inflammation. Incidentally, this man also has situs inversus. The lesion on his leg is pyoderma gangrenosum.

C Ogilvie's syndrome

Ogilvie's syndrome is associated with dilated large bowel, but not with inflammation.

A Crohn's disease

Crohn's disease produces skip lesions, so would not typically manifest with uniform involvement of the whole large bowel, as is the case here.

D Ischaemic colitis

The findings here are not suggestive of ischaemic colitis.

E Colonic carcinoma

No obstruction is seen on the barium study, ruling out colonic carcinoma.

questions.question:
An 80-year-old homeless man presents with punctuate haemorrhage around the hair follicles and coiling of the hair on his upper arms. He appears to be malnourished and lethargic, with a weight of 70 kg and blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)93 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)322 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.6 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea3.4 µmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)133 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Prothrombin test (PT)15 s10.6–14.9 s
Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)32 s23.0–35.0 s
Bleeding time3 minutes3–10 minutes

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Scurvy

Humans are unable to synthesise ascorbic acid (vitamin C), and its deficiency leads to a condition known as scurvy. The initial typical skin changes are of follicular keratosis with coiling of the hair. Later, patients develop perifollicular haemorrhages, bleeding gums and purpura over the legs. Patients often have an associated anaemia and their plasma ascorbic acid levels will be low. There is rapid clinical improvement following vitamin

C replacement.

E Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is an autoimmune syndrome of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia associated with renal and neurological dysfunction. Clotting studies may be abnormal.

A Ehlers–Danlos syndrome

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome refers to a group of inherited disorders in collagen and connective tissue synthesis and structure, resulting in hyperelastic skin, unstable and hypermobile joints, and fragile tissue and blood vessels.

B von Willebrand’s disease

von Willebrand’s disease is a hereditary clotting disorder associated with an increased bleeding tendency and easy bruising.

C Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

DIC is a coagulation disorder characterized by the widespread activation of the clotting cascade that results in the formation of clots in the small blood vessels throughout the body. Common causes include sepsis, malignancies, and large injuries.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old actress presents to her GP with worsening pruritus, which she finds embarrassing at work. She has a past medical history of hypothyroidism and mild rheumatoid arthritis. She is on levothyroxine only. She drinks on average one glass of wine a night.

On examination, she has mildly jaundiced sclera, xanthelasma, clubbing and hepatomegaly on examination. Her BP is 142/82 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular and her BMI is 25.

Given the likely clinical diagnosis, which of the following tests is most likely to be elevated /abnormal?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Anti-mitochondrial antibodies

This patient has a typical presentation of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), a condition of gradual destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to fibrosis and cholestasis and ultimately hepatic cirrhosis, usually presented in middle-aged women. Pruritis, fatigue and elevated alkaline phosphatase are some of the characteristic features seen in PBC. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies test is specific to PBC, as these antibodies are present in more than 90 % of cases.

E Haemoglobin

Patients with PBC can present with anaemia and low haemoglobin. However, this option is non-specific for the diagnosis of PBC.

A Serum IgG

Serum IgG levels are raised in cases of autoimmune pancreatitis, which is a predisposing factor of chronic pancreatitis, characterized by recurrent or persistent epigastric pain, steatorrhea and weight loss. None of these symptoms are present in this case and given the likely diagnosis of PBC, makes this option less likely to be correct. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies and raised serum IgM is also seen in cases of PBC.

C HDL cholesterol

High lipid and cholesterol levels (especially HDL) may be increased in patients with PBC. However, it is not the best option to select in the presence of anti-mitochondrial antibodies test, which is more specific and present in more than 90% of patients with PBC.

D Vitamin A

In patients with PBC, lack of bile can lead to inability to absorb fats and fat soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Abnormal vitamin A level is non-specific for the diagnosis of PBC, which is a possible diagnosis here.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman, known to have coeliac disease that is well controlled with a gluten-free diet, comes to the clinic for review. Over the past few months, she has developed a painful, blistering rash which also affects the inside of her mouth. Examination reveals extensive blisters, most of which have been deroofed within the oral cavity, affecting the trunk, arms and legs. Investigations;

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)128 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine85 µmmol/l50–120 µmol/L
Albumin41 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)36 IU/L5–30 IU/L

Skin biopsy, Intercellular IgG and C3 deposits mainly in the upper parts of the epidermis.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Prednisolone

While you might expect the underlying diagnosis to be dermatitis herpetiformis in a patient with coeliac disease, the biopsy description here is consistent with a diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris. Corticosteroids are the most effective and rapidly acting treatment for inducing remission in pemphigus vulgaris. Obtaining disease control typically takes several weeks to achieve. During this phase, the intensity of treatment may need to be built up rapidly to suppress disease activity. Once remission is achieved, steroid doses should be reduced and patients should also be prescribed a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) such as mycophenolate or rituximab. Studies have shown superiority of rituximab and prednisolone in maintaining remission over prednisolone as a standalone therapy.

A Aciclovir

Aciclovir is commonly used in the management of herpes simplex infections. The skin biopsy results in this case are not consistent with a diagnosis of herpes simplex. Therefore, aciclovir is not required here.

B Ciclosporin

Ciclosporin is an immunosuppressive drug first approved for use in organ transplantation to prevent rejection. Ciclosporinis also known to be used for the treatment of psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus and inflammatory bowel disease, among other indications. It is not used routinely in the management of pemphigus vulgaris, and therefore, it is not the correct answer here.

C Dapsone

Dapsone is used in the treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis, which is mostly associated with a neutrophilic infiltration on skin biopsy.

E Reinforcement of gluten free diet

Gluten-free diets are the mainstay of coeliac disease management. However, in this case, the patient has developed pemphigus vulgaris. She requires treatment for that, alongside the management of her coeliac disease.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with the sensation of something stuck in his throat. He reports to have been eating a steak dinner meal before a piece of meat became lodged when swallowing. On further questioning, he reports several episodes of dysphagia and has been told it is due to him not chewing properly. He occasionally takes over-the-counter antacids for heartburn but has no other past medical history of note.

He is referred for an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) and the food bolus is removed. Images are captured of his oesophagus:

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Eosinophilic oesophagitis

This patient likely has eosinophilic oesophagitis, given the history of repeated dysphagia and the presentation of an obstructed food bolus. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergen-mediated condition characterised by oesophageal dysfunction including dyspepsia, dysphagia, vomiting and abdominal pain, along with eosinophilic infiltration in the oesophageal epithelium on biopsy. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) and biopsy are necessary for diagnosis, and findings include oesophageal oedema, oesophageal rings and strictures with white plaques or exudates representing eosinophilic micro-abscesses. The endoscopic image shown here shows multiple oesophageal rings, which supports the underlying diagnosis.

Image source: By Samir, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=5161861

E Pharyngeal pouch

A pharyngeal pouch is caused by a herniation between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles that

causes symptoms of dysphagia, regurgitation, chronic cough, aspiration and halitosis. It is most commonly seen in men aged above 70 years. Barium swallow is preferred over OGD due to the risk of perforating the pouch.

A Achalasia

Achalasia is characterised by motor dysfunction of the oesophagus that causes symptoms of dysphagia and regurgitation due to loss of oesophageal peristalsis. Unlike oesophageal carcinoma, dysphagia for solids and liquids can present initially as the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax on swallowing. Nevertheless, OGD is indicated in the investigation of achalasia due to the concern of oesophageal carcinoma, and findings range from being normal to a dilated oesophagus with a tight lower oesophageal junction.

C Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) typically presents with dyspepsia and regurgitation. It is associated with Barrett’s oesophagus, oesophageal strictures and oesophageal carcinoma. Typically, GORD can present similarly to eosinophilic oesophagitis and, in some cases, both conditions can be present with GORD worsening eosinophilic oesophagitis by worsening the oesophageal mucosal wall. OGD is an initial investigation to request with findings ranging from being normal to showing oesophagitis with erosions, ulcerations and strictures. The oesophageal rings on this endoscopy make eosinophilic oesophagitis the most likely diagnosis.

D Oesophageal adenocarcinoma

Oesophageal adenocarcinoma is an important differential diagnosis to consider, given the history of dysphagia. However, additional symptoms tend to include odynophagia, weight loss and a progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids. The findings of OGD include oesophageal obstruction due to an oesophageal mass. 73943

questions.question:
A 26-year-old man is referred for investigation of profuse, watery diarrhoea that had been going on for the past 6 weeks. He had lost one stone in weight over this time, even though his appetite remained good. He had not seen any blood or mucus in the stool and had no abdominal pain, distension or vomiting. Apart from lethargy, he had no other symptoms. He had no significant past medical history and took no regular medication. He does not smoke and drinks ten units of alcohol per week. There was no relevant family history.

He had recently spent a year in Australia, travelling out and back through South East Asia, but had returned home over 6 months ago. His general practitioner had tried him on several anti-diarrhoeal agents that had not worked, and multiple stool cultures had come back negative.

On examination, he was thin, but not wasted. There was no lymphadenopathy, jaundice or clubbing. His abdomen was soft and non-tender with no masses, and normal bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination was normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.4 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)260 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)102 fL76–98 fL
Urea5.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)8.0 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)1.9 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
Bilirubin14 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)60 IU/L30–130 IU/L Gamma-glutamyl-transferase
48 IU/L5–30 IU/L (γGT) Aspartate aminotransferase
22 IU/L10–40 IU/L (AST)
Albumin30 g/L35–55 g/L Serum anti-endomysial - antibodies No abnormality seen, good views to the terminal Colonoscopy ileum Small bowel barium follow- Normal through
Abdominal ultrasound scanNormal

What would be the next most useful investigation to establish the cause of the diarrhoea?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B HIV test

This patient has diarrhoea of small bowel origin, with evidence of malabsorption (macrocytic anaemia, low calcium and albumin). Inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease have been excluded by the investigations performed so far. An HIV test should be performed after appropriate consent and counselling. Diarrhoea is a common problem in HIV infection and has many causes, mainly infective. Pathogens include Cryptosporidium parvum, Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Mycobacterium avium intracellulare, Isospora bella and cytomegalovirus (CMV), as well as those that can cause diarrhoea in immunocompetent patients. Intestinal lymphomas can also cause similar symptoms. As this patient has had multiple negative stool cultures, the diarrhoea could be due to HIV enteropathy which is caused by partial villous atrophy.

D Radio-isotope-labelled white cell scan

Radio isotope-labelled white cell scans are most useful in evaluating abscesses related to inflammatory bowel disease.

A Serum gastrin level

Serum gastrin level is most useful in evaluating potential Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which results in multiple gastric ulcers.

C Hydrogen breath test

Hydrogen breath testing is useful in the evaluation of bacterial overgrowth syndrome, which leads to symptoms of both diarrhoea and abdominal bloating.

E 24 h urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)

Urinary 5-HIAA is most useful in the evaluation of carcinoid syndrome, which is associated with episodes of diarrhoea and flushing. These occur against a background of hepatic metastases, which are not suggested by the normal LFTs seen here.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old devout Hindu woman who follows a vegan diet is referred to the Gastroenterology Outpatient Clinic by her general practitioner (GP). She complains of a 6-month history of lethargy and increasing breathlessness on exertion. Her blood pressure is 112/82, pulse is 70, BMI is 23. Neurological examination is normal. Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)86 g/L115–155 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)112 fL80–100 fL
White cell count (WCC)4.8 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)170 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)8 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Biochemical profileNormal
Serum gastrin42 pmol/l< 55 pmol/l

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Dietary deficiency of B 12

The most likely cause of a macrocytic anaemia with a mild reduction in white cell count and platelets in this patient is dietary deficiency. A Hindu diet is usually vegetarian. Vitamin B 12 is predominantly found in foods of animal origin, eg meat, fish and eggs. First-line investigations should confirm vitamin B 12 deficiency before undertaking further, more invasive investigations. The low white blood cell count is well described in B 12 deficiency and may be due to both co-existent low protein intake and to defective white cell maturation driven by B 12 itself.

Vegans do not eat food that originates from animals, including eggs and milk produce. This means that they are at an increased risk of vitamin B 12 deficiency. Vitamin B 12 is classically available from the following food sources: meat and fish (particularly cod and salmon), milk, cheese and eggs and is absorbed in the terminal ileum. However, many modern vegan foodstuffs, such as soya milk, are fortified with additional vitamins, including B 12. Even in cases where a patient's vegan diet is deficient in B 12, it is unlikely to be apparent for some time as the body typically has approximately five years of vitamin B 12 reserves.

Therefore, strict vegans and those who suffer from diseases which affect the terminal ileum (Crohn’s disease, bacterial overgrowth, coeliac disease and fish tapeworms, for example) are more likely to present with this deficiency. Other associated conditions include pernicious anaemia, chronic pancreatitis and the use of certain medications such as metformin. Clinical presentations of vitamin B 12 deficiency include oral findings like glossitis (‘beefy-red’ tongue), jaundice, depression, psychosis and neurological findings such as subacute combined spinal cord degeneration. Management is cause-dependent. If the cause is dietary, then oral vitamin

B 12 supplementation can be given; however, if the cause is malabsorption, then intramuscular vitamin B 12

injections are indicated.

D Myxoedema

Although hypothyroidism may cause macrocytosis, the degree of anaemia seen here would be unexpected. Additionally there is no evidence of weight gain or abnormal reflexes on physical examination.

A Pernicious anaemia

Pernicious anaemia is associated with elevated serum gastrin and decreased intrinsic factor. As such, the normal serum gastrin effectively excludes the diagnosis.

C Aplastic anaemia

There are no precipitating risk factors for aplastic anaemia, and in a strict vegetarian, B 12 deficiency is the likely cause of macrocytic anaemia seen here.

E Myelodysplasia

Myelodysplasia can be associated macrocytic anaemia, although the condition would be unusual in a woman of this age. Other features such as neutropaenia or low platelet count are absent here.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman has been referred to the Endocrine Clinic with a history of increasing shoe size and problems with her dentures fitting. She also complains of flushing and sweating.

Routine blood testing at the initial clinic appointment confirms an elevated random blood glucose and an elevated IGF-1. Because of a suspected diagnosis of acromegaly, an oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone is performed as well as a gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the pituitary. She attends for review after the tests have been performed.

The results of the oral glucose tolerance test are as follows:

Time (min) Growth hormone (GH) (mU)

0 8

30 8 (elevated)

60 7

90 8

120 9

180 9

The gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the pituitary is reported as not showing an adenoma, although the pituitary appears slightly enlarged overall.

Which step would you take next to best manage her case?
options: CT of the chest and abdomen
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B CT of the chest and abdomen

The oral glucose tolerance test shows non-suppression of GH secretion, with the 75 g glucose load indicating the diagnosis of acromegaly. However, the magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the pituitary shows no adenoma, which is unusual. This raises the possibility of other causes of acromegaly. The patient complains of flushing, which is a symptom of carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid tumours can rarely produce GH-releasing hormone (GhRH), causing pituitary hyperplasia and acromegaly. CT of the chest and abdomen would be used to look for a carcinoid tumour, and chromogranin A, also known as parathyroid secretory hormone 1, is a serum marker for carcinoid tissue.

E Inferior petrosal vein sampling

Inferior petrosal vein sampling is useful to localise a source of elevated ACTH. Given the MRI shows no adenoma, this is unlikely to be a useful step.

A Arginine test

Administration of arginine promotes GH release and is therefore used in the evaluation of GH deficiency.

C Refer for transphenoidal hypophysectomy

Without a discrete adenoma, pituitary surgery is not indicated here.

D Insulin tolerance test

Like the arginine test, the insulin tolerance test is used in evaluation of growth hormone deficiency, and therefore has no role here. Its use has also fallen off in recent years due to significant risk of serious hypoglycaemia.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old Greek man was referred to the Hepatology Clinic with abnormal liver function tests and a positive hepatitis B surface antigen. He works as a taxi driver and drinks three cans of beer in the evening. He has never had any blood transfusion or intravenous drug abuse.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Bilirubin24 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine transferase (ALT)78 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)143 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Albumin35 g/L35–55 g/L
Serum ferritin400 µg/L20–250 µg/L Further hepatitis B serology reveals the following:
InvestigationResult
Hepatitis B e antigenNegative
Anti-hepatitis B core IgMNegative
Total anti-HB corePositive
Hepatitis B DNAPositive

Which of the following best describes his likely diagnosis?
options: Hepatitis B with delta virus superinfection
Chronic hepatitis B carrier of high infectivity
Hepatitis B infection with pre-core mutant
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Hepatitis B infection with pre-core mutant

Chronic hepatitis B is defined as the persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in the circulation for more than six months after clinical infection. HBeAg is a marker of infectivity in all patients except those who have hepatitis B virus (HBV) pre-core mutant or the core promoter mutant, because they do not synthesise HbeAg (as seen in this case). This is most commonly due to a stop-codon mutation at nucleotide 1896. So the learning here is that although the e antigen is negative, this patient still has active hepatitis B and is still infective.

Response to interferon is not good and relapse rates tend to be high. Treatment of chronic hepatitis is aimed at patients with active disease and viral replication, preferably at a stage before cirrhosis has developed. Patients are selected for antiviral therapy if they have an increased alanine transferase on two occasions, detectable HBV DNA and/or HbeAg in their serum, and a liver biopsy that show fibrosis.

C Chronic hepatitis B carrier of high infectivity

Chronic hepatitis B carrier with high infectivity would be suggested by the presence of e antigen. As it is absent, this makes a less likely choice.

A Acute hepatitis B infection

This is unlikely, firstly because the clinical history does not suggest an acute infection as acute RUQ pain and jaundice are missing. Secondly, one would expect there to be a greater ALT rise and IgM to be positive.

B Hepatitis B with delta virus superinfection

Delta virus, or hepatitis D virus, is an incomplete RNA virus which needs hepatitis B to be able to complete its assembly, and can only occur as a superinfection. It can cause acute liver failure and cirrhosis, and can be tested for by serology. The absence of positive serology makes in unlikely.

E Previous hepatitis B infection

Previous hepatitis B infection would be suggested by the presence of anti-surface and anti-core antibodies and the absence of abnormal liver function. Also, the presence of detectable HBV DNA suggests the presence of active viral infection.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old man with chronic renal impairment and previous splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis presents to the Emergency Department with fever and rigors. He has been complaining of right upper quadrant pain over the past few days. His wife tells you that he has been avoiding fatty foods recently as he feels nauseous and sometimes vomits after eating them. On examination, he is pyrexial (39.2 °C) with BP 105/70 mmHg, pulse 102/min. There is obvious right upper quadrant tenderness.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)119 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)193 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)134 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Which of the following would be the most appropriate antibiotic intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Piperacillin with tazobactam

He is at increased risk of gallstones due to haemolysis related to his hereditary spherocytosis. It is likely that the presence of stones within the bile duct has led to ascending infection. Piperacillin with tazobactam has a broad spectrum of activity against community-acquired intra-abdominal infections covering streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae resistant to third-generation cephalosporins, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and anaerobes. Antibiotic treatment is usually followed by ERCP and sphincterotomy to allow any stones or sludge to pass.

D Vancomycin

Like gentamicin, vancomycin requires dose adjustment for kidney disease and is potentially nephrotoxic; it’s therefore a less appropriate choice versus ciprofloxacin.

A Gentamicin

This is an alternative although it must be carefully dosed given that creatinine is already elevated, blood pressure is at the lower end of the normal range and there is potential Gram-negative sepsis.

C Erythromycin

Erythromycin isn’t an appropriate choice here because it has poor coverage against potential Gram-negative pathogens.

E Amoxicillin

There is extensive resistance to amoxicillin amongst Pseudomonas and Gram-negatives, and so it isn’t an appropriate choice here.

questions.question:
A 74-year-old man, who has recently returned from Singapore, presents to the Emergency Department with severe pneumonia. He is treated with intravenous (iv) co-amoxiclav and then transferred to oral after four days, but begins to develop severe diarrhoea. This worsens over the next 24 h until he is opening his bowels 8-10 times per day and beginning to get dehydrated. On examination, his BP is 120/70 mmHg, his pulse is 92/min, but his BP decreases to 95/60 mmHg and his pulse increases to 105/min on standing. His temperature is 37.8 °C. His chest signs have significantly improved.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin129 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets187 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
C-Reactive protein (CRP)44 mg/L (down from 187)0–10 mg/L
Sodium (Na⁺)143 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine187 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Vancomycin

This patient in all likelihood has Clostridium difficile infection resulting in the development of pseudomembranous colitis. Symptoms are typically said to occur between 5 and 10 days after commencing antibiotic therapy. Diagnosis is via stool samples detecting Cl. difficile toxin. Sigmoidoscopy is not used routinely, but can reveal distal ulceration and a possible yellow slough or pseudomembrane in around half of patients. Treatment of choice for psuedomembranous colitis is oral vancomycin (125 mg four times a day for 10 days) which leads to slightly faster resolution of symptoms versus metronidazole. Second line treatment (if vancomycin is not effective) is fidaxomycin (200 mg twice a day for 10 days). If there is no oral administration possible, IV metronidazole can be considered. Supportive therapy with appropriate rehydration is also essential to avoid pre-kidney disease, and already debilitated patients have a significant mortality which may approach as high as 25%.

B Mebendazole

This is a medication used to treat parasitic worm infections, such as giardia and hookworm.

C Ciprofloxacin

This is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that is associated with Cl. difficile infection.

D Clindamycin

This is an antibiotic that is associated with Cl. difficile infection.

E Co-amoxiclav

This is amoxicillin with clavulanic acid and is the antibiotic the patient has received for his pneumonia; it is likely that this was a significant contributing factor to his Cl. difficile infection.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and vomiting. She has a long history of cramping abdominal pain, as does her younger brother. Her father has had two laparotomies.

Examination and investigation reveals signs of small-bowel obstruction. A picture of her mouth is shown below:

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Peutz-Jeghers syndrome

The history of small bowel obstruction with the classic signs of perioral pigmentation fits with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. This disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, with the defect being in a gene on chromosome 19 which encodes a serine threonine kinase.

The characteristic pigmentation occurs circumorally, on the buccal mucosa, and may also occur on the hands and feet, and/ or around the anus. The pigmented areas may fade with age. Hamartomatous polyps typically develop in the small intestine, although they may occur in the stomach and colon too. Small intestinal intussusception may lead to small bowel obstruction requiring laparotomy. Accordingly, once diagnosed, screening for small intestinal polyps is undertaken; surgery has been the conventional means by which these are removed if present, but developments in enteroscopy mean that this is increasingly another option.

Screening of the small bowel may be via radiological means, and/ or by capsule endoscopy. People with Peutz- Jeghers syndrome are also at increased risk of both other gastrointestinal (GI) tract malignancies, as well as non-GI malignancies (including breast and ovarian cancer).

C Familial adenomatous polyposis

FAP is a familial bowel cancer syndrome, but is also not associated with perioral pigmentation.

A Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia

HHT classically presents initially with epistaxis, occurring first at a mean age of 12 years; by 21 years of age, over 90% of affected people are symptomatic. Telangiectasia (rather than pigmented spots) occurs on the lips, oral mucosa, tongue, face, conjunctivae, ears and fingers. Upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage occurs frequently, causing anaemia which often requires transfusion. Other visceral angiodysplasias may also occur (including pulmonary AVMs), and vascular abnormalities in the liver may lead to cirrhosis.

B Juvenile polyposis

Juvenile polyposis may also cause small intestinal polyps, but not perioral pigmentation.

E Cronkhite-Canada syndrome

Cronkhite-Canada syndrome is a very rare disorder characterised by multiple intestinal polyps, alopecia, nail dystrophy and widespread skin pigmentation. It does not appear to have a familial tendency. The syndrome often first presents with diarrhoea. 70155

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man presents with pruritus, right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain and malaise. He has had ulcerative colitis for the past 10 years. He takes sulfasalazine and has had good control, with only two acute episodes since diagnosis. He now presents with a 6-month history of itching. He drinks fewer than 10 units of alcohol per week. On examination, he has hepatosplenomegaly, spider naevi and scratch marks.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Bilirubin150 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)40 μ/l7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)600 μ/l (45–105)30 - 150 U/L

What investigation is most likely to yield a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography/magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography

The history of a cholestatic illness (suggested by the itching) and evidence of chronic liver disease (cutaneous signs) against a background of inflammatory bowel disease suggests a possible diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). This is an inflammatory obliterative cholangiopathy that can lead to chronic liver disease cirrhosis and liver failure. It is commoner in men and presents in the second to fifth decade. A total of 3–10% of cases of ulcerative colitis will develop PSC. The diagnosis rests on the demonstration of destruction of the

biliary tree and this is best demonstrated by cholangiopancreatography. The disease is progressive with recurrent episodes of cholangitis complicating cirrhosis. Liver transplantation is now used in end-stage disease. The risk of cholangiocarcinoma is high, and the development of cancer is a contraindication to transplant and associated with a poor survival.

E Ultrasound scan (USS)

Ultrasound would be useful to exclude an extra-hepatic cause for cholestasis, but would not lead to the diagnosis. It is far more useful in jaundice secondary to gallstone and to diagnose cholecystitis.

A Liver biopsy

Rarely only smaller bile ducts are damaged and diagnosis is made at liver biopsy when PSC is mistaken for more focal liver disease, although this is only in exceptional circumstances where the liver biopsy is performed because of apparent local changes only.

C Anti-mitochondrial antibodies

AMA is positive in 98% of cases of PBC, not in primary sclerosing cholangitis. ANA, SMA and ANCA may be positive, but these are unlikely to lead to a diagnosis.

D Serum ferritin

High levels of serum ferritin may suggest haemochromatosis, but may be slightly raised as an acute phase reactant in most inflammatory conditions. 33074

questions.question:
A 36-year-old shop assistant presents with a 3-month history of diarrhoea. Her symptoms include increased stool frequency (particularly in the mornings) bloating and vague abdominal pains. The stool is soft with no blood.

On examination, her BP is 112/72 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and regular, she is thin with a body mass index (BMI) of 22, but apparently her weight is stable.

Initial blood tests arranged by the general practitioner (GP) are outlined below.

InvestigationResultNormal values
Urea and electrolytesNormal
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)350 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)100 fL80 - 100 fL
Vitamin B 12160 ng/L160 - 760 ng/L
Serum folate1.5 µg/L2.0 - 11.0 µg/L
Serum total protein63 g/L60 - 83 g/L
Immunoglobulin G (IgG)12.0 g/L6.0 - 13.0 g/L
Immunoglobulin A (IgA)0.2 g/L0.8 - 3.0 g/L
Immunoglobulin M (IgM)1.5g/l0.4 - 2.5 g/L

Which one of the following would be the most useful diagnostic test?
options: Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy with duodenal biopsies
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy with duodenal biopsies

Young people with diarrhoea should all be screened for coeliac disease, which is the commonest cause of small bowel disease in the West. The best initial screening tests are serological, either tissue transglutaminase or anti-endomysial antibodies, but these tests may be invalid in the presence of selective immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency, which is much commoner in patients with coeliac disease (2.6%). More modern tests now incorporate testing for IgG anti-TTG antibodies, which is a valid screening test. However, from the options provided here upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy with duodenal biopsies is the best investigation to exclude coeliac disease.

The symptoms in this case are non-specific and in the absence of abnormalities in screening blood tests would be sufficient to make a diagnosis of functional bowel disease without further investigation in someone under the age of 45 years. In this case however there is evidence of some small bowel malabsorption (folate deficiency) which would warrant further investigation. Small bowel examination would include in this case duodenal biopsy to exclude coeliac disease, and barium follow-through to image the terminal ileum.

A Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA antibodies

This would be a good initial screening test but may invalid in the presence of selective IgA deficiency which is seen in this patient.

B Anti-endomysial IgA antibodies

This would be a good initial screening test but may invalid in the presence of selective IgA deficiency which is seen in this patient.

C Colonoscopy

In the absence of red flag symptoms, such as weight loss, symptoms overnight and iron deficiency anaemia, colonoscopy would not be required in this patient.

E Three-day faecal fat collection

Three-day faecal fat determination is unpleasant and has a low yield in the investigation of malabsorption and is not recommended for routine use.

questions.question:
A 66-year-old woman is seen in clinic with a 3-month history of watery diarrhoea 5–10 times per day. She is otherwise in reasonable health but takes regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for her osteoarthritis. She also takes omeprazole. She has the watery diarrhoea regardless of whether she eats or not. She has no associated abdominal pain or vomiting and she has no blood mixed in with the stool. She has lost 5 kg in weight.

On examination, she looks well and is afebrile. Her abdomen is soft with no organomegaly.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Sodium (Na⁺)141 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)68 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin35 g/L35–55 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.4 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)10 mg/L< 0 mg/L Erythrocyte sedimentation
16 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour rate (ESR)
Stool microscopyLeukocytes present, no organisms seen

C difficile toxin -

Normal appearance macroscopically – increased Colonoscopy cellular infiltrate in the lamina propria

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Microscopic colitis

This condition is defined by the triad of watery diarrhoea, normal colonoscopy and increased inflammation of the lamina propria of the colon. This disease includes collagenous and lymphocytic colitis. It is an uncommon disease with an incidence of 5/100,000 per year and affects older patients (mean age 55–68 years) and women. There is a link with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), omeprazole, lansoprazole, ticlopidine and cimetidine. Treatment includes simply stopping the offending medication. Corticosteroids, azathioprine, cholestyramine and now bismuth have been used as treatment with some effect in patients who do not respond adequately to cessation of the causative agent. Recurrence however, does occur.

A Crohn’s colitis

Crohn’s disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease. It can affect any part of the GI tract, from mouth to anus, but commonly affects the terminal ileum and proximal colon. Presentation is with diarrhoea and urgency, weight loss, fever and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy would commonly show inflammation with skip lesions, and biopsy shows characteristic transmural inflammation. The absence of such histology findings makes this very unlikely.

B Ulcerative colitis

Ulcerative colitis is a type of inflammatory bowel disease. In UC, gut involvement starts from the rectum and may spread to involve the entire colon. It causes episodic or chronic diarrhoea, which can include blood and mucus. There is commonly crampy abdominal pain with bowel frequency and urgency relating to severity. Patients also develop fever, malaise, anorexia and weight loss. The age of the patient is higher than would be expected for UC, which normally presents between 15 and 30 years. In UC, colonoscopy would show continuous inflammation from the rectum with biopsy revealing goblet cell depletion, glandular distortion, mucosal ulcers and crypt abscesses.

D Giardiasis

Giardiasis is caused by Giardia lamblia, a protozoal organism, which following faecal–oral spread causes infection in the duodenum and jejenum,. Patients can present with abdominal pain and loose stools, explosive diarrhoea and flatulence. Over time, patients can have malabsorption and weight loss. The absence of pain and flatulence makes this a less likely diagnosis, alongside any history of potential exposure to faecal–oral spread.

E Amyloidosis

Amyloidosis is the deposition of amyloid, a fibrillar protein resistant to degradation, It can be primary due to an increase in plasma cell proliferation, leading to further amyloidogenic immunoglobulins. Alternatively, in secondary amyloidosis there is amyloid derived from serum amyloid A, an acute phase protein, seen in many chronic inflammatory conditions. Diagnosis is by biopsy, with a prognosis of 1–2 years. Clinically, primary problems are restrictive cardiomyopathy, glomerular lesions and peripheral neuropathy, but several other clinical presentations are possible.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with recurrent vomiting. She has been diabetic since the age of 14 years. She usually vomits several times in the evening and the vomitus often contains undigested residues of her morning meal. Apart from her insulin she also takes a statin and an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. Examination is unremarkable other than hypertension. She was given a 2-week course of erythromycin by her general practitioner (GP) for a chest infection, which she finished a week ago.

During her hospitalisation, she has an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, oesophageal manometry and a barium swallow, all of which are reported as normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin A1C (HbA 1c)79 mmol/mol (9.4%)< 53 mmol/mol (<7.0%)
Urea9.0 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Glucose8.0 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Sodium (Na⁺)134 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)155 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

What is the most likely cause of the vomiting?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Gastroparesis

The history of vomiting temporally removed from eating and with the vomitus containing recognisable food from hours before is the hallmark of a gastric-emptying disorder. The exclusion of gastric outflow obstruction (by normal endoscopy and barium studies) would lead towards a diagnosis of functional delayed gastric emptying, and in the context of long-standing diabetes, gastroparesis is correct as it is by far the most likely diagnosis. It is now recognised that some degree of delayed gastric emptying occurs in over 50% of diabetics, and the incidence seems to be related to the degree of glycaemic control. The aetiology is complex and may not be due to simple autonomic neuropathy as was thought in the past. Diagnosis depends on excluding other pathology and the demonstration of a significant delay of gastric emptying by scintigraphy. While many drugs list nausea and vomiting as side effects, these are usually mild and transitory.

A Side effect of erythromycin therapy

Although this medication is known for its gastrointestinal (GI) side effects, it usually causes an increase in GI motility.

B Uraemia

Although it can cause intractable vomiting, this usually occurs in the context of end-stage renal disease with much higher levels of uraemia.

D Addison’s disease

Vomiting is a symptom in about 50% of people with Addison’s disease, but this option is incorrect as the high glucose and hypertension make this diagnosis unlikely.

E Bulimia nervosa

Bulimia nervosa, while probably underdiagnosed in older people, is still rare in this age group and the vomiting is typically surreptitious and soon after eating.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old woman presents with a 9-month history of intermittent dysphagia to solids and liquids which appears to have worsened over the last two months. She is hungry, but finds it difficult to keep the food down. She regurgitates her food and describes frank vomiting recently. She thinks she has lost some weight.

Examination of all systems is normal, and her blood test shows mild dehydration.

Her general practitioner (GP) referred her for a barium swallow, which is shown as below:

An endoscopy is arranged.

What further investigation will you consider before proceeding to treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Oesophageal manometry study

The barium swallow shows characteristic sharp narrowing of the lower oesophagus exhibiting a typical ‘bird's beak’ appearance, with hold-up of barium. This is consistent with achalasia but doesn't totally rule out a carcinoma. It is characterised by aperistalsis of the body of the oesophagus and impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Manometry is the gold standard investigation, which shows a high resting lower oesophageal sphincter pressure and non-propagated lower oesophageal body contractions.

The aetiology remains unclear. The greatest incidence is between 30–50 years of age. Chest radiography can be non-specific, but may show a mediastinal shadow caused by the dilated oesophagus with an air/fluid level. Barium swallow is the mainstay of radiological diagnosis. Endoscopy is necessary in any patient to exclude a more sinister cause, because rarely a stenosing adenocarcinoma can present in a manner similar to achalasia (the so-called pseudo-achalasia).

B CT scan of the abdomen

CT scan of the abdomen is only really of utility here if oesophageal carcinoma is suspected, as a screen for hepatic metastases.

A CT scan of the thorax

Although this may reveal the dilated oesophagus with narrowing of the lower portion, it is less useful versus manometry with respect to confirming the underlying diagnosis.

D Endoluminal ultrasound scan

Endoluminal ultrasound scanning has a role in the initial evaluation of oesophageal cancer, with respect to the depth and lateral spread of any lesions identified.

E Gastric transit study

Gastric transit studies are used in the evaluation of gastroparesis, which is associated with autonomic neuropathy, for example in long-standing diabetes mellitus.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old female healthcare assistant is under investigation for chronic diarrhoea which has been going on for one year. She describes it as profuse and watery, but with no associated blood or mucus. She has also lost approximately one stone in weight over this period. The diarrhoea has not responded to multiple anti-diarrhoeal agents. She has had numerous investigations at multiple hospitals in the past, including negative stool cultures, a normal abdominal ultrasound scan and small bowel barium follow-through.

A recent sigmoidoscopy was normal except for some abnormally pigmented mucosa around the rectum.

On clinical examination, she was underweight, but there were no other specific findings.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)140 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)2.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)82 fL76–98 fL
Urea4.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)< 4 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Bilirubin14 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)70 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)32 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)44 IU/L5–30 IU/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Laxative abuse

Surreptitious laxative abuse is usually seen in young women who have an underlying eating disorder or psychiatric illness. It presents with large volumes (>1 l/day) of watery diarrhoea. This may lead to weight loss, dehydration and hypokalaemia as is seen here. These patients commonly deny laxative use, which they then continue to take during sometimes extensive investigations. The diagnosis is often difficult to make and may require hospital admission. Chemical analysis of the stools can sometimes identify which laxatives are being used. If the patient is abusing an anthraquinone purgative (e.g. senna), then pigmented mucosa (‘melanosis coli’) may be seen at sigmoidoscopy. In prolonged cases of laxative abuse the barium enema may show a dilated colon with loss of the normal haustral pattern. Management is difficult and usually requires psychiatric input.

C Bile salt malabsorption

Bile salt malabsorption results from bowel resection, and is seen in conjunction with use of certain drugs such as metformin that interfere with normal reabsorption of bile salts. Neither bowel resection nor use/abuse of metformin seems likely given the scenario here.

B Irritable bowel syndrome

Irritable bowel syndrome is only considered once organic pathology is ruled out. The hypokalaemia seen here counts against IBS as the likely diagnosis.

D Thyrotoxicosis

Diarrhoea associated with thyrotoxicosis would not usually be associated with the marked hypokalaemia seen here, or with melanosis coli seen on imaging.

E Carcinoid syndrome

Carcinoid syndrome is very rare in this age group, and is usually associated with hepatic metastases from carcinoid, which haven’t been seen here on the abdominal ultrasound scan.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman who is 17 weeks pregnant with her third child comes to the clinic complaining of right upper quadrant pain, worsening nausea and jaundice. Apart from nausea at the beginning of her pregnancy, things have followed a relatively uneventful course and the family has most recently returned from a trip to Tunisia. On examination, she has jaundiced sclerae and looks tired. Her blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg, she is tender over the right upper quadrant, and she is pyrexial at 37.8 °C.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 ×10⁹/L (mild lymphocytosis)4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)1200 U/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)420 U/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin230 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Hepatitis A

The fever, leukocytosis, history of recent travel abroad and transaminase >1000 U/L all point towards acute hepatitis A infection. Hepatitis A has a similar course to non-pregnant patients and fulminant hepatic failure is rare. In utero infection has been associated with postnatal complications, so if a pregnant patient is travelling to an endemic area then vaccination is recommended.

A Fatty liver of pregnancy

The patient is only in the 17th week of gestation. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare and potentially fatal obstetric emergency that occurs in the third trimester. Presentation can be non-specific with nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain or acute liver failure in the most severe cases. Bilirubin and transaminases tend to be significantly raised with a rise in WCC and hypoglycaemia/hyperlactaemia (hallmarks of acute liver failure).

B Cholestasis of pregnancy

With this answer, one would expect the patient to have pruritus. Bilirubin is normally not elevated. The condition is characterised by pruritus (typically starting on the palms and soles of the feet) with raised fasting and post-prandial serum bile acids. Total bilirubin is rarely raised. The condition occasionally presents with pale stool and dark urine. It typically presents within the third trimester and resolves up to 6 weeks postpartum. Treatment is for pruritus with ursodeoxycholic acid and rifampicin.

D Budd Chiari syndrome

This clinical picture could resemble Budd–Chiari, however the travel history and lymphocytosis would favour an alternative diagnosis of acute hepatitis A. One might also expect to see clinical features of portal hypertension. Budd–Chiari is characterised by obstruction of the hepatic vein, sinusoidal congestion and portal hypertension. Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state and the risk of Budd–Chiari is increased although it remains rare. Most patients presenting with de novo occlusion tend to have an undiagnosed underlying thrombophilia and should be investigated.

E HELLP syndrome

The platelet count and blood pressure are normal and the patient is only in the 17th week gestation. HELLP syndrome is an hepatic manifestation of pre-eclampsia. This occurs after the 20th week of gestation and tends to occur in the presence of hypertension (>140/90 mmHg). Thrombocytopenia occurs as a result of a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. This takes place within the sinusoids leading to congestion, hepatic ischaemia and a transaminitis.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman is referred to the clinic for abnormal liver function tests. She denies illicit drug or excess alcohol use. Her general practitioner (GP) is concerned as her alanine aminotransferase is twice the normal limit and alkaline phosphatase is also slightly elevated.

On examination, she is grossly obese with a body mass index (BMI) of 36; her BP is also elevated at 155/82 mmHg. No other significant findings are noted. Hepatitis B and C serology is negative.

Which of the following is the most useful initial investigation in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Abdominal ultrasound scan

This patient is obese with abnormal liver function tests and the most likely diagnosis is non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Ultrasound will rule out significant other disease of the liver or biliary tract and is likely to be hyperechogenic; fatty infiltration may be visualised when it is above 30% of the liver mass. Further investigations for NASH include an MRI to provide more accurate estimation of liver fat, magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) to estimate liver stiffness, and liver biopsy. Weight loss is the mainstay of treatment for this condition. Orlistat has been shown to reduce hepatic fat, as has pioglitazone, although neither is licensed for the treatment of hepatic steatosis.

A Ferritin estimation

Although ferritin may be elevated, it is a non-specific finding in chronic liver disease and is therefore not useful in further pinpointing the underlying diagnosis.

B Autoimmune profile

Transaminases are elevated, which makes autoimmune hepatitis a possibility, although with the marked elevation in BMI, NASH should be considered the most likely diagnosis.

C Abdominal CT scan

CT scan is less useful with respect to elucidating liver architecture than MRI. The correct sequence of investigations is therefore liver USS followed by MRI scanning later.

E Liver biopsy

Liver biopsy is usually required to confirm the diagnosis of NASH and provide evidence on histological staging of cirrhosis, although it is usually done after initial radiological investigations.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia. He initially presented to his General Practitioner, as he had noticed significant weight loss and mild fatigue over several months. There is no history of change in bowel habits. He has a history of hypertension, for which he takes ramipril, but is on no regular medication apart from this. He has a vegetarian diet and takes over-the-counter vitamins for iron, vitamin B 12 and folate.

On examination, his blood pressure is 142/82 mmHg. His body mass index is 20 kg/m 2, and abdominal and per rectum (PR) examinations are unremarkable. He has no skin rashes, bruises or joint pain.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)78 g/L135–175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)78 fL76–98 fL
White cell count (WCC)5.4 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets180 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)49 mm/h0–10 mm in the 1 sthour
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Endoscopy

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for colorectal cancer indicate referral via the 2-week wait pathway should be completed for all adults aged over 60 who present with iron deficiency anaemia or a change in bowel habit or a positive stool sample for occult blood. Both lower and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is recommended for these patients. The patient should have further investigations to establish the cause of his anaemia if these tests are negative.

C Haemolysis screen
