A haemolysis screen is indicated in patients with a significant, unexplained drop in their Hb concentration. In the

presence of haemolysis, these patients may have signs of jaundice as well as fatigue. However, this patient’s low Hb concentration can be explained by his iron deficiency and this, in itself, requires further investigation.

A Bone marrow biopsy

Bone marrow biopsy may be indicated in cases of iron deficiency anaemia where there is a need to differentiate iron deficiency anaemia from anaemia of chronic disease. However, in this case, the weight loss and patient’s age mean that colorectal cancer should be suspected.

D Immunoglobulin A (IgA) tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibody

In this patient, TTG antibodies should be tested for. However, the next most appropriate step is to proceed to further imaging to rule out the presence of colorectal cancer, as per the NICE guidelines which recommend that given this patient’s age of over 60 and the presentation with weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia, colorectal cancer should be ruled out with endoscopy.

E One unit of blood transfusion

The NICE blood transfusion guidelines recommend a treatment threshold of a Hb concentration of 70 for patients without acute coronary syndrome. Therefore, there is currently no indication to begin a blood transfusion for this patient.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is referred by his general practitioner (GP) for an upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy. He describes a 3-month history of worsening epigastric pain and anorexia. He suffers from chronic back pain following a road traffic accident 5 years ago. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day and drinks 30 units of alcohol per week. Examination is unremarkable and all his blood tests are normal. You perform a gastroscopy, and there is no blood in the stomach.

The oesophagus and duodenum look normal, but the appearance below is seen in the antral region of the stomach (see below).

Which of the following is the most appropriate management step
options: Refer back to the GP for smoking cessation advice
Adrenalin injection to the base of the lesion
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Eradicate pylori if present

The endoscopic appearance is that of a large gastric ulcer with a white sloughy base. H. pylori, aspirin, corticosteroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and smoking are aetiological factors for gastric ulcer. Other less common causes include Crohn’s disease, tuberculosis and vasculitides. Biopsy for histological analysis is important from the ulcer edge, to exclude malignancy. The association of H. pylori with gastric ulceration is weaker (60–70%) than with duodenal ulceration (90%), but eradication therapy may prevent recurrence.

C Refer for partial gastrectomy

Partial gastrectomy was the mainstay of therapy for gastric ulcers, although the advent of modern medical therapy (H2 antagonists and proton pump inhibitors) has massively reduced the need for surgery.

A Refer back to the GP for smoking cessation advice

Clearly reducing smoking and alcohol consumption is important, but this alone won’t lead to resolution of the ulcer without H. pylori eradication therapy.

D Repeat endoscopy in 2 weeks

There is no indication for repeat endoscopy after only 2 weeks. H. pylori eradication should be attempted first, with a follow-up endoscopy at least 4–6 weeks later.

E Adrenalin injection to the base of the lesion

As the ulcer is covered in slough and there is no active bleeding, injection therapy is not indicated; disturbing the overlying slough may actually increase the risk of further haemorrhage.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old man with a long-standing history of ulcerative colitis attends the clinic for review. He was also diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) some years earlier and his LFTs have been monitored. Recently, he has become severely jaundiced and requested an urgent hospital appointment.

Ultrasound demonstrated ductal dilatation with other areas of stricturing consistent with the PSC. MRI cholangiography demonstrated marked ductal dilatation and a hilar lesion consistent with a cholangiocarcinoma. There was evidence of local lymphatic invasion with enlarged lymph nodes around the porta hepatis.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate management of this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Stenting of the lesion

There is evidence from the MRI scan that this patient has cholangiocarcinoma with local invasion. As such, attempted surgical removal is likely to be unsuccessful. For this reason the treatment of choice is stenting via ERCP. The procedure is successful at relieving symptoms of jaundice and may also relieve associated lethargy and fatigue. Most patients with severe PSC are surveyed for the possible development of cholangiocarcinoma and are recommended for liver transplantation before this occurs. Stent replacement may be required every 3–6 months, and adjuvant radiotherapy post stent placement may prolong survival for as long as 17 months. Resectable lesions are associated with a 5-year survival as high as 40%.

E Referral for Whipple’s procedure

Whipple’s procedure or pancreaticoduodenectomy is performed for resectable carcinomas of the head of the pancreas. Only 10–20% of patients are actually suitable to undergo a Whipple’s procedure at the point of diagnosis.

A Referral for chemotherapy

5-FU and cisplatin are commonly used agents for cholangiocarcinoma, their effects are however limited, meaning that chemotherapy isn’t the preferred option.

C Referral for lobectomy

Local lymph node invasion has already occurred hence lobectomy isn’t an option for treatment here. In any case lobectomy risks a new focus of cancer developing in the unresected portion of the liver.

D Referral for liver transplantation

By the time local invasion has occurred, liver transplantation isn’t an option. Where lesions are resectable, however, 5-year survival may be as high as 40%. Transplantation is the aim for severe disease before cancer develops.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of diarrhoea and intermittent fresh rectal bleeding. She works as a shopkeeper and smokes ten cigarettes per day. Her brother suffers from colitis. Blood tests show microcytic anaemia and a raised C-reactive protein.

Colonoscopy shows inflammation in the recto-sigmoid colon and a normal terminal ileum. Histology suggests indeterminate colitis. She turns up to clinic very keen to know the exact diagnosis.

Which of the following will favour a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease?
options: Dilated colon on plain abdominal radiography
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA)

The diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease is based on clinical history, inflammatory markers, colonoscopy and histology results. In around 10% of patients, it is impossible to distinguish ulcerative from Crohn’s colitis and this is termed indeterminate colitis. Serological markers have been studied extensively in trials but are not yet in everyday clinical use. Ulcerative colitis is strongly associated with perinuclear anti-cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA – detected in 60–70% of UC vs 10–15% of CD). The presence of anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies favours Crohn’s disease (ASCA IgG + in 60–70% CD vs 10–15% of UC vs <5% in non-IBD colitis). The two antibodies can be used in combination, and a serological profile of ASCA±pANCA– has an 80% positive predictive value of progression to CD.

Reference: Mitsuyama K, et al. Antibody markers in the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. World Journal of Gastroenterology. 2016;22(3):1304–1310. doi:10.3748/wjg.v22.i3.1304.

E Arthritis

Although arthritis (including asymmetrical polyarthritis, spondylitis, sacroilitis and enthesopathy) is well described as an extra-intestinal manifestation of Crohn’s disease, their presence or absence is not a good predictive marker of underlying inflammatory bowel disease.

A Anti-endomysial antibodies

Anti-endomysial antibodies are seen in coeliac disease. Although there is an overlap with inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease, the positivity of these antibodies would not help clarify the diagnosis.

B Detection of perinuclear anti-cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA)

pANCA positivity has been well described in inflammatory bowel disease but is more commonly seen in UC rather than Crohn’s. In patients with indeterminate colitis (IC), pANCA and ASCA have been shown in studies to provide a predictive value. ASCA-/pANCA+ serology in indeterminate colitis is 64% predictive for a diagnosis of UC.

C Dilated colon on plain abdominal radiography

This is a non-specific finding that could represent multiple pathologies: obstruction, volvulus, ileus or toxic megacolon.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with intermittent episodes of diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal bloating and flatulence. She has not lost weight over the course of the past year.

Clinical examination is unremarkable. Her BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 65/min and regular, BMI 24 and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Faecal occult bloods are negative and haematological and biochemical investigations are unremarkable.

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Irritable bowel syndrome

In the presence of a normal physical examination and a series of normal investigations, irritable bowel syndrome is the most likely diagnosis here. Many patients with symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome also have lactose intolerance. Hence, a trial of dairy-free diet may bring about significant improvement in symptoms, as unmetabolised lactose contributes to large bowel symptoms of bloating and flatulence because lactose provides a substrate for metabolism by colonic bacteria. Other components of the diet may be excluded on a trial basis to assess the impact on symptoms.

C Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is usually a consideration when these symptoms present in association with iron deficiency anaemia, rather than the normal blood work up seen here.

A Colonic carcinoma

Given that there is no weight loss and investigations are normal, and the fact that this patient is only 28 years of age, a diagnosis of colonic carcinoma is very unlikely.

B Crohn’s disease

Crohn’s disease is associated with the development of chronic abdominal pain, weight loss and anaemia, rather than the picture seen here.

D Ulcerative colitis

UC is associated with distal bowel symptoms, which result in bloody diarrhoea with mucus and raised inflammatory markers, rather than the benign picture with normal investigations.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman is admitted comatose to the resuscitation room. Her husband describes a few days of increasing confusion.

Past medical history is of diabetes, primary biliary cholangitis and one episode of variceal haemorrhage. Drug therapy includes ursodeoxycholic acid, metformin and aspirin. She does not consume alcohol or any illicit drugs.

On examination, she is drowsy and unable to converse. There is no meningism, and pupils are equal and reactive. She has assumed a decorticate position, plantars are upgoing. Bedside blood glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. The remainder of systemic examination is unremarkable. As well as extensive investigations reported below, a full sepsis screen is sent to the lab. She was intubated for airway protection.

Initial blood tests reveal:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin89 g/L115–165 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets60 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine66 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Prothrombin Test (PT)19 s10.6–14.9 s
Urea16 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)45 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Bilirubin12 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase10 IU/L30–130 IU/L Aspartate aminotransferase
36 IU/L10–40 IU/L (AST)
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)38 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin28 g/L35–55 g/L
CT brainMild atrophy
EEGDiffuse symmetrical triphasic sharp waves

How should this patient be further managed?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

Although the patient has relatively normal transaminases (aminotransferases), we know from the history of varices that she has cirrhotic liver disease. We can also deduce from her low albumin and prolonged prothrombin time that her synthetic liver function is severely compromised. Thus a likely diagnosis of grade III– IV hepatic encephalopathy can be made. The electroencephalogram (EEG) picture is classical for hepatic encephalopathy. Her serum ammonia ought to be measured. The next stage of management is to identify any possible precipitants and reverse them.

In this patient, the likely precipitants are sepsis and gastrointestinal bleed; note the raised inflammatory markers, anaemia and disproportionate rise in urea. Therefore, an upper GI endoscopy is the best option presented here. Although commonly used, interventions such as non-absorbable disaccharides (lactulose), antibiotics and protein restriction have little evidence base.

A Lorazepam boluses intravenously

The diagnosis is hepatic encephalopathy, and drugs such as benzodiazepines ought to be avoided where possible.

B Intravenous aciclovir

It is sensible to consider viral encephalitis in patients with confusion, but in this case the features suggest hepatic encephalopathy and serum ammonia should be checked to confirm this.

C Magnetic resonance image (MRI) brain

Obtaining an MRI brain is likely only to delay treating the underlying problem – a probable upper GI bleed. In hepatic encephalopathy, basal ganglia high signal on T1-weighted images can be seen. In severe hepatic encephalopathy such as this, diffuse brain swelling may be seen.

E Plasma exchange

Plasma exchange is not helpful in treating hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old Russian immigrant with a background of haemophilia A is admitted after a road traffic accident. He is transfused with four units of blood and given recombinant factor VIII concentrate. He otherwise appears well. He drinks 10 units of alcohol per week and denies and previous intravenous (iv) drug use. He underwent surgery as a child whilst in Russia. Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)140 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT)88 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)120 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin25 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L

You suspect he has viral hepatitis.

What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Hepatitis C

Unfortunately, due to inadequate screening of donated blood and the pooling of multiple samples, significant numbers of haemophilia patients have been infected with hepatitis C virus following blood transfusions, so option C is correct. The picture seen here is most typical of hepatitis C infection, and around 50% of patients are

diagnosed on routine liver function testing with an isolated rise in alanine transferase (ALT). Diagnosis is made by confirming the presence of hepatitis C antibodies using ELISA.

D Hepatitis D

This is a less common virus that requires patients already infected with hepatitis B virus for its existence and replication.

A Hepatitis A

This is spread by the faecal oral route, and is usually a prodromal illness of jaundice, fever, nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain - but you are told this patient is fit and well.

B Hepatitis B

Although a good option here, it is not the best answer as hepatitis B screening was introduced some years before screening for hepatitis C, which came later, including in Russia. Given we are told the operation took place when he was a child, he’s more likely to have been exposed to hepatitis C

E Hepatitis E

This is spread by faecal oral transmission and the history of ingesting contaminated water or food. Hepatitis E is more common in pregnancy, but is usually self-limiting.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old man is seen in the clinic with a 6-month history of abdominal pain, 6 kg weight loss and intermittently he has noticed dark urine which lasted for a few days. He also has noticed night sweats, which soak his nightclothes. There is a history of ulcerative colitis which is currently well controlled; he does not smoke and drinks a couple of pints of beer at the weekend. On examination, he looks well and has no jaundice, clubbing or lymphadenopathy. He has a 4 cm non-tender hepatomegaly and the rest of his examination is normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
White cell count (WCC)6.7 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)135 g/L135–175 g/L
Platelets (PLT)379 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)61 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin21 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)245 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)256 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin36 g/L35–55 g/L
Serum electrophoresisPolyclonal increase in immunoglobulins
Auto-antibodies (ANA)1: 64
c-ANCANegative
p-ANCA1: 320
Abdominal ultrasound (US)Hepatomegaly but no bile duct dilation

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease of unknown aetiology. The diagnosis is based a combination of clinical features which often come on insidiously, including hepatomegaly, intermittent jaundice, fevers of unknown origin, pruritus, abdominal pain and weight loss. This, together with a cholestatic biochemical profile and typical cholangiographic abnormalities of generalized beading and stenosis of the intrahepatic and extra-hepatic biliary tree, characterise PSC. PSC is usually progressive, leading to cirrhosis, portal hypertension and liver failure. Ultrasound is normal in 50% of patients at an early stage of the disease. Pathognomonic histology shows a concentric obliterative fibrosis of interlobular bile ducts, with the presence of intrahepatic cholangiectasis and ductal obliteration.

Therapeutic interventions, such as dilation of strictures or placement of an endoprosthesis, can be performed during endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Many pharmacological therapies have been tried, without great success. Dietary replacement of vitamins A, D, E and K should be commenced. Liver transplantation is an option in terminal liver failure.

A Primary biliary cholangitis

Primary biliary cholangitis is interlobular bile duct damage caused by granulomatous autoimmune inflammation. This can result in fibrosis, cirrhosis and portal hypertension. It is associated with antimitochondrial antibodies and is far more common in females, typically at 50 years of age. Presentation is typically asymptomatic with incidental biochemical cholestasis but can cause lethargy and pruritus progressing to ascites. The presence of night sweats and absence of pruritis, as well as the demographics, makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

C Chronic active hepatitis

Viral hepatitis causes fever, malaise, anorexia and nausea, which can progress to jaundice. In patients with chronic infection this may progress to cirrhosis, which may lead to episodes of acute decompensation of liver disease. The blood tests suggest a primarily cholestatic injury as opposed to a hepatic cause, and there is no clear history of risk factors.

D Polyarteritis nodosa

Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotising vasculitis that causes thrombosis, and can also cause aneurysms, in medium-diameter arteries, which can lead to organ infarction. It is more common in men and with hepatitis B. The absence of systemic features and rash makes this an unlikely diagnosis, and the demographics of the patient are not supportive.

E Hydatid disease

Cystic hydatid disease occurs following transmission of ingesting the eggs of parasites such as Echinococcus. It is common in China, Russia, Japan, India, Pakistan and Wales. Clinically the organs most commonly affected are the liver and lungs. In the liver it can cause obstructive jaundice whilst in the lungs it can cause haemoptysis and dyspnoea, and rupture can lead to anaphylaxis. The absence of travel history and of potential exposure makes this very unlikely, as does the weight loss. 6871

questions.question:
A 19-year-old student presents to the university health service complaining of flu-like symptoms, lethargy and jaundiced sclerae and an inability to eat due to a sore throat. He remembered that his father may have suffered from a liver condition.

On examination, he is pyrexial 38.2 °C, BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular. He has signs of pharyngitis on examination of his throat.

Investigations reveal:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)23 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)28 U/L10 - 40 U/L
Bilirubin78 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Albumin41 g/L35 - 55 g/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention in this case given the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Observation

The clinical picture is highly suggestive of Gilbert’s syndrome, and as such, observation and supportive therapy for the acute flu-like illness is the management of choice. When jaundice is severe (as occurs only rarely in Gilbert's), phenobarbitone can rapidly decrease unconjugated serum bilirubin levels. This condition is autosomal recessive and is characterised by unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia caused by impaired glucuronyl transferase activity. Jaundice may be precipitated by fasting, excessive alcohol consumption or acute illness. Other liver function tests apart from bilirubin level are generally normal. It is likely that a viral illness has led to a period of fasting and the symptoms seen here.

E Hepatitis screen

Isolated elevated bilirubin in the context of an inherited liver condition is consistent with Gilbert’s syndrome, not with hepatitis. In hepatitis a marked elevation in transaminases would be expected.

A Phenobarbitone

Phenobarbitone is usually only considered for severe jaundice. At this stage it’s more appropriate to manage this patient conservatively.

B Diazepam

Phenobarbitone, rather than diazepam is used as an enzyme inducer in the treatment of acute Gilbert’s syndrome.

D Hepatic ultrasound scan

Given transaminases are normal, and this patient has evidence of an inherited liver problem, Gilbert’s is much more likely than obstructive liver disease.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old man is seen in neurology outpatients after being referred with disinhibited behaviour of 2 months’ duration. His family tells you that he passes urine in public and the police have brought him home on two occasions recently. He has been losing weight for the last year and was previously 110 kg, now weighing 92 kg. He has diarrhoea and his family tell you it smells bad and is difficult to flush. The patient complains of pain in his right knee, left ankle and lower back.

On examination, he looks pale and has angular cheilitis. He has a distended abdomen with some shifting dullness but no palpable organomegaly. His palmo-mental reflex is positive. The right knee and left ankle are both swollen with minimal tenderness and a good range of movement.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Sodium (Na⁺)134 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea4.8 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)45 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)1.74 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
Albumin27 g/L35–55 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)92 g/L135–175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)78.2 fL76–98 fL
Platelets (PLT)512 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.4< 1.1
Computed tomography (CT) brainNormal Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD) is performed and duodenal biopsy demonstrates expanded villi

containing macrophages staining positive with periodic acid–Schiff stain.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Whipple's disease

Whipple disease is a systemic disease caused by Tropheryma whippeli, a Gram-positive, non-acid-fast rod. It is usually found in white, middle-aged males, most commonly in Europe. The classic presentation, believed to be caused by organism infiltration of the body tissue, is that of a wasting illness characterised by four cardinal features: migratory arthralgia of the large joints, arthritis, intermittent diarrhoea and colicky abdominal pain. The disease can affect the central nervous system (CNS) and produce frontal signs (such as in our patient), meningoencephalitis or dementia.

The organism is taken up by the macrophages, and diagnosis is established by identifying ‘foamy’ macrophages that stain positive with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain on jejunal biopsy. PCR testing is also used for confirmation. Other infections, such as with endemic fungi (e.g. Histoplasma spp.), Rhodococcus and HIV- infected mycobacterial disease, can be histologically similar to Whipple’s disease, but many can be ruled in or out by additional testing (i.e. staining for organisms, culture, antigen testing). Antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment - usually co-trimoxazole or tetracycline is given for 1 year. Clinical failure is suggested by a positive PCR in the relevant specimen from patients who fail to respond clinically to adequate therapy or have recurrence of symptoms after initial improvement. One third of patients relapse.

B Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease could explain the gastrointestinal symptoms and malabsoption picture and, on rare occasions, has been associated with neuropsychiatric disease. However, the PAS positivity on the small bowel histology is not consistent.

A Hartnup disease

Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by impaired amino acid transport in the apical brush border membrane of the small intestine and the proximal tubule of the kidney. If symptomatic, it usually presents in childhood with pellagra-like skin eruptions, cerebellar ataxia and gross aminoaciduria.

C HIV enteropathy and dementia

HIV infection can lead to scarring of the lymphoid structures within the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in chronic malabsorption and weight loss. In addition, the gastrointestinal symptoms of Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI) enteropathy (almost exclusively seen in patients with AIDS, or those who are severely immunosuppressed) and Whipple’s disease are similar. Neurocognitive disorders can be seen in advanced or untreated HIV infection. However, there is no history of cough, which would be the usual first presentation of MAI infection. And while M. avium-positive duodenal biopsies are also PAS positive, contrary to Whipple’s disease, they also stain positive with Ziehl-Neelson. Whipple’s disease is more likely to explain the overall clinical picture.

D Tropical sprue

The gastrointestinal symptoms of tropical sprue and Whipple’s disease are indistinguishable. However, the cognitive changes as seen in this case would be more difficult to attribute to tropical sprue. Furthermore, histology of the duodenum would reveal flattened villi and inflammatory cell infiltrates, but no PAS-positive macrophages.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents to the Neurology Outpatient Clinic due to memory loss and ataxia. He reports recent weight loss of 10 kg over six months, associated with fatigue, change in bowel habits with watery diarrhoea and abdominal pain. He has a past medical history of osteoarthritis and hypertension.

On examination, he appears tanned, with loose clothing. A systolic murmur over the left fifth intercostal space is appreciated on cardiovascular examination. His abdomen is soft but distended, and there is palpable pelvic lymphadenopathy. Neurological examination reveals that cranial nerves are intact and peripheral power and sensation are normal in the upper and lower limbs, but there is clonus in the ankles bilaterally. When his gait is assessed, he has a broad-based stance and sways while mobilising from one end of the room to the other. Cognitive testing reveals an Abbreviated Mental Test Score (AMTS) of 8 out of 10.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Whipple’s disease

This patient has Whipple’s disease, an infection caused by the pathogen Tropheryma whipplei. Classical symptoms include gastrointestinal symptoms that resemble other malabsorption syndromes, migratory arthralgia and fever. Sacroiliitis is common and the HLA-B27 antigen is more commonly found among affected individuals. One-third of patients have cardiac involvement with pericarditis or endocarditis, which rarely causes significant symptoms. Neurological features include ataxia, confusion, seizures, delirium and cognitive impairment. Diagnosis is made by intestinal biopsy and identification of the organism. Periodic acid–Schiff staining shows foamy macrophages, and polymerase chain reaction will detect the bacterium. Treatment involves antibiotic therapy, with an initial phase of parenteral treatment, followed by 12 months of oral antibiotics. Relapse is common, often presenting with central nervous system (CNS) symptoms.

A Coeliac disease

This patient has Whipple’s disease which classically presents with migratory arthritis, intermittent diarrhoea and colicky abdominal pain. The main differential here would be coeliac disease, due to weight loss and diarrhoea. However, Whipple’s disease is the correct answer here because of the presence of systemic disease patterns (cardiac murmur indicating endocarditis, ataxia due to neurological involvement), due to the spread of the causative organism T. whipplei to other tissues. Coeliac disease may cause symptoms of malabsorption and other complications; however, it does not present with the typical features of endocarditis and neurological involvement seen here.

B Friedreich’s ataxia

Friedreich’s ataxia is an autosomal recessive disease, which usually presents in the teenage years with deafness, progressive spinocerebellar ataxia, optic atrophy and progressive muscle wasting. Patients may also present with cardiomyopathy; however, it is not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, as in the case here.

C Small bowel adenocarcinoma

Small bowel adenocarcinoma may present with changes in bowel habit, anaemia, weight loss, abdominal pain and bowel obstruction but is now relevant here.

E Wilson’s disease

Wilson’s disease is an inherited disorder characterised by accumulation of copper in the body, which results in chronic liver disease, CNS abnormalities, including tremors, muscle stiffness, dysarthria, dysphagia and incoordination, and psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depression and psychosis. It is not associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, as seen in Whipple’s disease. 72988

questions.question:
A 72-year-old female is admitted with a 2-month history of diarrhoea. She has loose motions with no blood, four times per day. Her stool cultures are negative and her examination is normal. She has a background of rheumatoid arthritis for which she is in remission; hypertension, chronic renal impairment with a creatinine of 151 µmol/L and depression. Colonoscopy demonstrates mild diverticular disease. Biopsy shows evidence of colitis with lymphocytic infiltration. Her daughter finds a list of her medications that she is taking and shows them to you.

Which one of the following medications is most likely to be causing her diarrhoea?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Lansoprazole

Many drugs contribute to causing diarrhoea and it is very important to get a good drug history when evaluating a patient with chronic diarrhoea. The list is endless and one must use the BNF to check whenever one is not sure. Drugs causing diarrhoea include broad-spectrum antibiotics, antihypertensives such as diuretics, digoxin, some cholesterol-lowering drugs, sodium valproate, thyroxine, levodopa, antacids, theophylline, colchicines, non-steroidals and oral hypoglycaemic drugs. Mechanisms leading to diarrhoea are diverse, including effects on transit time, alterations in bowel flora, and impact on colonic inflammation, such as the development of lymphocytic colitis seen with non-steroidals. With respect to lansoprazole it appears to result in the development of microscopic colitis.

E Spironolactone

Mild diarrhoea is a rare side effect of spironolactone therapy, although it isn’t as a result of microscopic colitis.

A Ramipril

Ramipril is associated with gastritis and pancreatitis, and in some cases diarrhoea, although this isn’t manifest as lymphocytic (microscopic) colitis.

B Amlodipine

Abdominal pain and intermittent nausea are the commonest associations with amlodipine use, and diarrhoea is uncommonly reported, although it isn’t thought to be due to microscopic colitis.

C Furosemide

Although loop diuretics have a recognised association with diarrhoea, this isn’t due to lymphocytic colitis. The changes in bowel habit are potentially due to an alteration in GI motility.

questions.question:
A 47-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic due to abnormal liver function tests which were a finding on a battery of blood tests checked by her GP. She attended the general practitioner (GP) because of increased fatigue and symptoms of itching. She was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome several years ago, but this has since become quiescent. She has no other significant past medical history except for hormone replacement therapy and takes no regular medication. She is a non-smoker and drinks 6 units of alcohol per week. She has no risk factors for hepatitis.

On examination she looked well, her BMI is 22. Some xanthelasmata were noted, but there was no jaundice, clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender and the liver edge was palpable 1 cm below the costal margin. Cardiorespiratory and neurological examination was unremarkable.

Investigation results are below:

Which further investigation would be most specific in making the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Anti-mitochondrial antibodies

Clinical features are pointing towards a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), which is a chronic progressive disorder with the gradual destruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to fibrosis and cholestasis and ultimately hepatic cirrhosis. PBC is usually presented in middle-aged females with early symptoms of pruritis, fatigue, which can progress to the development of obstructive jaundice and portal hypertension. 50% of patients may be asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis and are detected by abnormal liver function tests especially elevated alkaline phosphatase. Anti-mitochondrial antibody has a sensitivity of 95% with a specificity of 98%. Treatment options include colestyramine for pruritis (naltrexone and rifampicin may also help), ursodeoxycholic acid and liver transplantation for end staged disease (e.g. bilirubin > 100 µmol/L). Once jaundice develops, the survival rate is < 2 years without liver transplantation.

B Computed tomography (CT) scan of abdomen

CT scan of abdomen can be helpful in differentiating PBC from other biliary conditions e.g. carcinoma of bile duct, but not specific for PBC. There is a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with PBC.

A Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)

MRCP can help to exclude chronic biliary obstruction (stone or stricture), however, it is not specific for PBC.

D Hepatitis serology

PBC must be differentiated from chronic hepatitis (due to viral infections) by performing hepatic serology tests. Hepatic serology is not specific for underlying possible diagnosis of PBC.

E Anti-nuclear antibodies

Patients with clinical and histological picture of PBC but negative anti-mitochondrial antibodies are referred to as antibody –negative PBC or autoimmune cholangitis, which is associated with high levels of anti-nuclear antibodies and smooth muscle antibodies. Almost all cases of SLE show a positive serum ANA.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old girl is sent to you for assessment, as she is profoundly depressed. She has features of anhedonia and anorexia over the last 6 months. Before this, she had always been an excellent student and has many friends.

She has no known medical problems, but her mother has a history of schizophrenia. She does not smoke or drink, and both she and her parents deny that she has used drugs.

On examination, she is well-dressed but does not keep eye contact. She tells you that she is hearing second- person auditory hallucinations and has done so for 3 months. She has an expressionless face and when writing a sentence she has small, cramped handwriting. Her gait is slow and there is some increased tone in her right arm.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Albumin36 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)201 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)121 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin28 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Wilson’s disease

Wilson’s disease is an inherited disorder of hepatic copper disposition caused by mutations in the gene ATP7B on chromosome 13. The average prevalence is 30/million. It can present as either psychiatric (depression/neurotic behaviour), neurological (extrapyramidal signs) or with liver disease (asymptomatic hepatomegaly, elevated transaminase).

Biochemical findings include low serum ceruloplasmin and copper and elevated 24 h urinary excretion of copper. There is an increased copper concentration in the liver parenchyma. Kayser–Fleischer rings need to be looked for with a slit lamp and are present in 60% of cases. The mainstay of treatment is chelation therapy, with penicillamine. Second-line treatment involves trientine, and occasionally zinc. With effective and early treatment, most patients are well and live normally.

A Abuse of clozapine

The atypical antipsychotics carry a lower risk of extrapyramidal symptoms than typical antipsychotics. The more common signs and symptoms such as lethargy and sedation (histamine blockade), miosis, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension (alpha-adrenergic blockade) and confusion (muscarinic blockade). Clozapine abuse is not the best explanation for this patient’s presentation with extrapyramidal signs and deranged liver function tests.

B Chronic abuse of LSD

Lysergic acid use can cause a wide variety of neuropsychiatric symptoms, including visual illusions and distortion of time perception. Chronic use can lead to persistent psychosis, but is unlikely to account for the neurological signs and raised ALT.

C Ganser syndrome

Ganser syndrome is a dissociative disorder characterised by absurd or approximate answers to questions (paralogias), clouding of consciousness, somatic conversion symptoms, hallucinations and amnesia. The syndrome is associated with a history of head injury, Munchausen syndrome, solitary confinement or extreme stress. This diagnosis would not explain the extrapyramidal signs and abnormal liver function tests.

D Othello syndrome

Othello syndrome is a term used to describe morbid jealousy, which may involve delusions, obsessions and overvalued ideas. It would not explain this patient’s neurological signs or deranged liver function tests.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old Asian male, presents with a 3-week history of jaundice and pruritus. He has a 1-year history of diarrhoea which had been diagnosed as irritable bowel syndrome by his general practitioner. There is no history of foreign travel and he denies any illicit drug use or recent blood transfusion. On examination he appears jaundiced and has scratch marks on his trunk, but the liver is not enlarged and there is no evidence of ascites. A liver biopsy is performed and the histology shows typical onion skin-type periductal concentric ﬁbrosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)

Periductal concentric fibrosis (‘onion skin’) is a classic histopathologic finding of PSC on liver biopsy. The long history of diarrhoea should make you consider a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a condition strongly associated with PSC. In fact approximately 60-80% of patients with PSC have concomitant IBD.

E Alcoholic liver disease

There is no history of alcohol excess, and liver biopsy would usually show fatty change, cell necrosis and Mallory bodies.

A Primary biliary cholangitis

This typically shows a dense lymphocytic infiltrate in the portal tracts with granulomatous destruction and loss of medium-sized interlobular bile ducts, focal and variable within the liver.

B Haemochromatosis

When a liver biopsy is performed in this setting, Perls' Prussian blue stain would be performed to evaluate the degree and cellular distribution of hepatic iron stores.

C Autoimmune hepatitis

The findings on liver biopsy are described as interface hepatitis, formerly referred to as piecemeal necrosis. This is because portal inflammation is seen eroding through the limiting plate between the portal tract and liver parenchyma.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old man presents with a 10-month history of pain in his lower back, hips, ankles and feet. He has tried osteopathy, acupuncture and diclofenac, but had no relief. He has also been feeling increasingly tired and breathless on walking up steep inclines. He had lost 10 kg in the last 6 months despite eating reasonable meals. He had no dysphagia or night sweats, but does report intermittent abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. He smokes 30 cigarettes/day and drinks two pints of beer 3 times per week. His past history includes hypothyroidism for which he takes thyroxine, and his mother is a tablet-controlled diabetic.

On examination, his clothes fit loosely and he looks pale. He has no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. He had normal cardiac, chest and abdominal examinations.

On joint examination, there was pain when moving each joint but no obvious focus of the pain. Chest X-ray is normal, faecal immunochemical test (FIT) is negative. Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)71 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)512 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)71 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urea4.6 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L

International normalised ratio (INR)1.5< 1.1

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is common, with a prevalence of 1: 100 and as much as 1: 30 in the west of Ireland. Only one- third of patients present with chronic diarrhoea and steatorrhoea. Malabsorption in this case has caused vitamin

D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism, low albumin, impaired clotting, iron deficiency anaemia and

weight loss. The vitamin D deficiency has led to osteomalacia, causing the presenting feature of lower back and leg pain. Iron deficiency anaemia is the most common presentation of coeliac disease. Having other autoimmune conditions in coeliac patients is common, such as hypo/hyperthyroidism and type 1 diabetes mellitus (7%).

B Metastatic caecal carcinoma

Caecal carcinoma can present with anaemia, although it is much less likely to present with osteomalacia than coeliac disease.

A Crohn’s disease

Crohn’s disease is less likely to have an insidious presentation like this with predominant symptoms of osteomalacia, and is more likely to present with significant diarrhoea and abdominal pain.

D Whipple disease

Whipple’s disease is associated with diarrhoea and malabsorption, but it is also associated with small joint polyarthritis and is significantly rarer than coeliac disease.

E Intestinal lymphangiectasis

Intestinal lymphangiectasia is a protein-losing enteropathy and presents in childhood with symptoms of malabsorption and peripheral oedema.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man presents to the Colorectal Clinic with two discrete episodes of haematochezia. He has had no fresh bleeding per rectum, nor has he been experiencing abdominal pain. He has a healthy lifestyle recently and denies unintentional weight loss. He has no medical history of note. His father died of colorectal cancer at the age of 54 and his paternal aunt has a current diagnosis of thyroid cancer. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and a digital rectal examination reveals no visible cause of his haematochezia.

He is referred for a colonoscopy that shows 15 adenomatous polyps ranging from 3 mm to 1.5 mm.

What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Adenomatous polyposis coli genetic testing

This patient has a likely diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), given the young presentation of haematochezia and adenomatous polyps on colonoscopy. FAP is an autosomal-dominant condition caused by mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene causing hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. It comes with almost a 100% risk of colorectal cancer if not treated with a prophylactic pan-colectomy.

The family history of colorectal cancer and associated malignancies with FAP (eg thyroid cancer) makes FAP an even more likely diagnosis. Colonoscopy and biopsy form the mainstay of investigation for the condition. However, genetic testing is recommended for patients with ten or more adenomatous polyps on a single colonoscopy, as it helps to aid the diagnosis and decision for surgical intervention.

E Faecal immunochemical testing

Faecal immunochemical testing is used in the investigation of colorectal cancer. It detects the presence of blood within the stool by using antibodies specific for haemoglobin. As this patient is presenting with haematochezia, this result is likely to be positive. However, it is much more likely that this patient has FAP rather than colorectal cancer or FAP that has already malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer.

B Carcinoembryonic antigen testing

Carcinoembryonic antigen testing is a tumour marker used in the assessment of colorectal cancer. Although FAP has a very high risk of becoming colorectal cancer, this is usually in later years (35–40 years). Furthermore, it would not aid in the specific diagnosis of FAP. Rather, if FAP had malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer.

C CT abdomen

Carcinoembryonic antigen testing is a tumour marker used in the assessment of colorectal cancer. Although FAP has a very high risk for becoming colorectal cancer, this is usually in later years (35–40 years). Furthermore, it would not aid in the specific diagnosis of FAP. Rather, if FAP had malignantly transformed into colorectal cancer.

D Faecal calprotectin

Faecal calprotectin is used in the investigation of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which is a useful differential diagnosis to consider given the onset of rectal bleeding at a young age. However, this typically presents with abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss, and the absence of these features plus the family history of malignancy makes IBD less likely. 73504

questions.question:
A 32-year-old white bar owner returns from Spain and requires emergency consultation in the General Medicine Clinic. He feels lethargic and has not been able to maintain an adequate erection during intercourse or masturbation during the past few months. This is causing some marital difficulties. He also complains of swelling of his ankles and swelling around the abdomen. On examination, he appears tanned. There is a paucity of underarm and genital hair, and he has evidence of chronic liver disease and testicular atrophy. Past history of note includes arthritis and joint pain. He admits to drinking 12 units of alcohol per week (a glass of wine or half a pint of beer).

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Fasting glucose8.2 mmol/L< 5.6 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)183 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Bilirubin125 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L

What would be the next best investigation to lead to this patient’s diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation

Symptoms of haemochromatosis usually begin in men aged between 30 and 50 years and include increased skin pigmentation (due to iron deposition and melanin), cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, arthropathy, impotence in men and heart failure. First-line screening involves measuring patients’ serum transferrin saturation and ferritin

levels. Previously, liver biopsy with total hepatic iron estimation was considered the gold standard test for haemochromatosis. Now, however, genetic screening for the two identified mutations is seen as the next investigation of choice after transferrin saturation estimation. Around 10% of the Northern European population are heterozygous for each mutation (so-called compound heterozygotes), and this may account for the accelerated deterioration of liver function in patients with moderate alcohol intake corresponding to 15–30 standard drinks (units) per week.

C Liver ultrasound scan

A liver ultrasound scan is not indicated to diagnose haemochromatosis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver

is the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for the measurement of liver iron deposition in haemochromatosis.

A Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c)

This patient has a raised fasting glucose level, which is common in patients with haemochromatosis. Diabetes occurs in these patients due to iron deposition within the pancreas, affecting endocrine function, and/or liver cirrhosis. Although diagnosis and treatment of diabetes in these patients are important, HbA1c is not as accurate due to the increased turnover of red blood cells. Furthermore, HbA1c measurement will not lead to the diagnosis, making this an incorrect option.

B Liver FibroScan

Liver FibroScan is used to assess the degree of fibrosis in fatty liver disease, hepatitis and cholestatic disease. It can be used in haemochromatosis but is not the next best step in confirming this patient’s diagnosis.

D Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver

This patient likely has haemochromatosis, based on his symptoms, examination and investigation findings. Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver is a good, non-invasive investigation for measuring liver iron content in cases of haemochromatosis. However, the first-line investigations which can point toward the diagnosis of haemochromatosis are ferritin levels and serum transferrin saturations, which are both raised in cases of haemochromatosis.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old man is seen in clinic with a 3-month history of chronic epigastric discomfort. The pain comes and goes and radiates to his back and his right shoulder tip at times. It is worse after meals but there is no relieving factor. He feels nauseous most of the time and has foul-smelling stools. He has lost 2 stones in weight. He also complains of intermittent light-headedness. He drinks a bottle of wine on most nights and smokes 20 cigarettes/day.

On examination, he is thin and looks neglected. His abdomen is soft, but tender on deep palpation in the epigastric area. He has a 2 cm non-tender liver edge. He also has decreased sensation to light touch on both feet.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Chronic pancreatitis

This patient has a history of excess ethanol consumption and chronic abdominal pain. In early disease there may be no X-ray calcification of the pancreas, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatogram (ERCP) and computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen can also be normal. Faecal elastase is in the mild-to-moderate pancreatic insufficiency range, and the most likely diagnosis therefore is chronic pancreatitis. Treatment acutely is as for acute pancreatitis, but chronic pain control is often difficult and patients become opiate dependent. Pancreatic enzyme replacement is used. These patients also usually become diabetic and should be monitored for symptoms of hyperglycaemia such as polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy and dehydration.

B Bacterial overgrowth of the gut

Bacterial overgrowth syndrome presents with bloating, eructation and intermittent diarrhoea, weight loss is not as severe as that seen here, and faecal elastase remains in the normal range.

C Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is associated with symptoms of malabsorption, positive anti-TTG antibodies, and faecal elastase remains in the normal range.

D Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide-secreting tumour (VIPoma)

VIPomas are vanishingly rare and are associated with large-volume diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and dehydration. The chronic excess alcohol consumption counts towards an alternative diagnosis here.

E Caecal carcinoma

Caecal carcinoma is often symptomless in the early stages, and presents late with iron deficiency anaemia or ultimately obstruction, rather than the chronic diarrhoea seen here.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman is referred to the Cardiology Department with intermittent palpitations. She describes episodes of ‘feeling flushed’ associated with a fluttering feeling in the chest. She denies any chest pain or breathlessness. There are no risk factors for ischaemic heart disease or any history or rheumatic fever. She is also suffering from paroxysms of diarrhoea. On examination she appears well in herself. There are prominent v-waves noted on inspection of the jugular venous pulse. A pansystolic murmur is audible at the left sternal edge. The chest is clear on auscultation. A pulsatile liver is felt 2 cm below the costal margin on palpation of the abdomen.

Which of the following investigations is most likely to yield the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A 24 h urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)

This patient presents with features of carcinoid syndrome. This is a paraneoplastic syndrome secondary to a carcinoid tumour. The most common locations for a carcinoid tumour are in gut and arise from the enterochromaffin cells. Carcinoid tumours secrete serotonin, which is metabolised by the liver. If the carcinoid tumour metastasises to the liver, serotonin enters the systemic circulation. Release of circulation is associated with flushing, diarrhoea and bronchoconstriction. Continued serotonin exposure can result in restrictive cardiomyopathy secondary to fibrosis. This can lead to valvular pathology (in this case the tricuspid valve). 5- HIAA is a degradation product of serotonin, which is excreted in the urine. A level of >25 mg per 24 is diagnostic.

D Chest X-ray

Carcinoid syndrome can occur secondary to a carcinoid tumour in the lungs (a common extra-GI site for primary carcinoid tumours). However, the features supporting tricuspid regurgitation point towards a liver metastasis as the serotonin source. A chest X-ray in this patient may only show non-specific changes or appear normal.

B Echocardiogram

This patient likely has tricuspid regurgitation secondary to the carcinoid plaques on the tricuspid valvular apparatus,seen in 50% of cases of serotonin syndrome. The echocardiogram would likely demonstrate these cardiac abnormalities. However, it is not the investigation of choice to reveal the underlying cause.

C 24 h electrocardiogram (ECG)

Although this patient reports symptoms suggestive of palpitations (‘fluttering feeling in the chest’), there are no features suggestive of a sinister arrhythmic event. This patient likely has carcinoid syndrome, which does not commonly affect cardiac conduction.

E Abdominal ultrasound

This patient has an enlarged liver on clinical examination. This may be due to hepatic metastatic spread of a GI carcinoid tumour or secondary to the apparent tricuspid regurgitation. An abdominal ultrasound may show a hepatic tumour, but it is unlikely to be able to differentiate between a carcinoid tumour and a metastatic adenocarcinoma. Although it is an important investigation, it is unlikely to be the key to the underlying diagnosis. 6916

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man from Bangladesh comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a 6-week history of weight loss, fever, night sweats and dull abdominal pain. He lives in a rural community in Bangladesh that is mostly farmland and has been visiting his daughter for the past week. He has a past history of hypertension, for which he takes nifedipine, but is otherwise well. On examination, his BP is 105/60 mmHg; his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. Marked hepatosplenomegaly is noted on abdominal palpation. His BMI is 22 kg/m 2.

Investigations:

Explanation

C Direct agglutination testing

The most likely diagnosis is visceral leishmaniasis, typically presenting with the syndrome ‘kala-azar’, which causes insidious progressive fatigue, weight loss and night sweats, along with splenomegaly and fever. Anaemia and liver dysfunction are common on baseline blood testing. This travel history from a rural area of Bangladesh increases the likelihood of sandfly bites that transmit the disease. Direct agglutination testing and recombinant kinesin antigen (rK39) testing have high levels of sensitivity and specificity. They should be considered as non-invasive investigative options before moving towards more invasive testing, such as bone marrow aspiration.

B Dental scrapings

The most likely diagnosis is visceral leishmaniasis. Dental scrapings are usually considered for the diagnosis of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, which is not indicated here. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis presents with nasal symptoms, mucosal bleeding and increased secretions.

A Bone marrow aspiration

Bone marrow aspiration could be considered in myeloproliferative conditions. However, the normal LDH level and travel history are pointers against this. There is the added risk of complications of bone marrow aspiration that should not be taken lightly.

D Liver biopsy

Liver biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis but is not the most useful next step. It should be considered in cases where clinical suspicion is high and direct agglutination testing has not been suggestive of the diagnosis. There is the added risk of bleeding associated with this procedure and this should not be taken lightly.

E Splenic aspiration

Splenic aspiration biopsy, although it would provide a definitive diagnosis, is not the most useful next step in the management of this patient. questions.question:
A 32-year-old nurse presents with iron deficiency anaemia. She prefers mainly white meat and fish but claims that her diet is sufficiently varied. She also reports frequent diarrhoea and weight loss of 6 kg in the past year.

On examination, her BMI is 22, but no other abnormalities are found.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)104 g/L115–155 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)80 fL76–98 fL
Serum ferritin14 µg/L10–120 µg/L
Serum folate1.4 µg/L2.0–11.0 µg/L
Albumin34 g/L35–55 g/L
Immunoglobulin G (IgG)15 g/L5–16 g/L
IgA3.8 g/L1.0–4.0 g/L
IgM2.6 g/L0.5–2.0 g/L An OGD is performed, which shows some mild duodenitis. Small bowel biopsies are taken and are reported as showing subtotal villous atrophy.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is characterised by diarrhoea and malabsorption precipitated by sensitivity to gliadin, a protein fraction of gluten found in wheat, rye, barley and oats. Peaks of incidence occur in the third and seventh decades, there is a slight female preponderance and incidence is increased in Caucasian populations. Diagnosis is made by testing for tissue transglutaminase antibody (TTG) or small bowel biopsy, which shows the classical appearance of subtotal villous atrophy. Coeliac is also an important cause of iron deficiency anaemia caused by malabsorption of iron, as seen in this patient. Therefore, Option A is correct as it best fits the clinical picture and biopsy findings. Note that this patient has a normocytic anaemia, as she is both iron deficient (microcytic) and folate deficient (macrocytic) giving an overall normocytic picture. Treatment for coeliac is avoidance of gluten- containing foods.

C Small bowel lymphoma

This is extremely rare, and usually occurs in older individuals and one would expect to see abnormal plasma cells on biopsy such as abnormal T-cell proliferation.

B Crohn’s disease

Although this can cause villous atrophy of the small bowel, the classical biopsy findings are non-caseating granulomas and transmural inflammation. This may also be associated with aphthous ulcers in the mouth.

D Whipple’s disease

This is a rare malabsorptive disease caused by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei and occurs in conjunction with neurological, cardiac or rheumatological sequelae. This patient did not elicit any of these symptoms.

E Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

This usually gives a high folate as a result of bacterial synthesis, and is more commonly associated with patients who have diabetes or other autoimmune conditions such as scleroderma.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman was admitted via the Emergency Department complaining of intermittent epigastric pain. She had had a cholecystectomy 1 year ago for these symptoms but continued to have pain after the procedure. The pain was severe, typically coming on when she was eating, radiating to the back and was accompanied by nausea and sometimes vomiting. It tended to last for several hours and did not vary in intensity. She has had five such attacks over the last year.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Bilirubin21 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)100 U/L10 - 40 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)110 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)176 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Amylase220 U/L23 - 65 U/L

An ultrasound scan showed a moderately dilated common bile duct (12 mm) but no stones were seen. Consequently, she underwent an endoscopic retrograde cholangiogram which, again showed mildly dilated ducts. A sphincterotomy was performed along with trawling of the bile duct, again revealing no cause. Post- procedure she developed acute pancreatitis from which she recovered with conservative management. Subsequently, her symptoms resolved. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction

The symptoms described by this woman and her response to sphincterotomy are characteristic of sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD), which causes non-calculous obstruction of flow of biliary and/or pancreatic fluid.

In SOD, the sphincter is hypertonic (>40 mmHg on manometry) and may also be dyskinetic. SOD typically occurs in middle-aged women, but may present in any age group, including children. The usual presenting symptoms are those of biliary-type pain, i.e. epigastric or right hypochondrial pain that is severe, steady and may radiate to the back or shoulder.

Since the symptoms of SOD are usually so similar to that of gallstone disease, the diagnosis of SOD is often only made after cholecystectomy. SOD may also manifest as recurrent episodes of apparently idiopathic pancreatitis, but jaundice is rare.

There are three categories of SOD:

Type I: People with typical biliary pain, abnormal liver enzymes and radiological evidence of impaired biliary drainage Type II: People with typical biliary pain, with either abnormal liver enzymes or radiological evidence of impaired biliary drainage Type III: People with typical biliary pain, but no other abnormalities.

Definitive diagnosis of SOD is made by manometry, although delayed drainage of contrast at ERCP is also a classic sign (>45 min). Rates of post-ERCP pancreatitis are increased five-fold in people with SOD.

Treatment of SOD with smooth muscle relaxants (such as nifedipine) improves symptoms in a proportion of affected people, but at rates similar to placebo overall. Endoscopic sphincterotomy is often effective in treating people with type I SOD, and may help people with type II SOD, but is usually of no benefit in people with type III SOD. Botulinum toxin injection into the sphincter of Oddi may have a role in treatment, particularly for people with type III SOD.

E Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Primary sclerosing cholangitis only typically causes biliary pain in the presence of cholangitis, and is associated with a beaded pattern to the biliary tree on cholangiography.

A Recurrent biliary stones

Recurrent biliary stones may be ruled out given that none were seen on her ERCP.

B Non-ulcer dyspepsia

Non-ulcer dyspepsia does not explain this woman’s abnormal liver enzymes and imaging findings.

C Chronic pancreatitis

No typical risk factors for chronic pancreatitis are given, and it is unusual for chronic pancreatitis to cause such marked biliary dilatation.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man visited his general practitioner (GP) some 10 days after returning from holiday with his friends in Turkey. He admitted to drinking up to 10 pints of lager per day during his 2-week holiday and frequently bought food from street sellers.

Since his holiday, he has given up smoking as he said he did not enjoy it any more. There was a history of paracetamol use in the past few days for a sprained ankle sustained when slipping in the street, and there was some concern that he may have taken a couple of extra tablets while on holiday. Most recently, he has been suffering from fever and anorexia.

On examination, he was jaundiced.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Bilirubin345 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransaminase (AST)400 U/L10 - 40 U/L

Which of the following investigations is most likely to give the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Hepatitis serology

It seems likely that this man has an acute hepatitis. This is unlikely to be an acute alcohol-related phenomenon as he has taken some 10 days to present. The clue is in his visit to Turkey, where he is likely to have been exposed to hepatitis A. This is the commonest cause of viral hepatitis worldwide, transmitted via the faeco-oral

route, and is associated with non-specific symptoms such as nausea, anorexia and distaste for cigarettes. Hepatitis A is not associated with progression to chronic liver disease. During the convalescent period, 5–15% of patients may have relapses of their hepatitis but these resolve spontaneously. Occasionally a more severe jaundice with prolonged cholestasis may occur over the course of 7–20 weeks. Mortality (due to fulminant hepatic necrosis) is rare at around 0.1%, but increases with age.

C Paracetamol level

In a patient presenting 10 days after his holiday, paracetamol levels are not of value in determining whether excess paracetamol during the trip contributed to his symptoms.

A Conjugated bilirubin

Given that transaminases are elevated, Gilbert’s disease can be ruled out as a cause of his symptoms.

B Clotting screen

Although this man has acute hepatitis, synthetic liver function is highly unlikely to be affected and clotting won’t reveal an underlying cause of liver disease.

E Serum ammonia

Serum ammonia is most useful in the evaluation of hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old farmer is admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward with a 3-week history of intermittent abdominal pain, nausea, reduced appetite and 5 kg weight loss. He had no past medical history of note and has no allergies.

On examination, his temperature is 37.9 °C with a heart rate of 99 bpm and a BP of 119/60 mmHg. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant with palpable hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)140 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.7 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils4.6 ×10⁹/L1.8–7.5 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes4.5 ×10⁹/L1.0–4.0×10⁹/L
Eosinophils1.6 ×10⁹/L0.1–0.4×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.5 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)109 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

An ultrasound scan (USS) liver is requested:

What is the recommended management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Albendazole and surgical resection

This patient likely has hydatid disease, given the symptoms of abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia and weight loss, in addition to findings of eosinophilia and multiple liver cysts on ultrasound imaging. Hydatid disease is a zoonotic infection caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus which is commonly transmitted by infected dogs and foxes. Contact with animals is a risk factor for the infection and the occupational history of being a farmer is significant in this instance. Importantly, unlike other causes of hepatic cysts (eg amoebic liver abscess), hydatid disease can remain asymptomatic for some time before being diagnosed. Treatment of hydatid disease involves a combination of albendazole, corticosteroids and surgical resection to ensure complete clearance of the infection.

Image source: By R. Badea and Simona Ioanitescu, (CC BY 3.0), CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=65099337

A Amphotericin B

Amphotericin B is a potent antifungal agent used in the treatment of invasive Candida albicans and Cryptococcus neoformans. Fungal infections do not typically cause eosinophilia as seen in this patient. Rather, it is much more likely that the patient is suffering from a parasitic infection (eg helminth) for which amphotericin B has no efficacy.

B Mebendazole

Mebendazole is used in the management of parasitic infections, particularly threadworm, hookworm and roundworm. In contrast, albendazole is more commonly used in the management of hydatid disease with mebendazole reserved as the second line. Nevertheless, surgical cyst removal is generally necessary, making an antiparasitic agent used in isolation less likely to achieve complete clearance.

C Metronidazole

Metronidazole is an antibacterial agent with good activity against anaerobic bacteria. Therefore, it is generally a useful antibiotic to treat intra-abdominal infections. Metronidazole is also used to treat amoebic liver abscesses which can present very similarly to hydatid disease. However, some distinguishing factors include eosinophilia and the presence of multiple cystic liver lesions (representing daughter cysts) which are more common in hydatid disease. In contrast, an amoebic liver abscess is a smooth cystic mass without numerous daughter cysts.

D Praziquantel

Praziquantel is used in the treatment of helminthic infections including intestinal tapeworm infection. However, hepatic disease requires alternative forms of treatment including albendazole and surgical resection. 74096

questions.question:
A 45-year-old banker is referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver function tests. He had a heart attack 2 years ago and is regularly seen in the Diabetic Clinic for poor glycaemic control. He currently takes metformin, atenolol and atorvastatin. He drinks socially and smokes 10 cigarettes per day. There is no history of blood transfusion or drug abuse. On examination, he is overweight and there is an enlarged, non-tender liver. Ultrasound scan of the liver is reported as showing a generalised, hyper-echogenic appearance with no focal lesions.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)240 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)83 fL76–98 fL
International normalised ratio (INR)1.1< 1.1
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.7 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea9.0 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin39 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)96 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)70 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)135 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Hepatitis and autoimmune serologyNegative
FerritinNormal20–250 µg/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis

Most patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) are asymptomatic. The condition is usually discovered incidentally after abnormal liver tests. Diffuse fatty change can be detected on ultrasonography as a hyper- echogenic appearance. It is part of a metabolic syndrome and is commonly associated with obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolaemia and drugs. In patients with NASH, the ratio of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is usually <1, whereas in alcoholic liver disease the ratio is usually >2. Liver biopsy reveals macrovesicular steatosis. Treatment is that of underlying cause, encouraging moderate weight loss, exercise, improved diabetic control, treatment of hyperlipidaemia and avoidance of alcohol. Bariatric surgery is perhaps the best therapeutic modality in the presence of severe obesity.

A Drug-induced hepatitis

While statins can cause abnormal liver function tests, the history does not suggest that this has been recently commenced. Furthermore, a true drug-induced hepatitis would likely result in a more marked rise in liver enzymes. Given the risk factors, and ultrasound findings suggestive of fatty change, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis is a better answer.

C Alcoholic-induced hepatitis

The history does not suggest that the patient drinks alcohol to excess, and the ratio of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is <1, suggestive more of NASH than alcoholic liver disease, where the ratio is usually >2.

D Chronic active hepatitis

There are no particular risk factors given in the history, and viral serology is negative.

E Amyloidosis

Hepatic amyloidosis occurs in the setting of primary (AL) or secondary (AA) amyloidosis. Hepatomegaly is present in 80% of patients, but one would expect the presentation to include other signs and symptoms of systemic illness such as weight loss, abdominal pain, anorexia, ascites, peripheral oedema and splenomegaly. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is frequently raised. Ultrasonographic findings of hepatic amyloidosis include heterogeneous echogenicity. The diagnosis of gastrointestinal amyloid requires a tissue biopsy with positive staining of amyloid by Congo red or the presence of amyloid fibrils on electron microscopy.

questions.question:
A concerned 29-year-old woman attends her general practitioner (GP) practice complaining of two days of painless rectal bleeding. There has been no change in her bowel habit. She denies any other constitutive symptoms and has no significant travel history. She is particularly concerned since her mother, who is 48 years old, has recently been diagnosed with cancer of the bowel. On further questioning, it appears that her maternal grandfather also died after suffering from bowel cancer.

The GP suspects that there may be an inherited tendency towards this disease and is especially concerned about familial adenomatous polyposis.

What physical feature is most commonly found in this condition?
options: Hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by the presence of hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. There is a wide phenotypic spectrum of FAP, with all phenotypes having an underlying germ-line mutation in the adenomatous polyposis coli gene. The average age of the polyposis is 16 years, with all patients having this syndrome developing colon cancer if left untreated. The average age of onset of colorectal cancer is 39 years. Physical features associated with this condition include congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, dental abnormalities including supernumerary teeth and dentigerous cysts, osteomas of the skull and mandible, and fibromas and epidermoid cysts in prepubescent patients.

D Cutaneous lipomas

Lipomas per se are not associated with increased risk of cancer, although weight gain is associated with a range of cancers including colon and breast cancer, which are linked to increased insulin resistance.

B Early onset cataracts

Early onset cataracts may be associated with decreased antioxidative activity, and have been shown in epidemiological studies to be associated with increased risk of head and neck cancer and hepatoma.

C Axillary freckling

Axillary freckling is identified in hereditary non-polyposis cancer, rather than FAP.

E Pre-auricular skin tags

Abnormalities of the ear cartilage are more commonly associated with renal and cardiac abnormalities. They are not thought to be associated with increased risk of colonic polyps. 33410

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with known rheumatoid arthritis complains of generalised pruritis.

On examination, she is mildly jaundiced and has periorbital xanthelasmata. Abdominal palpation reveals hepatomegaly 2 cm below the right costal margin. She has no lymphadenopathy.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)112 g/L115–155 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)89 fL76–98 fL
White cell count (WCC)4.6 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)310 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)34 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Albumin30 g/L35–55 g/L
Bilirubin30 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)260 IU/L30–130 IU/

Which of the following tests would be most useful?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A M 2 subtype anti-mitochondrial antibody

Primary biliary cholangitis is a slowly progressive inflammation and destruction of the intrahepatic ducts leading to eventual cirrhosis. The cause is unknown but it is thought to be an autoimmune disease, and there is a strong association with other autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome and CREST syndrome. Most patients are diagnosed between the ages of 40 and 70 years, and 90% of patients are female.

D M 5 subtype anti-mitochondrial antibody

Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are found in over 90% of patients, the M 2 subtype being specific. Therefore M 5 is not the most specific for primary biliary cholangitis.

B Anti-smooth muscle antibody

Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic hepatitis characterised by immunologic and auto-immunologic features, generally including the presence of circulating auto-antibodies and a high total serum gamma globulin, usually confined to the IgG fraction. The main circulating auto-antibodies, although not specific for the disease, are antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA) in type 1 disease and, in type 2 autoimmune hepatitis, anti-liver-kidney microsome-1 antibodies (ALKM-1) and anti-liver cytosol antibody-1 (ALC-1). In this case, it is primary biliary cholangitis that we are wanting to diagnose so anti-smooth muscle antibody is not particularly useful.

C Hepatitis serology

Hepatitis serology is negative in primary biliary cholangitis and there is no association.

E Serum electrophoresis

Serum electrophoresis is abnormal in disorders such as multiple myeloma, but not in primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman is being investigated for intermittent dysphagia and has had a normal upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.
