She undergoes oesophageal manometry and some of the results are outlined below. She has symptoms of Raynaud’s, and some skin thickening over her hands, but no other significant medical problems.

InvestigationResultNormal values
Lower oesophageal sphincter resting pressure8 mmHg17 - 36 mmHg
Residual lower oesophageal sphincter relaxing pressure7 mmHg< 8 mmHg Peristalsis:
InvestigationResultNormal values
Proximal amplitude80 mmHg33 - 91 mmHg
Distal amplitude25 mmHg64 - 154 mmHg

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnoses?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Scleroderma

The finding of a low resting lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) pressure is a requirement for a diagnosis of scleroderma-associated dysmotility. It may also be found in the hypocontractile oesophagus associated with reflux disease. However, in the presence of skin thickening and symptoms of Raynaud’s, the most likely diagnosis is systemic sclerosis.

D Achalasia

Absent distal peristalsis, high resting LOS pressures and failure of LOS relaxation would be expected in cases of achalasia.

B Diffuse oesophageal spasm

This is a condition characterised by uncoordinated oesophageal contractions, which can lead to pain on eating, dysphagia and regurgitation in some cases.

C Globus

Globus is a psychological condition which would only be diagnosed in the absence of abnormal finding on investigation.

E Non-specific oesophageal dysmotility

This is a disorder of peristalsis but would not be associated with the other features of systemic sclerosis (thickened skin and Raynaud’s) that are present in this case.

questions.question: A 46-year-old Malaysian woman with hepatitis C-related liver cirrhosis is seen in clinic for her 6-monthly follow-up. She remains well and a surveillance ultrasound shows two small focal lesions in the liver. Her alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is 78 ng/ml (10–20). It was 30 ng/ml six months ago. Spiral computed tomography scan of the liver and thorax confirms two liver lesions, both measuring 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm and no pulmonary lesions. What is the most definitive way to manage these two liver lesions?
options: Percutaneous ethanol injection of the lesions
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Liver transplantation

The only proven potentially curative therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains surgical, either hepatic resection or liver transplantation. Liver transplantation should be considered in any patient with cirrhosis and a single small HCC (<5 cm) or up to three lesions (<3 cm). Hepatic resection should be considered as a primary therapy in any patient with HCC and non-cirrhotic liver. A rising alpha-fetoprotein indicative of a hepatoma and biopsy is not always necessary to avoid seeding of tumour.

D Trans-catheter embolization of the lesions

Chemo-embolisation can produce tumour necrosis and has been shown to affect survival in highly selected patients with good liver reserve, although in this case it would only be considered if liver transplantation was not an option.

A Partial hepatic resection

This is not advised because of the potential to generate new areas of dysplasia within the remaining abnormal liver.

C Percutaneous ethanol injection of the lesions

Percutaneous ethanol injection has been shown to produce necrosis of small HCC and is best suited for peripheral lesions. Given the two lesions here are small, liver transplantation if possible is the preferred intervention.

E Intravenous interferon

Systemic therapies including interferon have a poor response rate in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma and would not be curative. Transplant is therefore preferred.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old man presents to accident and emergency complaining of a 4-day history of upper abdominal pain which radiates to his back, along with nausea and diarrhoea. He has been admitted to hospital twice in the past 8 months with similar symptoms and has lost approximately 5 kg in weight over this time.

His past medical history includes hypertension, gastric ulceration and a partial gastrectomy 12 years ago. His current medication includes atenolol 50 mg once daily and omeprazole 20 mg once daily.

The following blood results were obtained:

InvestigationResultNormal values
White cell count (WCC)12.6 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)124 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)112 fL80 - 100 fL
Platelets (PLT)110 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea2.4 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)64 mmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.24 mmol/L2.2 - 2.7 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)64 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)250 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Bilirubin26 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Albumin30 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Random glucose18 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L 3-day faecal fat excretion 21 g/day = 63 g total (normal < 30 g/3 days)

Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Alcohol abuse

In view of this man’s history, the most likely diagnosis is recurrent pancreatitis secondary to alcohol abuse or gallstones. Alcohol is a cause of chronic pancreatitis, whereas gallstones may be associated with recurrent acute pancreatitis. Other causes of chronic pancreatitis include cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis and sclerosing cholangitis. Chronic pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition which is characterised by irreversible damage to both the exocrine and endocrine pancreas. This patient’s faecal fat excretion is high (> 30 g/3 days) indicating pancreatic enzyme insufficiency. This is further supported by an elevated random glucose consistent with a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. Initial further investigations in this patient should include abdominal ultrasound and, if indicated, abdominal CT or MRCP.. Chronic pancreatitis is treated with pancreatic enzyme supplementation and complete abstention from alcohol. Approximately 60% of patients survive two years.

B Haemochromatosis

There is an absence of other symptoms of haemochromatosis including increased pigmentation, endocrine dysfunction and costochondritis, and presentation at an age earlier than 64 years would be expected.

C Sclerosing cholangitis

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and usually presents at an earlier age than 64 years.

D Gastric carcinoma

Gastric carcinoma is less likely as the underlying diagnosis, given very gradual weight loss over the past 8 months, and no symptoms suggestive of gastric obstruction.

E Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is a possible differential, but given the duration of symptoms, more pronounced anaemia and associated conditions such as dermatitis herpetiformis would be expected.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old previously fit and healthy woman is knocked over by a cyclist on the pedestrian crossing. She is admitted to hospital and has an abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan. This shows that the spleen and liver are normal except for a cyst in the pancreas. The cyst shows features of a 1 cm serous cystadenoma.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Do nothing

Serous cystadenomas (SCAs) are benign tumours of the pancreas commonly picked up on imaging. They are rarely >2 cm and usually remain benign, and therefore do not require follow-up. The differential in this case would be a mucinous cystadenoma, which has malignant potential (in about 25% of cases). CT and MRCP can differentiate between the two but occasionally EUS with FNA of serous fluid may be required. High levels of CEA are typically observed in a mucinous cystadenoma (but are normal in a serous cystadenoma). The international consensus guidelines (2012) recommend all mucinous cystadenomas should be resected.

Other cystic lesions of the pancreas that may be noted incidentally include intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), which also has a malignant potential and requires MRCP surveillance; pancreatic pseudocysts (in a patient with a history of pancreatitis); retention cysts (simple cysts, seen in association with Von Hippel–Lindau disease and polycystic kidney disease); and papillary cystic neoplasm (typically seen in young females, in the tail or body of the pancreas).

Reference: Tanaka et al. Pancreatology 12 (2012): 183–197.

E Resection of whole pancreas

There is no malignant potential of SCAs. Pancreatectomy would be considered in mucinous cytadenoma or in IPMN with high-risk radiological features (see consensus guidelines mentioned above).

B Annual follow-up

As there is no malignant potential of SCAs, this is not recommended. Annual follow-up is recommended for patients with low-risk or stable IPMNs with MRCP and clinical examination.

C Resection of cyst alone

This is not recommended as there is no malignant potential for SCAs. A mucinous cystadenoma would be resected, but pancreatectomy with lymph node dissection remains the standard of care in these cases.

D Resection of tail of pancreas

There is no malignant potential for SCAs. This option could be considered in a patient with a papillary cystic adenoma, as this tends to occur in the pancreatic tail and metastasis is rare.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids, and a persistent productive cough. He is a long-term smoker but otherwise is fit and well; he reports no significant weight loss.

Clinical examination is unremarkable and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy report from another hospital is normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Bilirubin19 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)22 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)31 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin42 g/L35–55 g/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)148 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)258 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
InvestigationResultNormal values
Lower oesophageal sphincter resting pressure60mmHg17–36 mmHg
Residual lower oesophageal sphincter relaxing pressure12mmHg< 8 mmHg Peristalsis reveals the following:
InvestigationResultNormal values
Proximal amplitude80 mmHg33–91 mmHg
Proximal duration3s2.0–3.6 s
Distal amplitude0 mmHg64–154mmHg
Distal durationAbsent2.9–5.1 s

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Achalasia

Achalasia describes a failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, and affects an estimated 10 in 10,000 people. Endoscopy is often normal but can show lower oesophageal dilatation and failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) to relax. The hallmark feature of manometry is absence of peristalsis in the distal oesophagus, accompanied by failure of the LOS to relax during swallowing (i.e. a high residual relaxing pressure). These features may be accompanied by a high resting LOS pressure, but this is not necessary for a diagnosis. Achalasia often causes intermittent symptoms, with residual food and liquid in the distal oesophagus causing halitosis and recurrent chest sepsis due to nocturnal aspiration.

B Nutcracker oesophagus

Nutcracker oesophagus is an oesophageal dysmotility disorder characterised by dysphagia of both liquids and solids, with chest pain. In nutcracker oesophagus, there is oesophageal pressure exceeding 180 mmHg, which this patient does not have.

A Scleroderma

Scleroderma is an autoimmune connective tissue disorder which causes fibrosis of organs. It can cause fibrosis of the oesophagus leading to dysphagia, but is unlikely without other features such as calcinosis, Raynaud’s, sclerodactyly and telangiectasis. Scleroderma can also lead to reduced or occasionally absent distal peristalsis, but this is accompanied by low resting LOS pressures.

C Diffuse oesophageal spasm

Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes intermittent dysphagia and chest pain. A barium swallow can differentiate from achalasia by demonstrating abnormal oesophageal contractions such as a corkscrew pattern. In this patient there is interruption of peristalsis, which does not fit.

D Carcinoma of the oesophagus

Oesophageal cancer is associated with male gender, smoking history, oesophageal reflux, Barrett’s oesophagus and achalasia. Management is via an MDT approach. The presence of intermittent rather than progressive dysphagia makes this unlikely, as does the abnormal manometry. 6437

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of chronic diarrhoea. She underwent an extensive small bowel resection for Crohn’s disease 2 years earlier and has not been well since.

On examination, she has a BMI of 17, with multiple scars on the abdomen. Additionally she is suffering from dermatitis, glossitis and angular stomatitis.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)104 g/L115–155 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)106 fL76–98 fL
White cell count (WCC)5.6 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)232 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)12 mm/hour< 10 mm/hour
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin29 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)52 IU/L5–30 IU/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Short bowel syndrome

Short bowel syndrome has many causes, but in adult patients it is usually the result of extensive surgery undertaken for either Crohn’s disease or mesenteric infarction. We can see from the patient’s blood results that she has a macrocytic anaemia, likely indicating a failure to absorb B 12. Her low albumin of 29 also suggests significant malabsorption. Dermatitis is a feature of failure to absorb essential fatty acids (linoleic acid and linolenic acid). These patients also commonly exhibit dehydration and signs of hypovolaemia due to extensive gastrointestinal fluid losses. In some individuals adequate oral intake may be impossible; parenteral nutrition may be the only option, but is associated with significant long-term morbidity and mortality.

A Reactivated Crohn’s disease

The fact that the patient has a low ESR level makes a diagnosis of active inflammation unlikely. The chronicity of her symptoms going back 2 years also makes an exacerbation of her Crohn’s less likely as the answer here.

B Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease more often presents with generalised symptoms of tiredness, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia, though it can present with features of florid malabsorption in severe cases. However, given that we already know that this patient has had an extensive small bowel resection, that represents a far more likely explanation for her clinical picture.

D Bacterial overgrowth

Bacterial overgrowth tends to present with chronic diarrhoea and/or steatorrhoea with anaemia. Given that both Crohn’s disease and extensive small bowel resection can predispose to the condition, it should certainly be considered in this case. However, the fact that the patient has evidence of chronic malabsorption is more easily explained by a loss of surface area for digestion and absorption caused by short bowel syndrome.

E Cryptosporidium infection

Cryptosporidium is a protozoal parasite and generally causes a short illness with voluminous watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. The exception is in severely immunocompromised patients such as those with AIDS, where it can develop into a serious chronic condition with persistent severe diarrhoea and weight loss. We are given nothing in the history to suggest that degree of severe immunocompromise in this patient.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of lower abdominal pain for the past day that has worsened over the past few hours. He had two episodes of vomiting on his way to the hospital.

On examination, his blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg and his heart rate is 108 bpm. Abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the right iliac fossa. There was no guarding or rigidity. After further radiological examination, the patient was taken up for surgery and the surgical specimen is shown below.

Which of the following is the most likely pathology in this patient?
options: Infection of the terminal ileum resulting in granuloma formation
Inflammation of a congenital outpouching of the small intestine
Inflammatory bowel disease with stricture formation
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Inflammation of a congenital outpouching of the small intestine

This is descriptive of Meckel’s diverticulitis. The surgical specimen shows the presence of a Meckel’s diverticulum, which is the most common congenital abnormality of the small intestine. The most common presentation is with bleeding, followed by diverticulitis which can be confused with appendicitis. In a large

majority of cases, Meckel’s diverticulum may be incidentally found during surgery. A computed tomography (CT) abdomen may be helpful in the diagnosis, whereas a Meckel scan with technetium-99m pertechnetate may be more accurate in identifying it.

Image Source: Milliways, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons

D Inflammatory bowel disease with stricture formation

This is descriptive of Crohn’s disease, which presents with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss, rather than with the acute presentation seen here. Besides, there are no strictures observed in the gross specimen presented here.

A Infection of the terminal ileum resulting in granuloma formation

This is descriptive of ileocaecal tuberculosis, which usually does not have such an acute presentation. Besides, an outpouching of the small intestine is suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum.

C Inflammation of the appendix

This is descriptive of acute appendicitis. However, the gross specimen shows an outpouching of the small intestine in the anti-mesenteric border, suggestive of Meckel’s diverticulum.

E Salmonella enteritis resulting in perforation

Typhoid due to Salmonella infection can cause longitudinal ulcers which may result in intestinal perforation. However, intestinal perforation usually occurs after more than two weeks of illness. Besides, there is no evidence of perforation in the gross specimen shown here.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old Iraqi student was admitted to the Emergency Department on a number of occasions with abdominal pain associated with arthralgia and fever.

Previous medical history included appendicectomy and cholecystitis. Pain was often associated with constipation that became diarrhoea when the pain resolved.

Clinical examination revealed a pyrexia of 38.5 °C, with generalised rebound tenderness in the abdomen and diminished bowel sounds. Bilateral swollen knees were noted and clear fluid was aspirated from each joint. Computed tomography (CT) examination was unremarkable.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)135 g/LMales: 135–175 g/L Females: 115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)300 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin10 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)16 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)21 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin40 g/L35–55 g/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)72 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)50 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Synovial fluidNo organisms
UrinalysisProtein+++
Urinary porphyrinsNormal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Familial Mediterranean fever

Familial Mediterranean fever is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by sporadic paroxysmal attacks of fever and serosal inflammation. Patients are recurrently admitted to hospital and undergo extensive investigation and often abdominal surgery, but no specific pathology is found. Constipation accompanying the fever is common and diarrhoea may follow its resolution. Synovitis has been reported in up to 75% of patients. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are elevated, and serosal (peritoneal or pleural) or synovial fluid may show large numbers of neoutrophils with no organisms. Amyloidosis manifesting as proteinuria can occur, particularly in Sephardic (Middle Eastern and North African) Jews. Therefore, Option A is the best answer here. A specific genetic test is now available to aid diagnosis, and the treatment of choice is colchicine.

B Crohn’s disease

It could explain many of these symptoms, including the abdominal pain with associated joint pains, as Crohn’s is associated with extra-intestinal manifestations such as arthritis. However, this patient has a fever and, in the context of Crohn’s disease, you would be concerned about an abscess or another complication of Crohn’s such as a perforation, which would usually be apparent on a CT scan.

C Acute intermittent porphyria

Normal urinary porphyrins effectively rule out acute intermittent porphyria.

D Adult Still’s disease

This condition is usually associated with a classic salmon-coloured rash and a raised ferritin. Splenomegaly can also be present.

E Irritable bowel syndrome

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man presents to the Colorectal Clinic for a review of his test results. He had presented earlier that year with a 6-month history of lower abdominal pain and constipation. An urgent CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis shows an ill-defined mass in the lower rectum measuring 30 mm × 28 mm × 16 mm. A diagnosis of stage 2a colorectal adenocarcinoma is made. He has no significant past medical history of note and is normally fit and active. In the clinic today, the patient is keen to explore treatment options.

What is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Surgical resection alone

Surgical resection is the mainstay of treatment for stage 2a colorectal cancer, aiming for complete removal of the tumour with clear margins. Adjuvant chemotherapy is not routinely indicated in stage 2a disease, unless specific high-risk features are present. However, chemotherapy would be considered in stages 2b and 2c.

D Palliative chemotherapy without surgery

This would not be suitable for stage 2a colorectal cancer, which is potentially curable with surgery. Palliative chemotherapy is typically reserved for advanced or metastatic disease where surgery is not a curative option. Given that this patient is relatively young with a good performance status, surgery should most definitively be considered as an option for managing his cancer.

A Adjuvant chemotherapy following surgery

This is not the most appropriate initial management for stage 2a colorectal cancer. Adjuvant chemotherapy is generally not recommended for stage 2a disease, unless there are high-risk features such as poor histological differentiation or lymphovascular invasion. It would be considered in later stages of the disease such as stages 2b, 2c and 3.

B Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery

This would not be appropriate for stage 2a colorectal cancer, as neoadjuvant chemotherapy is typically reserved for locally advanced (stage 3) or metastatic (stage 4) disease. Stage 2a patients usually undergo surgery as primary treatment without neoadjuvant therapy.

C Observation with close surveillance

While surveillance is important following treatment for colorectal cancer, including stage 2a disease, observation alone without surgical intervention is not appropriate as it does not address the primary tumour.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man with a long history of diabetes and previous cerebrovascular accident is admitted with early satiety, postprandial vomiting and abdominal distension. There is no history of haematemesis or abdominal pain. He opens his bowels regularly. He is on insulin therapy, digoxin and aspirin.

On examination, he is overweight and he is in atrial fibrillation. His abdomen is distended and tympanic, but is otherwise soft and non-tender with active bowel sounds. Rectal examination reveals soft brown stool. Neurology examination reveals a residual right-sided paralysis.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)134 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.7 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)319 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)133 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.1 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)117 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)81 fL80 - 100 fL
International normalized ratio (INR)1.2< 1.1
Urea10.4 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Albumin36 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.06 mmol/L2.2 - 2.7 mmol/L
Glucose11.2 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L
Chest X-rayNormal
Abdominal X-rayDilated stomach Upper GI endoscopy is normal.

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Trial of domperidone

Gastric motility is frequently affected in diabetes mellitus, with a reported prevalence of gastroparesis of 10%, although in reality this is probably significantly higher. Patients should initially be investigated with an endoscopy to exclude anatomical lesions such as pyloric stenosis. Gastric emptying scans using solid-phase meals are usually necessary. Treatment is often difficult and improving diabetic control can be beneficial, but a prokinetic drug has the added effects of increasing locally released acetylcholine at the myenteric plexus. Domperidone is now the initial intervention of choice, with metoclopramide having fallen out of favour because of long-term neurological sequelae associated with its use.

B Trial of high-fibre diet

High-fibre diets may result in significant residual solid material remaining within the stomach, exacerbating symptoms of gastroparesis.

A Recommend less frequent meals

Patients should be encouraged to eat smaller, more frequent meals with a lower potential residual solid component, to minimise solid food retention in the stomach.

C Trial of nifedipine

Nifedipine is a potential intervention for the treatment of oesophageal spasm in achalasia, but it has no role in the treatment of diabetic gastroparesis.

D Trial of a gastric pacemaker

Gastric pacemakers are viewed by NICE as a research intervention for patients with gastroparesis resistant to other interventions.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old woman is seen to take a large quantity of paracetamol tablets following an argument with her boyfriend. At 72 h later, she presents to the Emergency Department with jaundice and vomiting.

On examination, her BP is 105/72, pulse is 85 and regular. She is tender in the epigastrium and tells you she is passing only small amounts of dark urine.

Which of the following would be the best indicator of her overall prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Prothrombin time

Paracetamol can cause liver failure even at relatively low doses (>7 g). The transplant criteria published by King’s College Hospital are based on prognostic factors from a large retrospective cohort of patients. In these criteria, coagulopathy (prolonged prothrombin time/increased international normalised ration (INR)) is an important prognostic indicator along with encephalopathy, development of kidney disease and acidosis not corrected by fluid resuscitation.

Maximal liver damage will occur approximately 72 h after ingestion when prothrombin time will be maximally prolonged – it will then either return to normal (recovery with no sequelae) or remain prolonged (acute liver failure – recovery unlikely).

E Urea

Creatinine, not urea is used as an indicator of impending acute kidney disease in paracetamol overdose. Measurement of urea is confounded as a measure of renal failure because of it’s absorption as part of a 'blood meal'.

B Liver transaminases

Transaminases are released by damaged hepatocytes and are always raised in significant paracetamol poisoning, reaching levels of >10 000 IU/L. Transaminase levels are, however, not good indications of whether progression to acute liver failure will occur.

C Serum paracetamol levels

Although raised serum paracetamol levels at >48 h would suggest a large or staggered overdose, both more at risk of progressing to acute liver failure, the value has no prognostic role.

D Bilirubin

Although serum bilirubin is included in some prognostic indices in paracetamol poisoning, it is nowhere near as reliable as prothrombin time. Transaminases, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGt), albumin and alkaline phosphatase are of no benefit.

questions.question:
You are asked to review a 42-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis who is an inpatient on the Gastroenterology Ward. His spironolactone has been withdrawn, but the nurses are concerned as his creatinine has risen to 180 µmol/L. He has received albumin infusions.

On examination, his BP is 110/70 mmHg, with pulse 75/min and regular. He has marked ascites consistent with cirrhosis. You suspect hepatorenal syndrome.

Which of the following is the most effective intervention with respect to his renal function?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Terlipressin

The class of drugs known as splanchnic vasoconstrictors has been studied regarding treatment of individuals with hepatorenal syndrome. One of the drugs terlipressin, has a positive impact on both blood pressure and glomerular filtration rate (GFR), when used in combination with albumin. Terlipressin is a non-selective V1 vasopressin agonist, with lower incidence of ischemic complications as compared to ornipressin. Also, terlipressin can be given as a bolus. Albumin is useful in expanding the plasma volume and maintenance of cardiac output. Liver transplantation is the ultimate definitive treatment of hepatorenal syndrome. Over the longer term, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be of value, although ultimately liver transplantation is the most effective option. In a study by Sarwar et al. (see below), complete response to terlipressin–albumin therapy was seen in 58.3% patients, 29.2% achieved partial response with > 25% creatinine reduction, while 12.5% showed no response.

Reference: Sarwar, S., Khan, A.A. (2016). Hepatorenal syndrome: Response to terlipressin and albumin and its determinants. Pakistan Journal of Medical Sciences 32(2):274–8.

E Midodrine

Midodrine (an alpha-agonist) is used the treatment of postural hypotension and is non-selective in constricting splanchnic vessels, and thus cannot be used in this case. Where terlipressin therapy is not available, initial treatment with a combination of midodrine, octreotide and albumin is suggested. Investigations of midodrine alone or in combination have shown conflicting results for systemic and renal haemodynamics and renal function in patients with cirrhosis-related complications.

B Lactulose

Lactulose is used in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It reduces ammonia production in the intestine. Lactulose is the mainstay of treatment and results in improvement in approximately 70–80% of patients with overt hepatic encephalopathy. It would not be effective in this particular scenario.

C Furosemide

Furosemide, a diuretic, is not indicated as the patient is already on spironolactone and his blood pressure needs to be maintained at an optimal level.

D Dobutamine

Dobutamine is less selective in vasoconstriction of the splanchnic vasculature as compared to terlipressin, and would be ineffective in maintaining blood pressure in this situation.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with shortness of breath. He is a known alcoholic and has a past history of ischaemic heart disease.

On examination, he looks jaundiced but his abdomen is soft and non-tender. His blood pressure is 109/82 mmHg, pulse is 80 and regular and his chest sounds clear with good breath sounds bilaterally.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)70 g/L (elevated reticulocytes)135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)92 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)85 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin35 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT)400 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Cholesterol10 mmol/L< 5.2 mmol/L

Which of the following diagnoses do you think he has?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Zieve syndrome

Zieve syndrome occurs in patients with excessive alcohol consumption, with haemolysis and severe hyperlipidaemia, abdominal pain and transient mildly raised bilirubin. It usually occurs in males and resolves once alcohol consumption is stopped.

D Gilbert syndrome

Gilbert syndrome is a benign cause of isolated hyperbilirubinaemia episodes of jaundice can be triggered by illness, surgery or dehydration.

B Whipple’s disease

Whipple’s disease is a cause of gastrointestinal (GI) malabsorption, and is caused by the Gram-positive bacterium Tropheryma whippelii. It is also associated with joint pains.

C Crigler Najjar syndrome

Crigler–Najjar syndrome is a rare congenital disorder of bilirubin conjugation. It has two distinct forms, type 1 and type 2: type 2 patients can survive to adulthood without any neurological impairment, whereas this impairment is seen in neonates in type 1 cases.

E Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis syndrome (NASH)

NASH is fatty liver disease unrelated to alcohol exposure and is seen in obese patients with insulin resistance, including those with type 2 diabetes.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department for review. For the past four weeks, he has had increasingly frequent diarrhoea, opening his bowels up to eight times per day. Over the past few days, the diarrhoea has become increasingly mixed with blood. He has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medication. He tells you he has lost 5 kg in weight over the past few months and has suffered from intermittent night sweats.

On examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg while his pulse is 85 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and he has mild left-sided tenderness. Bowel sounds are normal and PR reveals no masses. Repeated stool cultures taken by his General Practitioner are negative.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)133 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)421 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)189 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)42 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)75 mm/1 st h< 10 mm/1 st h
Albumin31 g/L35–55 g/L
Bilirubin17 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most useful investigation to establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Flexible sigmoidoscopy

Given the history of chronic bloody diarrhoea, coupled with multiple negative stool cultures, ulcerative colitis is the main diagnosis to exclude. Bearing in mind that distal disease is always present, a flexible sigmoidoscopy coupled with biopsy is the most useful step in establishing the diagnosis. Oral and rectal corticosteroids are the key to achieving remission, coupled with a 5-ASA compound.

B Barium enema

While a barium enema can show evidence of colonic pathology in ulcerative colitis, it is contraindicated in patients with acute severe colitis due to the risk of perforation and should not be performed here.

A Abdominal X-ray

An abdominal X-ray would not lead to a confirmed diagnosis of the underlying condition (ulcerative colitis) which is the question here. It would, however, be useful in the work-up of patients presenting with an acute severe flare of colitis, as is the case here, in order to investigate for toxic megacolon. Truelove and Witt’s criteria define acute severe colitis as more than six bloody stools per day along with any one of the following:

tachycardia > 90 bpm fever > 37.8 °C Hb < 105 g/L Raised inflammatory markers.

D Hydrogen breath test

Hydrogen breath testing is useful in confirming a diagnosis of bacterial overgrowth syndrome. Patients with bacterial overgrowth typically present with bloating and abdominal pain along with diarrhoea and flatulence.

E Ultrasound scan (USS) abdomen

While a USS abdomen can be useful in the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease it cannot differentiate between ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease. It is a more useful in the investigation the of the hepatobiliary disorders which are complications in these patients. Ulcerative colitis is an important risk factor for primary sclerosing cholangitis and gallstone disease.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old man who recently emigrated from China had some routine blood work by his general practitioner (GP).

His hepatitis-B screen came back showing positive HBs and hepatitis-B IgG core antibodies. Anti-HBe was positive, but he is e-antigen negative and s-antigen negative.

The GP immediately referred the patient to your clinic, but before doing this sent some liver function tests.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Bilirubin12 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)42 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)67 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Albumin36 g/L35–55 g/L
HBV DNANegative

The patient seems to be in good health.

What is the most appropriate management of this patient?
options: Start combined lamivudine and interferon therapy
Offer an HIV, Hep-C test and discharge the patient back to the GP if negative
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Offer an HIV, Hep-C test and discharge the patient back to the GP if negative

A patient who is HBs antibody positive indicates previous infection unless they have been vaccinated against

Hep-B. The phenomenon of loss of HbeAg and seroconversion to anti-Hbe-positive status indicates a reduction of inflammation accompanied by histological change from active to inactive hepatitis. E-antigen negativity implies that he no longer has active infection. Guidance suggests that in this case it is worth offering an HIV test, as exposure to hepatitis B may well indicate exposure to other blood-borne viruses.

For indications for treatment, refer to NICE guidance CG165.

D Start combined lamivudine and interferon therapy

Antiviral therapy is not currently indicated for a man over 30 years old, with LFTs and negative HBV DNA. Antiviral treatments for HBe-Ag-negative chronic hepatitis-B include PEGinterferon alfa-2a (first line), entacavir and tenofivir.

A Elective liver biopsy

In patients with HBe-negative chronic hepatitis and mildly raised ALT, liver biopsy is usually only considered in those patients who have serum HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/ml, to determine whether treatment is warranted. This patient has nearly normal LFTs and negative HBV DNA.

B Discharge back to the GP

He should be tested for other blood borne viruses, and offered transient elastography testing.

C Start interferon therapy

Antiviral therapy is not currently indicated for a man over 30 years old, with normal LFTs and negative HBV DNA.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old bar owner comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. He has suffered from chronic diarrhoea for many years, accompanied by intermittent abdominal pain, and is finding it impossible to maintain his weight. He admits to drinking excess alcohol in the past, although now he claims to have reduced his intake to one glass of whisky per day. He also smokes 20 cigarettes per day. On examination, his blood pressure is 135/75 mmHg and pulse 80 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft, although he complains of vague tenderness in the epigastrium. His body mass index (BMI) is 21 kg/m 2.

Investigations:

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)108 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)151 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine90 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin29 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)121 U/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)172 U/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin17 µmol/L< 17 µmol/L

You suspect him to be suffering from chronic pancreatitis.

Which of the following is the best way to confirm functional pancreatic insufficiency?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Faecal elastase

Faecal elastase measurement is the preferred approach to evaluating chronic pancreatitis because it requires a single random stool sample, with values of elastase of < 200 ug/g being suggestive of pancreatic insufficiency.

D Lipase

Like amylase, random lipase measurement is not useful in the diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis. It is only useful in diagnosing acute pancreatitis where patients usually present with acute epigastric pain and vomiting.

A Amylase

Random measurement of amylase and lipase is of no value in detecting either chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic insufficiency. Minor elevations may be seen in patients with obesity and diabetes, but this has no prognostic value with respect to pancreatic disease.

B Faecal fat estimation

Faecal fat estimation is both time-consuming and unpleasant in terms of collection and analysis. Qualitative staining for fat with sudan staining is not recommended. A quantitative approach looking at thresholds of > 7 g/fat excretion per day (possible pancreatic insufficiency) and > 10 g/fat excretion per day (likely pancreatic insufficiency) is therefore required.

E SeHCAT test

The SeHCAT test is used for determining bile acid malabsorption. It uses a radiolabelled taurine-conjugated bile acid analogue, and retention is measured at seven days using a gamma camera.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease at the age of 17 years. He has been admitted to hospital on a yearly basis since his diagnosis with acute flare-ups requiring courses of systemic corticosteroids.

He has no extra-enteric manifestations of Crohn’s disease, but has had a problematic perianal fistula requiring frequent courses of antibiotics. He is finding it difficult to maintain attendance at work because of ill health.

Which of the following steps is recommended next to maintain remission in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A 6-Mercaptopurine

Thiopurines (azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine) are the most effective agents in maintaining remission in Crohn’s disease long term. If not tolerated, methotrexate could be used as an alternative. Thiopurines are thought to be particularly effective in patients with fistulating disease. Infliximab is of value in long-term remission in fistulating Crohn’s disease (and possibly in non-fistulating disease) but is generally used alongside a thiopurine. Over the long term, it may prove a superior option to methotrexate, but currently it is still considered only after a traditional second line therapy has failed to gain control.

E Sulphasalazine

ASA (5-Aminosalycilic acid) compounds such as balsalazide and sulphasalazine have a role in maintaining remission and are generally well tolerated but are not as effective as thiopurines.

B Polymeric diet

This has most value in reducing the severity of acute flares and their frequency, rather than resolving fistulae.

C Budesonide

Steroids do not have a role in maintaining remission, their main value is in treating acute flares of Crohn’s disease.

D Ciclosporin

Cyclosporine is of most use in the treatment of severe ulcerative colitis which is unresponsive to high dose corticosteroids and 5-ASA compounds.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of jaundice, nausea and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. There is no history of fevers or recent travel. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis, for which he has been taking methotrexate for the past four months. He drinks two glasses of wine three times a week and denies smoking or recreational drug use. Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
White cell count (WCC)10.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µm/l50–90 µmol/L
Bilirubin60 µmol/L1–21 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)150 U/L1–40 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)180 U/L1–40 U/L
Albumin40 g/L35–50 g/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)80 U/L30–130 U/L
Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)50 U/L1–54 U/L

What is the most likely cause of this patient's liver injury?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Drug-induced hepatitis

The most likely cause of the patient’s liver injury is drug-induced hepatitis, given the recent history of methotrexate use. The patient’s blood results demonstrate evidence of acute hepatitis with raised AST and ALT levels, with a normal ratio, and raised bilirubin levels. Methotrexate, a commonly used medication for rheumatoid arthritis, is known to cause hepatotoxicity. It is important to promptly recognise and discontinue the offending medication in cases of drug-induced hepatitis to prevent further liver damage and facilitate recovery. Bilirubin levels of more than twice the upper limit of normal are indicative of severe hepatotoxicity and are associated with a 10–15% mortality rate.

A Alcoholic hepatitis

This patient’s history does not suggest significant alcohol consumption, with six standard glasses of wine totalling 12 units across the week. This makes a diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis less likely. Additionally, alcoholic hepatitis would typically cause a raised AST: ALT ratio of more than 2 and elevated GGT levels, which are not seen here.

B Autoimmune hepatitis

While autoimmune hepatitis is a consideration in patients with elevated liver enzyme levels and jaundice, the onset of symptoms within a short time frame from starting methotrexate makes drug-induced hepatitis a more likely diagnosis in this case.

D Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) typically presents with elevated liver enzyme levels and may progress to liver fibrosis and cirrhosis. LFTs tend to show an AST: ALT ratio of less than one. Bilirubin levels are typically normal and are only elevated with decompensated disease. Adding to this, the patient’s history of methotrexate use makes drug-induced hepatitis a more likely explanation for the liver injury in this case.

E Viral hepatitis

The absence of fever or recent travel and a normal WCC make viral hepatitis unlikely. The history of recent methotrexate use with the LFT results seen above makes a drug-induced cause more plausible.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old patient with a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) has suffered a number of episodes of pan-colitis over the last 11 years. He is currently managed with infliximab and has stable disease.

He has read on the Internet that people with UC have an increased risk of cancer and liver disease and wishes to discuss this. He has not had any weight loss or additional bloody diarrhoea.

The general practitioner (GP) measures his carcino-embryonic antigen level (CEA) and alpha fetoprotein, and a surveillance colonoscopy is arranged.

Which of the following is the correct advice to give him?
options: CEA is a useful screening test for bowel cancer
Faecal calprotectin elevation indicates a possible neoplasm
Cancers tend to present earlier in patients with UC and are therefore easier to treat
Alpha-fetoprotein is a good marker for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) in this case
He is at risk of PSC despite good control of his UC at the current time
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E He is at risk of PSC despite good control of his UC at the current time

Although this patient’s UC is currently well controlled, it won’t significantly impact on future risk of PSC, which is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

C Cancers tend to present earlier in patients with UC and are therefore easier to treat

Due to the fact that symptoms may be confused with active inflammatory bowel disease, diagnosis is often made late.

A CEA is a useful screening test for bowel cancer

CEA is not reliable as a test for diagnosing early colon cancer, but is considered as a test for cancer recurrence in those who have undergone a surgical resection.

B Faecal calprotectin elevation indicates a possible neoplasm

Faecal calprotectin is a measure of active inflammatory bowel disease.

D Alpha-fetoprotein is a good marker for primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) in this case

Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, not for PSC.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and an upper GI haemorrhage. She admits that she went foraging for mushrooms some 3 days earlier and cooked some that she found in the forest, but no one else in the family wanted to take the risk of eating them. A sample of leftover mushrooms suggests they were Death Cap. On examination, her BP is 110/72 mmHg, with pulse 92/min and regular. She is tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant of her abdomen. There is dried blood around her lips and evidence of bruising on her arms and legs.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)91 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)121 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)255 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L

Which of the following would be an indicator for transplant according to the King’s College Hospital criteria (non-paracetamol induced liver failure)?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Bilirubin 320 µmol/L

Bilirubin levels of >300 µmol/L is one of the prognostic indicators that determines referral for liver transplantation.

Several factors are important in the prognosis of patients with acute liver failure. Several criteria have been developed to predict when liver transplantation is indicated, the most widely accepted being the King's College Hospital criteria:

INR >6.5; or,

Three of the following five criteria:

Patient age <11 or >40; Serum bilirubin >300 micromoles per litre; Time from onset of jaundice to the development of coma >7 days; INR >3.5; or Drug toxicity, regardless of whether it was the cause of the acute liver failure.

C Alkaline phosphatase 430 U/L

ALP levels are not included in the King’s College Hospital criteria for predicting when to refer the patient for liver transplantation.

A Age 34

Age of less than 11 years or more than 40 years is considered to be one of the prognostic indicator criteria for liver transplantation.

B ALT 2300 U/L

ALT level is not included in the King’s College Hospital criteria of prognostic indictors for liver transplantation.

E INR 3.2

INR of >6.5 is considered one of the positive indicators that determines referral for liver transplantation.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She complains of weight loss, intermittent abdominal bloating and diarrhoea which has increased over the past few months. She also has a history of type I diabetes, for which she takes a basal bolus insulin regimen.

Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/75 mmHg; pulse is 85 bpm and regular. She looks pale and has a body mass index (BMI) of 20 kg/m 2.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)101 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.7 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)178 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)95 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin26 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)85 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin17 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)183 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Calcium (Ca)2.15 mmol/L2.2–2.6 mmol/L
Anti-endomysial antibody (IgA)Negative

Which of the following is the most useful next step given the negative anti-endomysial antibody result?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Immunoglobulin electrophoresis

Insufficient levels of IgA lead to falsey negative coeliac serology (both IgA tTG and IgA endomysial antibodies). As IgA deficiency can coexist in up to around 5% of patients with coeliac disease. It is therefore necessary here, given the suspicious clinical scenario and concurrent autoimmune disease, to rule out IgA deficiency before excluding coeliac disease based on negative serology alone. Duodenal biopsy would be appropriate after IgA testing.

A Duodenal biopsy

Although anti-endomysial antibody is negative, this test requires sufficient levels of IgA which has not been tested for. It raises the possibility of IgA deficiency and would be required for testing before a duodenal biopsy is clinically indicated.

B Gluten-free diet

Although this is a treatment option for coeliac disease, it may obscure the diagnosis if further requiring duodenal biopsy after IgA testing. A gluten-free diet is a significant undertaking for which coeliac patients must strictly adhere to lifelong. It should not, therefore, be advised to be started without a diagnosis first.

D SeCHAT testing

SeCHAT testing is not clinically indicated. This is a test of bile acid malabsorption which is common in inflammatory bowel disease. The clinical scenario would indicate she may have coeliac disease.

E 24hr fecal fat collection

24-hour faecal fat collection is a test for fat malabsorption which is not currently indicated by the clinical scenario.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old man complains of acute epigastric pain radiating to his back. This is associated with vomiting. The pain is improved when he sits forward. He drinks half a bottle of whisky per day.

On examination, he is mildly pyrexial. He looks jaundiced and unwell. He is tachycardic and slightly hypotensive. There is generalised tenderness of the abdomen. There is no guarding or rebound rigidity. Bowel sounds are normal.

Electrocardiography, erect chest and abdominal radiography are normal. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a small liver, normal bile ducts and minimal fluid around the pancreas.

Which of the following is an indicator of poor prognosis for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Serum calcium = 1.91 mmol/L

The patient has acute pancreatitis secondary to alcohol (95% of acute pancreatitis is attributable to gallstones and alcohol). The pain in pancreatitis can be very severe and is relieved by leaning forward. In severe cases, patients are shocked.

There are several severity scoring systems used to assess prognosis/predict mortality. The Ranson criteria use the following parameters (assessed at admission and 48h) to predict mortality in alcoholic pancreatitis: age > 55, WCC > 16.0 ×10⁹/L, fasting blood glucose > 11 mmol/L, LDH > 350 IU/L, serum AST >250 IU/L; within 48 h of admission: haematocrit decrease by >10%, arterial Pa0 2 <8 kPa, serum calcium < 2.0 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen increase > 1.8 mmol/L, base deficit > 4 mmol/L, fluid sequestration > 6 l. Mortality ranges from 1% for those with <3 criteria to 90% for those with >6 criteria.

Other assessment systems include the Glasgow score and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II scoring system.

There are limitations to most scoring systems (as most require 48 h to determine predicted outcome) and the patient needs to be aggressively fluid resuscitated early to reduce the chance of progression to end organ dysfunction (250–500 ml/h isotonic crystalloid during first 12–24 h). The most recent British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines are from 2005. For more recent guidelines see American College of Gastroenterology: Management of Acute Pancreatitis (2013), Am J Gastroenterol 2013; 108:1400–1415.

E Serum creatinine = 150 mmol/L

This creatinine may be indicative of early kidney disease, which is a marker of severe pancreatitis, but serum creatinine in isolation is not in the recognised severity criteria.

A PaO 2 = 9.5 kPa

In the Glasgow prognostic criteria for alcoholic and gallstone pancreatitis, a Pa O 2 of <8kPa in room air is a marker of poor prognosis. Other criteria include:

Age >55

Serum albumin <32g/l

Serum Ca <2 mmol/L

Blood glucose >10 mmol/L

Serum LDH >600 units/l

Serum urea nitrogen >16.1 mmol/L

WBC >15

With a score <3, severe pancreatitis (defined as the presence of persistent organ failure >48 h) is unlikely to occur.

B Serum albumin = 34 g/L

In the Glasgow prognostic criteria for alcoholic and gallstone pancreatitis, an albumin of <32 g/L is a poor prognostic indicator.

D Aspartate aminotransferase = 98 IU/L

An AST >250 would be predictive of severity in the Ranson criteria.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man was found on the street by the police. He complains of right upper quadrant pain and anorexia. He works at a building site but has recently lost his job.

On examination, he smells very strongly of alcohol. He has icteric sclera. His temperature is 37.6 °C. There is spider naevi and palmar erythema. Heart sounds and chest examination are unremarkable. Abdominal examination reveals dull flanks and a tender liver edge. There is no focal neurology but a hepatic flap is present.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L135–175 g/L
White blood count (WBC)17.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)80 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean cell volume (MCV)103 fL76–98 fL
International normalised ratio (INR)1.6< 1.1
Sodium (Na⁺)132 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea1.7 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)70 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin35 g/L35–55 g/L
Bilirubin102 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)45 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)100 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)156 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Ferritin987 µg/L20–250 µg/L
Hepatitis and autoimmune serologyNegative

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Alcoholic hepatitis

Alcoholic hepatitis commonly occurs after a prolonged period of alcohol abuse or return to alcohol after period of abstinence. It often presents with malaise, anorexia, mild fever, tender hepatolomegaly, and (if severe) jaundice. Investigations usually reveal mildly increased serum transaminases, macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia, poor hepatic synthetic function, leukocytosis irrespective of infection and increased acute phase reactants. Usually the AST: ALT > 2.

The prognosis depends on its severity. Malnutrition, jaundice, fluid retention and encephalopathy are associated with poor outlook. Histology can help to confirm diagnosis.

The mainstay of treatment is supportive in nature:

Alcohol abstinence Prevention and treatment of alcohol withdrawal Fluid management Nutritional support Infection surveillance Prophylaxis against gastric mucosal bleeding

The discriminant function (DF) can be used to identify patients for treatment. Those who have a value > 32 may benefit from corticosteroids. If there is a contraindication to steroids, pentoxifylline is an alternative.

A Hepatoma

The development of a hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with liver cirrhosis is a possible cause of decompensation. However, the history of alcohol, low-grade fever and high WCC, make alcoholic hepatitis a more likely cause.

C Choledocholithiasis

Acute gallstone impaction in the common bile duct is likely to present with right upper quadrant pain, with possible complicating cholangitis causing a fever. But this would not account for the macrocytosis, signs of chronic liver disease, and decompensation with jaundice, ascites and asterixis.

D Viral hepatitis

This could be the cause of chronic liver disease, which has now decompensated, but we are told that viral serology is negative.

E Haemochromatosis

There is no suggestion of other organ involvement, and haemochromatosis is less likely to explain the tender hepatomegaly, raised WCC, and mild fever. The raised ferritin in this case is likely due to alcoholic liver disease and not haemochromatosis.

questions.question:
You are seeing a 25-year-old woman in clinic with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC). She had extensive colitis 10 years ago, which has improved with medical treatment.

Last year, she had been diagnosed with early primary sclerosing cholangitis after an MRCP and liver biopsy. Her last colonoscopy was 6 months ago, which detected no active disease, and random biopsies were normal. She is remaining well and asymptomatic.

Physical examination is unremarkable, with a normal BMI of 23.

When should colonic screening be performed on this patient?
options: Colonoscopy should be performed only when there are symptoms of colitis
Colonoscopy should be performed in 10 years’ time
Colonoscopy should be performed in 3 years’ time
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Colonoscopy should be performed annually

This patient has had ulcerative colitis (UC) for 10 years and has developed associated primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) of the liver. Patients with concomitant UC and PSC are at a higher risk of developing colonic cancer, and it is recommended that they be screened annually with colonoscopy. Those with history of colon cancer in a first-degree relative under 50 years of age should also be subject to annual surveillance.

D Colonoscopy should be performed in 3 years’ time

Those with intermediate-risk disease, extensive colitis with mild active endoscopic/histological inflammation or post-inflammatory polyps or family history of colorectal cancer in a first-degree relative aged 50+, should be surveyed 3-yearly.

A Colonoscopy should be performed only when there are symptoms of colitis

Given there is significant risk of colonic dysplasia and subsequent carcinoma, expectant colonoscopy only when there are symptoms runs the risk of missing a lesion that could be advanced at the point of diagnosis.

B Colonoscopy should be performed in 10 years’ time

Even those patients with low-risk disease (those with previous extensive colitis with no active endoscopic/histological inflammation or left-sided colitis or Crohn's colitis of <50% colon) should be surveyed 5-yearly.

E Flexible sigmoidoscopy should be used 2-yearly

Flexible sigmoidoscopy is inappropriate because it would fail to detect right-sided colonic lesions.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old man complains of lethargy and progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He has a long history of intermittent heartburn and has occasionally passed some dark red blood mixed with his stools.

Other past medical history includes hypertension and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has not lost any weight recently, is an ex-smoker and drinks only occasional alcohol.

Physical examination confirms hypertension, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, but is otherwise unremarkable.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)84 g/L135–175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)70 fL76–98 fL
White cell count (WCC)9.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils5.4 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.58 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)258 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L

Renal and hepatic function are normal.

Gastroscopy and barium enema are normal.

Mesenteric angiography showed an abnormal vascular blush in the ascending colon.

What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Angiodysplasia

This patient has a microcytic anaemia and a history of gastrointestinal bleeding. The findings on mesenteric angiography, combined with a normal barium enema, suggest a diagnosis of angiodysplasia. Angiodysplasia may be found throughout the gastrointestinal tract, although it most commonly occurs in the caecum and ascending colon. It is a significant cause of chronic anaemia and can also cause acute haemorrhage. Treatment is either by heat coagulation at endoscopy or by embolisation of the bleeding vessel during angiography.

C Colonic varices

Colonic varices would produce distension of the veins in the colon and would not appear as an abnormal vascular blush on mesenteric angiography.

A Colonic carcinoma

Barium enema would not be normal in colonic carcinoma – we would expect a colonic mass in carcinoma. The mesenteric angiography would be normal.

D Meckel’s diverticulum

Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. It results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct leading to the formation of a true diverticulum of the small intestine. Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum, containing all layers of the small bowel wall. It arises from the anti- mesenteric surface of the middle-to-distal ileum. The diverticulum represents a persistent remnant of the omphalo-mesenteric duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac in the foetus. Meckel's diverticulum is uncommon and often clinically silent, particularly in adults. Asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum may be discovered during abdominal exploration for the evaluation of unrelated pathology. Less commonly, it is found incidentally on diagnostic imaging. When symptomatic, Meckel's diverticulum may present with abdominal pain or symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction. Mesenteric angiography is not abnormal as in this case.

E Ulcerative colitis

Ulcerative colitis is characterised by recurring episodes of inflammation limited to the mucosal layer of the colon. It commonly involves the rectum and may extend in a proximal and continuous fashion to involve other parts of the colon. Patients with ulcerative colitis usually present with diarrhoea, which may be associated with blood. Bowel movements are frequent and small in volume as a result of rectal inflammation. Associated symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, urgency, tenesmus and incontinence. Patients with mainly distal disease may have constipation accompanied by frequent discharge of blood and mucus. The endoscopic findings in patients with ulcerative colitis include loss of vascular markings due to engorgement of the mucosa, giving it an erythematous appearance. In addition, granularity of the mucosa, petechiae, exudates, oedema,

erosions, touch friability and spontaneous bleeding may be present. More severe cases may be associated with macro-ulcerations, profuse bleeding and copious exudates. Mesenteric angiography is not abnormal as in this case.

questions.question:
A 71-year-old woman with a background of previous non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and atrial fibrillation presents with generalised abdominal pain. The pain is grumbling in character and has been worsening over the last 24 hours. She notes that she has had blood in her stool occasionally for the past few weeks. She is haemodynamically stable, and an inpatient colonoscopy is arranged. Her histology is shown below.

Following the colonoscopy, she deteriorates rapidly, developing worsening abdominal pain and vomiting. Examination of her abdomen demonstrates guarding.

Chest X-ray: normal Abdominal X-ray: no acute abnormality detected

Normal Values

Lactate 6.2 mmol/L 0.5 - 2.2 mmol/L

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Ischaemic colitis

This patient has vascular risk factors and vague-sounding abdominal pain, with relatively rapid deterioration and a raised lactate level. These are all red flags for ischaemic colitis. Moreover, the histology shows crypt loss with thickening of the mucosa and hyalinisation of the submucosa. There is also inflammatory cell infiltrate. Taken together these features indicate ischaemic colitis.

D Perforation following colonoscopy

While this history may well be suggestive of perforation following colonoscopy, the deterioration post- procedure, the lack of X-ray findings and the ischaemic changes on histology suggest that this condition was likely pre-existing before the colonoscopy and the deterioration was coincidental. However, it is important to note that colonoscopy can be a cause of ischaemic colitis, the diagnosis here.

A Bowel cancer

While malignancy must be suspected in patients with blood in the stool, this presentation is much too acute for bowel cancer, and an alternative diagnosis must be suspected.

B Infectious colitis

Infectious colitis, eg caused by Escherichia coli, is an important differential. However, this is made less likely by the age of the patient and the fact that the history points to an ischaemic cause. These cases tend to present in epidemiological clusters.

E Ulcerative colitis

The patient’s age and the lack of change in bowel habit point away from ulcerative colitis, while the vascular risk factors are much more suggestive of an ischaemic cause.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with a history of chronic diarrhoea. She also complains of bone pain.

On examination, she has a number of small blisters on the skin that are extremely itchy, as shown below over her shoulder.

Blood testing reveals low corrected calcium, raised alkaline phosphatase and low albumin levels. She is also found to be anaemic.

Which of the following represents the best treatment option for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Gluten-free diet

The history of anaemia with associated hypoalbuminaemia, hypocalcaemia and raised alkaline phosphatase all point to a malabsorptive process secondary to coeliac disease and associated osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency. There are dual peaks of incidence in the 3rd and 7th decades, and the disease is commoner in women. An OGD with duodenal or jejunal biopsy is the gold standard test, and demonstrates sub-total villous atrophy. Treatment is the commencement of a gluten-free diet, so Option D is correct. This will also help treat the skin rash from which the patient is suffering, called dermatitis herpetiformis - a chronic blistering skin rash linked to coeliac disease.

C Topical corticosteroids

Topical corticosteroids have no role in the management of this skin condition.

A Calcium and vitamin D supplementation

It would help with the low calcium but would not treat the underlying cause, so is not the best option here and is therefore incorrect.

B Intravenous albumin

This is rarely used as a treatment strategy to correct hypoalbuminaemia and would not be the best treatment in this patient.

E Oral 5-aminosalicyclic acid

The diarrhoea is caused by malabsorption from coeliac disease. 5-ASAs have no role in the management of coeliac disease and are more commonly used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis complains of diarrhoea, abdominal bloating, lethargy and weight loss.

On examination, she is pale. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations are normal. The abdomen is distended, but soft and non-tender. Bowel sounds are present. She has bilateral pitting ankle oedema. There is a proximal weakness of her arm and leg muscle. The tone, reflexes and sensation are normal. Blood pressure is 122/82, pulse is 75 and regular.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)80 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)400 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)60 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)106 fL76–98 fL
Urea2.5 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Albumin34 g/L35–55 g/L
Serum B 12123 pmol/l160–900 pmol/l
Folate22 µg/L2.0–11.0 µg/L

A barium meal is reported as showing multiple rounded jejunal diverticulae.

What other test may best help to confirm the underlying cause of her presentation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Hydrogen breath test

Bacterial overgrowth is common in patients with jejunal diverticulae, which in this case has led to malabsorption of vitamin D and calcium and muscle weakness. The bacteria can also lead to B 12 deficiency, although folate levels are not normally depleted. Bacterial overgrowth can be confirmed by the hydrogen breath test after giving lactose or glucose. Small-bowel diverticula develop secondary to intestinal dysmotility and connective tissue disorders – for example, Marfan syndrome and systemic sclerosis. Patients are usually asymptomatic, but on bacterial colonisation they develop malabsorption. Treatment is empirical, and options include metronidazole and tetracycline. If this fails, jejunal aspiration is recommended to identify the organism.

B Urea breath test

The urea breath test is used to confirm a diagnosis of H. pylori, which is associated with peptic ulceration, rather than the symptoms of malabsorption seen here.

C Schilling’s test

Schilling’s test is used to diagnose pernicious anaemia, but the jejunal diverticulae seen here drive us more towards bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption as the cause of the abnormal metabolic picture seen here, rather than pernicious anaemia.

D Thyroid function test

Stable pulse and blood pressure, coupled with normal reflexes, count against thyroid dysfunction as the underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms.

E Faecal calprotectin

Faecal calprotectin is a cytoplasmic protein from neutrophils which is almost always increased with colonic inflammation related to ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease.

questions.question:
This chest radiograph is from a 36-year-old man who presented with severe abdominal pain, having collapsed at home. He has suffered from intermittent bloody diarrhoea, which has increased in severity over the past few months.

On examination, his blood pressure is 100/70, pulse is 90 and regular. He is pyrexial at 38.4 °C. Abdomen is generally tender and rigid with guarding.

His chest X-ray is shown below:

What is the most likely underlying cause of his presentation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Ulcerative colitis

The chest radiograph shows free air under the diaphragm, which is due to perforation of an abdominal viscus. Although the heart shadow looks a little large, remember that it is an AP film. The most likely cause in this patient would be perforated large bowel secondary to ulcerative colitis, which fits well with the previous history of chronic diarrhoea.

C Acute cholecystitis

Cholecystitis presents with epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, and gall bladder perforation is very rare.

B Acute pancreatitis

Acute pancreatitis presents with vomiting and epigastric pain, rather than the clinical picture seen here.

D Ischaemic bowel

Ischaemic bowel does cause diarrhoea, although it usually occurs in patients with a history of atherosclerosis and who are considerably older than 36.

E Diverticulitis

Diverticulitis is seen in a more elderly population, although it does present with left-sided abdominal pain and diarrhoea.

questions.question:
A 78-year-old retired banker was reviewed in the Outpatients Department after a recent admission with right lower lobe pneumonia. She has had two similar episodes, managed by her GP, over the last 2 years. She has mild angina for which she is taking Aspirin and Atenolol and problems swallowing that she has never addressed before. She is otherwise fit and well. She smoked 15 cigarettes a day from the age of 20, and drinks 15 units of alcohol per week. Throughout her life, she has travelled widely in Africa and Asia.

Examination revealed no abnormal signs and her blood tests were unremarkable.

Her plain chest X-ray is shown below:

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Achalasia

A fluid level is visible behind the heart and the oesophagus is dilated. This is suggestive of chronic oesophageal

obstruction. From the scenario given and the radiological evidence supplied, achalasia is the most likely diagnosis.

Achalasia can present at any age but is rare in childhood. Dysphagia is universal, and occurs for liquids and solids relatively early in the condition. Other typical symptoms may include regurgitation, weight loss, chest and abdominal pain, as well as possible aspiration pneumonitis (which may be the presenting complaint). Achalasia is caused by degeneration of the myenteric plexus, causing failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS), and absent peristalsis in the body of the oesophagus. Diagnosis is confirmed by oesophageal manometry, but prior upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is mandatory to exclude a tumour of the cardia. Tumours of the cardia may mimic achalasia, and chronic achalasia slightly increases the risk of oesophageal carcinoma.

A number of treatment options are available. Pharmacological therapy includes calcium channel blockers

(including Nifedipine) and nitrates, but tends to be only minimally effective. Injection of botulinum toxin into the LOS also produces variable degrees of success, but has a role in affected people who are unable to tolerate more invasive therapies. The major definitive choice of therapy, however, is between endoscopic dilatation (which carries the risk of perforation), or surgical intervention (Heller’s myotomy). There is also a growing role for an alternative combined surgical and endoscopic treatment called peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM).

https://www.eurorad.org/case/14900

D Chagas’ disease

Chagas' disease can also mimic achlasia and is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi. Chagas’ disease, however, is confined to South and Central America; this woman has travelled abroad but to Africa and Asia, meaning it is unlikely to be the diagnosis here.

A Tracheo-oesophageal fistula

Outside of the paediatric setting, tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TOF) is most associated with locally advanced oesophageal carcinoma, and/or as a complication of oesophageal carcinoma treated with radiotherapy or chemotherapy. This woman does not have a diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma, making TOF unlikely.

B Carcinoma of the lung

The description of a significant smoking history and recurrent pneumonia may make candidates think of carcinoma of the lung. However, an X-ray demonstrating oesophageal obstruction/ dilatation – without evidence of a lung lesion – makes achalasia and aspiration pneumonitis more likely as a diagnosis rather than primary lung carcinoma.

E Pharyngeal pouch

A pharyngeal pouch may cause recurrent aspiration pneumonitis, but is not associated with oesophageal

obstruction.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old man with a history of COPD and severe arthritis presents to the Emergency Department of the university hospital with haematemesis. You get his old notes and find that his lung function is quite poor. He is managed with both salmeterol/fluticasone high-dose inhaler and tiotropium. Medication for his arthritis includes diclofenac. On examination, he is very unwell, with a pulse of 105/min and BP of 85/50 mmHg. You resuscitate him with fluids and 2 units of blood and arrange an endoscopy; the endoscopist visualises a large bleeding duodenal ulcer, but he is unable to reach it properly to control the bleeding via the scope. The patient has a further large haematemesis.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)89 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.4 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)130 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)189 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Electrocardiogram (ECG)Lateral ST depression

Which of the following represents the most appropriate management in this case?
options: Further fluid resuscitation and delayed endoscopy
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Angiography and selective embolization

This patient is a very poor surgical candidate, with severe COPD and an ECG which reveals signs of ischaemia, potentially related to hypovolaemia as a result of blood loss.
