In these patients, and patients at increased risk of transmission, such as surgeons, treatment is usually initiated at the time of diagnosis (rather than wait the 12 weeks from the time of suspected inoculation before starting therapy, to allow time for spontaneous viral clearance to occur).

E He requires no treatment as the probability of developing cirrhosis is less than 5%

50-85% of those individuals who acquire hepatitis C will remain chronically infected. Of those individuals who do develop chronic hepatitis C, approximately 5-30 % will develop cirrhosis over a 20- to 30-year period of time. Early treatment to eradicate HCV infection is associated with increased and sustained viral response rates, and can reduce the risk of complications such as end-stage liver disease and HCC.

A He requires a liver biopsy before consideration of treatment

Liver histology is used to evaluate the degree of fibrosis in chronic HCV infection, and to exclude other causes of liver disease. A liver biopsy is rarely indicated in the work-up of uncomplicated acute hepatitis C infection.

C He should be vaccinated to prevent spread of the virus

At present, there is no commercially available vaccine for hepatitis C.

D An endoscopy should be arranged soon to exclude oesophageal varices

The development of oesophageal varices is seen in the context of portal hypertension, usually related to cirrhosis, resulting from chronic HCV infection. This scenario concerns the management of acute hepatitis C, and hence there is nothing in this case to suggest that an endoscopy is required.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old student presents to Clinic with recurrent episodes of melaena requiring admission and blood transfusions.

He has been investigated by upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, both investigations proving negative. Between episodes of melaena he is asymptomatic.

Which of the following investigations would you organise from the Clinic?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Wireless capsule endoscopy

Meckel’s diverticulum should always be considered in a young adult presenting with intermittent malaena, despite normal OGD and colonoscopic findings.

Wireless capsule endoscopy is increasingly used for the work-up of gastrointestinal bleeding of uncertain origin, and case reports have demonstrated its ability to identify Meckel’s diverticulum. The use of capsule endoscopy in diagnosis will undoubtedly grow, but not all centres yet have easy access to this service and it is not offered as an option for the above case.

Alternatively, In the stable outpatient setting, a Meckel’s scan can be useful in investigating the presence of gastrointestinal diverticula containing ectopic gastric mucosa.

E Octreotide scan

The patient’s symptoms of intermittent, significant, gastrointestinal bleeding are not the typical presentation of a neuroendocrine tumour, and therefore an octreotide scan is not warranted.

A Barium swallow

A repeat oesophago-gastroduodenoscopy (OGD) may be indicated, as lesions within reach of a standard upper

gastrointestinal endoscope may be missed for a variety of reasons. However, a barium swallow would not be of benefit in the investigation of the upper gastrointestinal tract for a cause of bleeding not previously seen on OGD.

B Mesenteric angiogram

The patient’s blood loss is severe and occurs intermittently. A mesenteric angiogram is most effective during active blood loss (usually >1 ml/min) and, as such, is not an appropriate investigation for use in the stable outpatient setting.

D Barium enema

A repeat colonoscopy may be indicated, as proximal colonic lesions may be missed for a variety of reasons.

However, a barium enema does not have a role in the investigation of suspected small bowel bleeding in a patient with a normal colonoscopy.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is seen in clinic with pain in his wrists and knees. He has recently found it difficult walking because of pain mainly in his right knee. He also tells you that he has been feeling more tired recently, is feeling thirsty all the time and has abdominal pain which is mainly in the RUQ and worst in the evenings.

He smokes 20 cigarettes/day, drinks half a bottle of wine with his evening meal and has recently returned from a safari in Mozambique. He took precautions by only drinking boiled water and took anti-malarial medication.

He looks tanned but tired. His wrist joints and knees are tender and his right knee is swollen. His examination is otherwise unremarkable. You aspirate his right knee and the report is of crystals, which exhibit positive birefringence.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Sodium (Na⁺)134 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.1 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.5 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)95 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)0.68 mu/l0.4 - 5.0 mu/l
Free Thryoxin (FT4)8.5 pmol/l10.0 - 26.0 pmol/l
Glucose13.1 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)216 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)123 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Bilirubin16 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Transferrin saturation55%

Of the options given, which is most useful in making the diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Genetic screening

This patient has hereditary haemochromatosis (HHC), which usually presents in the fourth or fifth decade. It manifests earlier in men because women have regular iron loss through their periods. The C282Y mutation of the haemochromatosis, HFE gene on chromosome 6p is homozygous in 1/300 of the UK population, but iron overload manifests in only a few. Blood loss, iron intake and alcohol have a role to play. Iron is deposited in the anterior pituitary (loss of libido, tiredness), skin (pigmentation), heart (cardiac failure/dysrhythmia), joints (mainly metacarpal (MCP)/wrist/knee – with chondrocalcinosis and pseudo-gout), maturity-onset diabetes mellitus and liver failure. Cirrhosis develops and the patient may present with hepatocellular carcinoma, which is often metastatic before symptoms develop. Genetic testing is widely available and liver biopsy is helpful. Serum ferritin is pathologically elevated in these patients; however, it can be acutely elevated in acute inflammatory states. HHC should be diagnosed before organ damage, as the prognosis is poor once the patient has cirrhosis. Treatment is regular phlebotomy. Cardiac and liver damage may improve with treatment, but joint pain and diabetes often remain. Screening first-degree relatives is crucial.

A Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pituitary

Whilst there may be deposition in the pituitary of iron, this is unlikely to be seen on MRI and would therefore not help diagnosis.

B Liver biopsy

A liver biopsy in haemachromatosis would demonstrate iron load and be able to assess disease severity.

However, genetic testing can be sufficient and non-invasive in HHC and establish the specific mutation which has caused the disease, and is therefore a better option.

C Alpha-fetoprotein

AFP is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, metastatic cancer in the liver and some germ cell tumours. It is a useful test to monitor for liver cancer in patients with established cirrhosis of the liver, but would not help in diagnosing haemachromatosis.

D Rheumatoid factor

Rheumatoid factor is unlikely to be positive in haemachromatosis. Had the patient had symmetrical small joint polyarthritis associated with early morning joint stiffness, then this would be a far more appropriate answer, but the presence of liver abnormalities and symptoms makes it unlikely to be diagnostic. 33017

questions.question:
A 64-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and distension and a 2-day history of persistent vomiting. He has had intermittent abdominal pain for the last 5 weeks and diarrhoea for 3 days prior to the onset of vomiting. He has not passed a bowel motion since.

His past medical history includes hypertension and coeliac disease, from which he has been asymptomatic for the past 10 years although he admits to being poorly compliant with his diet. He has lost 4 kg in weight over the past 5 months.

Physical examination shows a distended abdomen. Bowel sounds are tinkling in nature.

What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Small bowel lymphoma

Coeliac disease is a common and underdiagnosed condition, which may present at any age. It is a hypersensitivity to gluten found in wheat, rye and barley. The gliadin fraction of the protein provokes an inflammatory response causing subtotal or total villous atrophy of the small bowel, resulting in malabsorption. It classically presents with a history of diarrhoea, weight loss, lethargy and anaemia (folate, B 12 or iron- deficient). It is associated with an increased risk of developing small bowel lymphoma, which thankfully only occurs in a very small proportion of coeliac patients. It is the rapid deterioration seen here, with weight loss, which points us towards malignant transformation of the coeliac to small bowel lymphoma.

E Small bowel carcinoma

The history of coeliac disease makes small bowel lymphoma a more likely cause than carcinoma of the bowel, although carcinoma of the small bowel can also cause weight loss and small bowel obstruction.

A Adhesions

There is no previous history of bowel surgery or abdominal surgery to suggest that adhesions may be present to cause small bowel obstruction.

B Carcinoma of the colon

The history of coeliac disease makes small bowel lymphoma a more likely cause than carcinoma of the bowel, especially in the absence of lower GI symptoms before the presentation with acute abdomen.

C Meckel’s diverticulum

Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. It results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct leading to the formation of a true diverticulum of the small intestine. Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum, containing all layers of the small bowel wall. It arises from the anti- mesenteric surface of the middle-to-distal ileum. The diverticulum represents a persistent remnant of the omphalo-mesenteric duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac in the foetus. Meckel's diverticula are uncommon and often clinically silent, particularly in the adult. Asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum may be discovered during abdominal exploration for the evaluation of unrelated pathology. Less commonly, it is found incidentally on diagnostic imaging. When symptomatic, Meckel's diverticulum may present with abdominal pain or symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction. In this scenario, the past medical history of coeliac disease makes Meckel’s diverticulum a less likely diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old woman, who works as an accountant, presents to her general practitioner (GP) with fatigue. She has also noticed troublesome itching over the past few months, which is worse at night and in hot weather. She is teetotal.

Examination reveals jaundice, evidence of excoriation, telangiectasia and mild ascites. Alkaline phosphatase is elevated at 242 IU/L.

Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be positive in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Anti-mitochondrial antibodies

Given this clinical picture, the most likely diagnosis is primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), and AMAs are found in 95% of patients with the condition. Onset typically occurs between the ages of 30 and 65 years, the condition is much more common in women, and it may be asymptomatic or present most commonly with tiredness and itching. Ursodeoxycholic acid improves bilirubin and symptoms of jaundice, but may mask the need for transplantation. A limited number of studies have shown positive effects on survival although there is still some debate in this area. Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment and there is 85–90% post-transplant survival at 1 year. Overall, survival from time of diagnosis with PBC is put at between 7 and 16 years.

E Anti-nuclear antibodies

Anti-nuclear antibodies are less specific indicators of autoimmune disease, most likely to be associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.

A Anti-thyroid antibody

Anti-thyroid antibodies are found in Grave’s disease and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, a small percentage of patients with thyroid carcinoma, and approximately 3% of normal individuals.

B Anti-endomysial antibody

Anti-endomysial antibodies are found in association with coeliac disease which is not suggested by the symptoms seen here. It is usually associated with weight loss and diarrhoea.

C Anti-smooth muscle antibody

Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis, not with PBC. In autoimmune hepatitis, a hepatocellular picture of liver function test abnormalities would be expected.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department complaining of worsening nausea and vomiting, general malaise and anorexia. She is 36 weeks’ pregnant with her first child.

On examination, there is pain in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant of the abdomen on palpation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)420 U/L7–55 U/L
Bilirubin85 µmol/L1–22 µmol/L
Albumin27 g/L35–55 g/L Prothrombin time (PT) and Activated partial thromboplastin time Prolonged (APTT)
Haemoglobin (Hb)101 g/L135–175 g/L 13.2 ×
White cell count (WCC)4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L10 9/l
Platelets (PLT)75 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

This condition presents with nausea and vomiting and pain in the epigastrium or right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Mean gestational age at presentation is 37 weeks, although it may occur in the 28–42-week range. Abnormal investigations include hypoglycaemia, raised ammonia levels, elevated aminotransferase levels, elevated white cell count, low albumin and disseminated intravascular coagulation in up to 75% of cases. Ultrasound is the best imaging modality and allows the exclusion of other conditions such as cholecystitis. Spontaneous resolution of the condition usually follows delivery. Stabilisation on the intensive therapy unit (ITU) may be required first, and this may involve the use of intravenous (IV) fluids and glucose, correction of coagulopathy with fresh-frozen plasma, and reduction of exogenous ammonia intake through protein restriction or dietary laxatives to speed evacuation of nitrogenous wastes.

A Hepatitis A

Hepatitis A can be contracted by faecal–oral spread or consumption of shellfish. It is present in Africa and South America and causes fever, malaise, anorexia and nausea, followed by jaundice. The absence of a travel history and fever, as well as a pro-dromal period, makes this unlikely.

B Cholecystitis

Acute cholecystits follows impaction of the neck of the gall bladder. This causes right upper quadrant pain, fever, vomiting and peritonism locally. It is also associated with Murphy’s sign and there may be a mass on palpation. The absence of fever and RUQ pain, as opposed to tenderness, makes this unlikely.

C Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

This condition is caused by a bile acid transporter defect and usually manifests in the last trimester. It is not associated with significant constitutional symptoms for the mother, although the risk of stillbirth and post- partum haemorrhage is slightly increased. Milder episodes may have occurred earlier in life associated with hormonal contraception, and it recurs in subsequent pregnancies. Prothrombin time may be prolonged in any cholestatic process due to deficiency of vitamin K. The presence of constitutional symptoms makes this diagnosis less likely.

E Hyperemesis gravidarum

Hyperemesis gravidarum is intractable vomiting associated with weight loss, dehydration and disruption of electrolytes. It is more common in the first trimester and, if the patient is ketotic or has severe derangement of electrolytes, they will need hospitalisation. The presence of abnormal liver function tests, that the patient is at 37 weeks and the presence of abdominal pain make this less likely.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage. He admits to vomiting on multiple occasions over the last 12 hours and states that he vomited 250 ml of blood on the last occasion. He is an alcoholic who has been previously treated for hepatitis C and has some evidence of cirrhosis, although he is poorly compliant with medications prescribed by his hepatologist. On examination, his blood pressure is 85/60 mmHg and pulse 95 bpm and regular. He is tender in the epigastrium. 6 units of blood are cross matched initially.

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)89 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)55 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)142 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)82 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urea15.7 mmol/L2.5–7.8 mmol/L

Which of the following is the most important intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B IV terlipressin

This patient has a likely variceal haemorrhage, given his previous evidence of cirrhosis and ongoing alcohol consumption, with poor medication compliance. Since 2012, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines have recommended terlipressin in this situation, although a 2016 meta-analysis suggested there may be little difference between outcomes when terlipressin is used, compared to somatostatin or octreotide. Use of terlipressin is recommended until haemostasis is achieved or for a maximum of five days.

C IV fresh frozen plasma (FFP)

FFP may be required for massive variceal haemorrhage, and this patient’s clotting status should be assessed. In this situation, however, it is the use of terlipressin, a vasopressin analogue, that has been shown to have the biggest effect on outcomes.

A Intravenous (IV) pantoprazole

Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) used acutely (both in the oral and IV forms) are only recommended for the treatment of peptic ulcer disease. They have no impact on outcomes when used acutely in the management of variceal haemorrhage.

D IV cryoprecipitate

IV cryoprecipitate is used to reverse anticoagulation due to warfarin excess. It does not have a role in the acute treatment of variceal haemorrhage, unless there is concomitant use of vitamin K antagonists.

E Platelet transfusion

Although this patient is thrombocytopenic, there is limited evidence to support effectiveness of platelet transfusion in reducing haemorrhage, unless the platelet count is below 20 ×10⁹/L.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old woman is reviewed in the Psychiatric Clinic for monitoring of her response to lithium therapy. She has a history of previous alcoholism, although she is now alcohol free, and has begun lithium therapy for bipolar disease some 6 months earlier.

Physical examination in the clinic is unremarkable.

You are concerned about the possibility of this leading to hepatic dysfunction.

Which of the following is the most sensitive measure for lithium related hepatotoxicity?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)

ALT may elevated in patients taking lithium may be due to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease caused by weight gain that occurs in at least one-quarter of treated patients.

D Bilirubin

Acute liver injury with hyperbilirubinaemia is not usually associated with lithium use.

A Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)

AST is most useful in monitoring for alcoholic liver disease, where a ratio of AST:ALT >2 is suggestive of alcoholic liver disease.

C Alkaline phosphatase

Elevation in transaminases and gamma GT representing hepatocellular dysfunction, rather than raised alkaline phosphatase, is more likely to be seen.

E Gamma GT

Liver test abnormalities (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/n/livertox/glossary/def-item/glossary.liver-test- abnormalities/) have been reported to occur in a small proportion of patients on long term therapy with lithium. ALT may elevated in patients taking lithium may be due to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease caused by weight gain that occurs in at least one-quarter of treated patients

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic. She is 30 weeks pregnant and has a previous history of Crohn’s disease. However, this was quiescent before becoming pregnant and she discontinued her treatment 18 months ago. She was previously managed with sulfasalazine. She now complains of severe diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Abdominal examination is consistent with a 30-week pregnancy, and it is difficult to assess for specific tenderness, which may be related to active Crohn’s disease.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)190 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)47 mm/hour< 10 mm/hour
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

She is treated with oral steroids. However, after seven days there is no clinical improvement.

Which of the following would be the next most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Infliximab

Infliximab is an appropriate second-line therapy in pregnant patients who have failed to achieve a response to corticosteroids. Infliximab is thought to be low risk in pregnancy, although it does cross the placenta. Patients on maintenance infliximab therapy should stop treatment by week 26 of gestation. In patients who require treatment in the last trimester, live vaccines should be avoided in the newborn for the first six months.

A Azathioprine

Recent meta-analyses have shown that thiopurines, such as azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, are not associated with an increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes when compared with inflammatory bowel disease patients on no treatment. As such, patients should remain on thiopurines during pregnancy; better maternal and fetal outcomes are strongly associated with good disease control during pregnancy. However, patients should not be started in azathioprine during pregnancy due to the long delay of action and unpredictable risk of developing medullary suppression or pancreatitis.

C Metronidazole

There is no role for induction of an acute flare. Although metronidazole can be used safely in pregnancy, its use in acute Crohn’s disease tends to be limited to patients with infective complications such as abscess formation, perianal disease and acute pouchitis.

D Methotrexate

Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy due to its teratogenicity, particularly in the first trimester. For patients trying to conceive, there is an approximately 6-week washout period.

E Sulfasalazine

This patient has an acute flare of Crohn’s disease and needs induction of remission. Sulfasalazine has not been shown to be efficacious in inducing remission in an acute flare, and despite the fact she was previously taking this, its role as maintenance therapy in Crohn’s disease is no longer recommended.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man is being investigated for recurrent gastric and duodenal ulceration diagnosed at endoscopy. He has suffered from bouts of abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhoea, although his weight is stable. On examination, his abdomen is soft and there is no organomegaly.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)310 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)92 fL76–98 fL
Urea and electrolytesNormal
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)45 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)128 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)38 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin17 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Basal acid secretion20 mEq/h1–5 mEq/h
Fasting gastrin200 pg/ml< 100 pg/ml
Basal gastrin200 pg/ml
Post-secretin gastrin500 pg/ml

Which of the following are responsible for the elevated gastrin levels?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Gastrinoma

All of the above conditions are associated with hypergastrinaemia. Gastrinoma is the correct answer and can confidently be diagnosed in patients with gastrin levels > 1000 pg/ml and basal acid output > 15 mEq/l. The secretin test can be used to differentiate low-output gastrinomas from other causes of hypergastrinaemia – this will only be positive (rise in gastrin of > 200 pg/ml 10 min after secretin injection) in the presence of a gastrinoma.

A Omeprazole therapy

Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy with omeprazole is associated with hypergastrinaemia but low acid secretion, so is therefore an incorrect option.

B Pernicious anaemia

Loss of normal gastric mucosa, such as in pernicious anaemia, where there is gastric atrophy results in an increase in gastrin levels, but acid secretion levels would be low, so this option is incorrect.

D H. pylori infection

This has been associated with high basal acid secretion and hypergastrinaemia. G-cell hyperplasia is an increase in the number of gastrin-producing cells in the normal gastric mucosa and is associated with H. pylori, and is thought to account for the raised gastrin levels seen in H. pylori infection.

E Carcinoma of the stomach

This condition, in which normal gastric mucosa is replaced with cancerous cells, will lead to an increase in gastrin levels, but again one would not expect to see high levels of acid secretion, and secretin usually inhibits gastrin production. Therefore this option is incorrect.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old girl is referred by her general practitioner (GP) with weight loss and vomiting. During the consultation, it becomes apparent that she has an altered body image.

Which of the following would best assess her nutritional status?
options: Mid-arm muscle circumference and skin-fold thickness
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Mid-arm muscle circumference and skin-fold thickness

Anthropometry allows for an assessment of body composition, and a number of anthropometric measurements can be used.

E Height (m)/weight (kg)

The body mass index (BMI) can be used to stratify patients, but is calculated by weight/(height) 2 rather than height/weight. The BMI measurement takes into account neither the difference between fat and non-fat mass, such as bone and muscle, nor the changes in body composition that occur with age.

A Serum albumin

The serum albumin level can fall in conditions such as sepsis and liver disease, and should therefore not be considered a good indicator of nutritional status.

B FSH:oestrogen ratio

Amenorrhoea is associated with anorexia nervosa, but the FSH:oestrogen ratio is not routinely used to assess nutrition.

C Mid-thigh:hip ratio

The waist:hip ratio is a useful measure in the context of central obesity, but the mid-thigh:hip ratio is a fictitious measurement.

questions.question:
You are asked to see a 72-year-old woman who is under the care of the orthopaedic surgeons, following an elective left total hip replacement. She has been treated with codeine for pain relief over the last six days. For the past 24 hours, she has complained of left iliac fossa cramping pain and watery diarrhoea. Blood pressure is 155/92 mmHg, and pulse 82 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination reveals palpable faeces on the left side of the abdomen, and per rectum examination reveals an empty rectum. She has active bowel sounds.

Investigations;

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)112 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)178 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potasium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)18 mg/L0–10 mg/L

Abdominal X-ray: Paucity of bowel gas, left-sided faecal loading.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Overflow diarrhoea

This patient has normal inflammatory markers and a normal white cell count. This, coupled with a history of codeine use and initial constipation, now followed by profuse diarrhoea and faecal loading on the X-ray, fits best with overflow diarrhoea as the underlying diagnosis. The most appropriate management is use of an oral stool softener such as sodium docusate. A switch away from a severely constipating opiate, such as codeine, to an option with less gastrointestinal liability, such as meptazinol, or an attempt to reduce the total opiate dose and switch to other medications such as regular paracetamol would be indicated.

C Ischaemic colitis

Ischaemic colitis is usually associated with severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea and significant metabolic derangement, including raised lactate/metabolic acidosis.

A Pseudomembranous colitis

Pseudomembranous colitis is expected to be associated with severe diarrhoea, often with blood and mucus and other evidence of compromise such as pre-renal impairment. Carriage of Clostridium difficile, the causative organism can spread within institutions, although frank diarrhoea normally follows exposure to antibiotics.

B Diverticulitis

Diverticulitis is associated with left-sided abdominal pain and diarrhoea, with evidence of systemic inflammation, usually with raised CRP and white cell count.

E Ulcerative colitis

Ulcerative colitis would be unusual to present for the first time at the age of 72. Elevation of white cell count and/or inflammatory markers would be expected.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department for review. She has been feeling unwell and off her food over the past few days and is concerned because she has become jaundiced. There is particular concern as she is 26 weeks pregnant. This is her third episode of jaundice over the past five to six years. Although her diet is rich in fruit and vegetables, she continues to drink 4–5 glasses of wine per week. On examination, her blood pressure is 105/60 mmHg and her pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 24 kg/m 2. She has jaundiced sclerae. Abdominal examination reveals an enlarged uterus, consistent with her current stage of pregnancy.

Investigations:

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)119 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.9 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)191 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine88 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Glucose7.8 mmol/L4.0–7.0 mmol/L
Bilirubin80 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Albumin42 g/L35–55 g/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)110 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)38 IU/L5–30 IU/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.01.1

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Gilbert’s syndrome

Given this presentation represents a third episode of jaundice over the past few years, an acute episode (eg viral hepatitis or cholestasis of pregnancy) is unlikely. The liver function test picture with an isolated rise in bilirubin is very consistent with Gilbert syndrome where periods of jaundice often follow an intercurrent illness. No treatment is required in this case; where fasting has occurred, encouraging the patient to eat may lead to a more rapid resolution of symptoms.

A Cholestasis of pregnancy

The isolated hyperbilirubinaemia in this case makes the diagnosis of cholestasis of pregnancy unlikely. In that scenario, you would expect to see an elevated ALP.

C Hypercaroteinaemia

Hypercarotenaemia is rare where skin colouring from carotene is confused with jaundice.

D Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis

The isolated hyperbilirubinaemia in this case makes the diagnosis of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis unlikely. In that scenario, you would expect to see an elevated ALT.

E Viral hepatitis

The recurrent nature of this patient’s presentation makes a viral hepatitis unlikely. Also, the isolated hyperbilirubinaemia is not associated with hepatitis. You would expect to see deranged ALT levels, coupled with abnormal bilirubin levels, in viral hepatitis. It would be prudent in this case to screen the patient for viral hepatitis as there is a risk for transmission to the fetus during delivery if the mother has hepatitis.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old has returned from a trip to Tunisia approximately one week ago. She now has symptoms of a gastrointestinal (GI) upset and attends the Emergency Department. She is most concerned because she has become jaundiced and has increasing dull abdominal pain. There is a history of smoking heroin and using cocaine on two occasions as a student, although she denies illicit drug use at other times. Prior to her trip, she received a vaccination against hepatitis A.

On examination, her blood pressure is 110/82 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. Her temperature is 37.9 °C. Abdominal palpation reveals tenderness in the right upper quadrant.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.3 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)1821 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)203 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Albumin35 g/L35–55 g/L
Prothrombin time (PT)13.2 s10.6–14.9

Infection with which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Hepatitis E

The distribution of cases of hepatitis E is similar to that of hepatitis A, including North Africa; hence, the trip to North Africa on holiday is a significant risk factor for the disease. Transmission is via faecal-oral route and the incubation period of the disease is between 15 and 60 days. It generally results in an acute self-limiting hepatitis with symptoms lasting between one and two weeks, although there are increased risks of fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy and patients who are immunocompromised.

C Hepatitis B

Given that she has denied high risk factors related to hepatitis B, it would be unlikely that this could be attributed to hepatitis B. Clearly, one would test for all causes of viral hepatitis.

A Epstein–Barr virus

Epstein–Barr virus is commonly associated with pharyngitis rather than GI upset and therefore would be unlikely to be the cause.

B Hepatitis A

Hepatitis A, although has a similar transmission mode and distribution of cases as Hepatitis E, is unlikely here due to the vaccination history.

D Hepatitis C

Given that she has denied high risk factors it would be less likely that the acute hepatitis is due to hepatitis C. Clearly, one would test for all causes of viral hepatitis.

questions.question:
A 31-year-old woman has been diagnosed with seronegative arthritis. She has a long history of fatigue, malaise and joint pains. She now attends for review because of the development of tremors and ataxia. Previous blood tests include elevated transaminases, serum immunoglobulin G (IgG), positive antinuclear antibody and positive anti-smooth muscle antibody. Anti-LKM antibodies are negative. Examination reveals stigmata of chronic liver disease and a gold-yellow ring at the periphery of the iris.

Which of the following additional blood tests would fit best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Low serum caeruloplasmin

This patient has a picture of chronic active hepatitis, with fatigue, arthralgia and abnormal autoimmune screen, coupled with stigmata of chronic liver disease and raised transaminases. The additional new neurological symptoms point to the possibility of Wilson’s disease, characterised by low serum caeruloplasmin, increased serum “free” copper, raised urinary copper excretion, low serum uric acid and phosphate and haematuria. Wilson’s disease is caused by defective metabolism of dietary copper and its incorporation into caeruloplasmin, leading to decreased biliary copper excretion. Penicillamine in a dose range 0.75–1.5 g/day is standard maintenance copper chelator therapy for Wilson’s disease. The starting dose is 1.5-2g daily in divided doses. Urea and electrolytes and urine analysis should be frequently undertaken. Zinc may also be employed at a standard dose of 50 mg per os tds as it inhibits intestinal absorption of copper. Prognosis for Wilson’s disease is generally good with early chelator treatment.

D Raised serum uric acid

Uric acid is actually low in patients suffering from Wilson’s disease.

A Low serum “free” copper

Due to defective incorporation of copper into caeruloplasmin, serum free copper is actually increased.

B Raised serum caeruloplasmin

Low serum caeruloplasmin is a hallmark of Wilson’s disease, although in patients with significant hepatic inflammation, caeruloplasmin may be falsely increased.

E Raised serum phosphate

Wilson’s may present with features of renal tubular disease, leading to increased phosphate excretion. Hence normal or low phosphate, rather than increased phosphate levels are usually seen in association with the disease. 33059

questions.question:
A 65-year-old builder presents with a 4-week history of increasing abdominal swelling. There has been one admission with acute pancreatitis a few years ago and he reports a similar episode of severe vomiting and epigastric pain after a curry and beers a few weeks earlier.

He has a history of hypertension and normally takes a ß-blocker. He smokes 30 cigarettes per day and drinks 28 units of alcohol per week. His abdomen is soft and non-tender with shifting dullness. Ultrasound scan of his abdomen shows large amount of ascites.

A diagnostic ascitic tap reveals the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Polymorphic neutrophil count30 cells/mm 3
Fluid amylase1800 IU/L< 40 IU/L
Total protein30 g/L10–20 g/L
Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG)8.0 g/L
Glucose concentration2.0 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)1 ng/ml< 5ng/ml

Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of his ascites?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Pancreatitis

This question tests knowledge on causes of ascites, traditionally ascites was divided into transudates and exudates. This case would have thus been classified as an exudate (protein content 30 g/L). Causes of transudate ascites are cirrhosis and portal hypertension, cardiac failure, Budd–Chiari syndrome, myxodema. Causes of an exudate ascites include hepatic or peritoneal malignancy, intra-abdominal tuberculosis, and pancreatitis. However the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) has now largely replaced this concept and is the best single test for classifying ascites into portal hypertensive (SAAG > 11 g/L) and non–portal hypertensive (SAAG < 11 g/L) causes. (N.B. this may also be expressed in g/dl in which case the cut-off is 1.1 g/dl). Calculated by subtracting the ascitic fluid albumin value from the serum albumin value, it correlates directly with portal pressure. The specimens should be obtained relatively simultaneously. The accuracy of the SAAG results is approximately 97% in classifying ascites. The terms high-albumin gradient and low-albumin gradient should replace the terms transudative and exudative in the description of ascites. An increased ascitic amylase concentration generally of the order of 2000 IU/L, is typical of pancreatic ascites. The ascitic total white cell count of > 500/µl or neutrophil count of > 250/µl is diagnostic of bacterial peritonitis.

E Nephrotic syndrome

Nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and oedema) has many causes, including primary kidney diseases such as minimal-change nephropathy, focal glomerulosclerosis, and membranous nephropathy. Nephrotic syndrome can also result from systemic diseases that affect other organs in addition to the kidneys, such as diabetes, amyloidosis, and lupus erythematosus. In patients with nephrotic ascites, usually, the SAAG is < 11 g/L, but with a total protein in the ascites of < 25 g/L.

A Congestive cardiac failure

Congestive cardiac failure would usually cause a transudative ascities (with a SAAG > 11). The biochemistry from this case suggests an exudative (non-portal hypertensive) cause.

C Budd–Chiari syndrome

Budd-Chiari syndrome (Option C) is incorrect. Budd-Chiari syndrome usually presents as a classical trial of abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and ascites, and is caused by occlusion of the hepatic vein. The ascites in Budd- Chiari syndrome is a transudate (with a SAAG > 11) via portal hypertension. The biochemistry from this case suggests an exudative cause.

D Alcoholic cirrhosis

Alcoholic (Option D) is incorrect. The ascites in the context of cirrhosis is a transudate (with a SAAG > 11), as a result of portal hypertension. The biochemistry from this case suggests an exudative cause.

questions.question:
You review a 27-year-old man who has recently moved house and is referred by his GP for investigation of jaundice. His blood results reveal raised conjugated bilirubin with normal haptoglobins. A liver biopsy is performed, which reveals a number of dark granules within the hepatocytes.

What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Dubin–Johnson syndrome

Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a rare cause of isolated conjugated bilirubinaemia. This is due to mutations in the MRP2 transporter gene, responsible for transport of bilirubin and a number of other compounds. It is an autosomal recessive disorder; the granules seen in the liver histology of this patient are thought to arise from melanin deposition.

E Haemolytic anaemia

This patient’s haptoglobulin level is normal, and this would be expected to be low in intravascular hemolysis, as the free haemoglobin released into circulation binds with haptoglobin to form a complex, so circulating levels of free haptoglobulin become lower.

B Crigler–Najjar syndrome

This rare disorder causes an unconjugated, not a conjugated, bilirubinaemia. A gene mutation results in the defective production or absence of the enzyme glucuronosyl transferase in the liver – a key enzyme involved in the conjugation of bilirubin.

C Rotor syndrome

Although this rare benign disorder can cause a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, it is associated with normal liver histology.

D Gilbert syndrome

This condition is associated with an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with unintentional weight loss, frequent watery diarrhoea and fatigue. He recently underwent extensive bowel resection following mesenteric ischaemia, leaving him with approximately 100 cm of the small intestine. Despite adherence to dietary modifications and supplementation, he continues to experience malabsorption and electrolyte imbalances. Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)105 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)280 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)130 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Magnesium (Mg 2+)0.5 mmol/L0.7–1.0 mmol/L

What is the primary physiological mechanism leading to malabsorption in this patient?
options: Loss of gastric intrinsic factor production
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Insufficient small intestinal surface area

Short bowel syndrome (SBS) results from reduced intestinal surface area after extensive resection, leading to impaired nutrient and fluid absorption. This reduced absorptive capacity explains the malabsorption and electrolyte imbalances.

B Reduced pancreatic enzyme secretion

Pancreatic enzyme insufficiency can lead to malabsorption, but it is typically associated with pancreatic disease rather than with bowel resection. This patient’s pancreatic function is not mentioned as impaired.

A Decreased bile salt reabsorption

Decreased bile salt reabsorption occurs in patients with resection of the terminal ileum, leading to fat malabsorption. While this may contribute, the primary issue in SBS is reduced absorptive surface area along the small intestine.

D Decreased chylomicron formation

Decreased chylomicron formation is related to fat absorption in the intestine. However, the primary issue in SBS is a reduced absorptive surface area affecting multiple nutrients, not just fat.

E Loss of gastric intrinsic factor production

Intrinsic factor is required for vitamin B₁₂ absorption, but this patient’s primary symptoms suggest malabsorption of multiple nutrients. Intrinsic factor production is unrelated to the small intestine length. 74430

questions.question:
A 76-year-old woman is found to have abnormal blood results during a pre-operative assessment for hip replacement. She suffers from severe arthritis, hypercholesterolaemia, complex partial epilepsy and hypertension. She was treated for cystitis by her general practitioner (GP) 3 weeks ago. She is teetotal and a non-smoker. Blood test results are as below:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Bilirubin25 µmol/L1.7 - 20.5 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)174 U/L3 - 35 U/L
Aspartate aminotransferase(AST)180 U/L10 - 40 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)160 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Hepatitis and autoimmune serologyNegative
Ferritin89 µg/L11 - 307 µg/L (females)
Ultrasound scanNormal

Which of the drugs listed below would be most likely to account for her deranged liver function tests?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Simvastatin

The incidental discovery of asymptomatic patients with mild to moderate increases in serum transaminase concentrations represents a common clinical problem. Hydroxymethyl glutaryl co-enzyme A reductase inhibitors (statins), are well recognised to cause deranged liver function tests, classically causing a hepatocellular pattern of derangement, although other biochemical patterns of injury are possible. Over-the- counter medications and herbal remedies may also be associated. If viral, autoimmune and metabolic causes are excluded, patients should be advised to discontinue medications that may be the cause.

B Carbamazepine

Carbamazepine can be associated with a drug-induced liver injury, but more classically causes a cholestatic pattern of derangement in liver function tests, although other biochemical patterns of injury are possible. The pattern of liver injury in this case is predominantly hepatocellular, and hence Carbamazepine is not the best answer.

A Co-amoxiclav

Amoxycillin-clavulanic acid (co-amoxiclav) can be responsible for a drug-induced liver injury, but this classically causes a cholestatic pattern of derangement in liver function tests, although other biochemical patterns of injury are possible. The pattern of liver injury in this case is predominantly hepatocellular, and hence co-amoxiclav is not the best answer.

D Bendrofluazide

Although any drug can theoretically result in a drug-induced liver injury, only rare instances of clinically apparent liver injury have been linked to thiazide diuretics.

E Codeine phosphate

Codeine phosphate has not been convincingly shown to cause liver injury. Clinicians should be wary of patients taking co-codamol analgesia, as the paracetamol component puts patients at risk of liver injury if the drug is taken over and above the recommended dosage. 71300

questions.question:
A 25-year-old art student is brought into the casualty department by her flatmates following one cupful of haematemesis. She has been vomiting earlier that day after an alcohol binge over the weekend. There is no past medical problem and she is on the oral contraceptive pill. She drinks 15 units of alcohol per week, mainly during the weekends. Her mother suffers from primary biliary cholangitis. On examination, her heart rate is 82/minute and her blood pressure is 124/70 mmHg. There is mild epigastric discomfort. The rest of the examination is normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)120 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)192 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean cell volume (MCV)85 fL76–98 fL
International normalised ratio (INR)1.1< 1.1
Sodium (Na⁺)133 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.0 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)61 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin14 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)24 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)125 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)40 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin38 g/L35–55 g/L Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy shows no source of active bleeding, although a small linear tear is identified

in the mucosal surface. There is no evidence of blood in the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum.

What is the most appropriate step of management?
options: Discharge home with General Practitioner follow-up
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Discharge home with General Practitioner follow-up

This is a case of Mallory–Weiss tear, which is a longitudinal mucosa tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction as a consequence of forced retching or vomiting. This is produced by a sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure. It is a common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in the young, classically after an alcohol binge, and the linear tear can be seen on endoscopy. Bleeding is usually mild and transitory; therefore, management is largely conservative and patients do not require further specialist follow-up.

B Liver ultrasound

There are no clinical signs of chronic liver disease, and liver function tests are normal. Further imaging of the liver is not indicated.

A Check autoantibody screen

There are no clinical signs of chronic liver disease, and liver function tests are normal. The endoscopic findings are not suggestive of a variceal bleed, which would prompt the clinician to search for an underlying cause of cirrhosis.

C Prescribe non-selective beta blocker

Non-selective beta blockade has proven benefit in the prophylaxis of variceal bleeding. There is no role for beta blockade in the management of a Mallory-Weiss tear.

D Repeat endoscopy in 2 weeks

Provided the patient remains well, with no further bleeding, a simple Mallory-Weiss tear prompted by an obvious trigger event (vomiting after an alcohol binge) does not require a repeat endoscopy.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman presents to the clinic feeling very depressed about weight gain that has occurred over the past two to three years. This is against a background of caring for three young school-age children.

She takes no medication of note, and has no significant past medical history.

On examination, her BP is 144/82 mmHg and her BMI is 31. A fasting glucose is measured at 6.2 mmol/L.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Group-based dietary intervention

Group weight loss programmes have been shown to be superior to individual effort with respect to dieting. As such, WeightWatchers, Slimming World and other such clubs are recommended to patients for initial weight management.

A Metformin

Metformin causes very modest weight loss and in this context (impaired fasting glucose), diet and exercise are superior to pharmacological intervention.

B Liraglutide

Liraglutide 3 mg is licensed for weight loss, but in this case with a BMI of 31, a period of attempted diet and exercise alone is advised.

C Gastric banding

Gastric banding is recommended for patients with morbid obesity and who are unable to lose weight by other means, and have significant co-existing medical complications of obesity.

E Prescribed exercise

Although prescribed exercise will significantly impact on cardiovascular fitness, it has little impact on weight control.

questions.question:
A patient with known ulcerative colitis presents with an exacerbation. He has eight bloody motions per day. He has lost 3 kg of weight in one week. He has had a temperature of 38 °C, a heart rate of 100 bpm and blood pressure of 100 mmHg systolic for three consecutive days. His abdomen is soft and he has active bowel sounds, with significant tenderness, particularly on the left-hand side. Abdominal X-ray reveals no evidence of colonic dilatation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Albumin33 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.0 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea3 mmol/L2.5–6.7 mmol/L
Creatinine75 mmol/L70–150 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)57 mg/L< 3 mg/L He is started on intravenous (IV) hydrocortisone 100 mg three times a day and IV fluid resuscitation. He is reviewed daily and on day three of his admission, he reports that he is still passing seven motions per day, which are less bloody, but he still has abdominal pain. Observations reveal a temperature of 37.5 °C, a heart rate of 95 bpm and blood pressure of 100/65 mmHg. Abdominal examination reveals left-sided tenderness, with active bowel sounds. Repeat blood tests reveal the following:
InvestigationResultNormal values
Hb100 g/L135–175 g/L
Albumin30 g/L35–55 g/L
Na⁺135 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
K⁺2.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea7.5 mmol/L2.5–6.7 mmol/L
Creatinine105 mmol/L70–150 mmol/L
CRP75 mg/L< 3 mg/L

Which of the following is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Surgical consult

Absolute indications for colectomy in patients with acute severe colitis are complications such as toxic megacolon, perforation, uncontrolled severe bloody stool and multiorgan dysfunction. The risk of surgical complications increases with delays in surgery and therefore, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend consideration of surgery if there is a lack of response within 3–5 days. As this patient has had a refractory response to medical therapy and is showing ongoing signs of systemic toxicity, with further organ involvement (kidney injury), surgical consultation is the next best option.

C Repeat abdominal X-ray

This patient has acute severe colitis, as indicated by > 6 bloody stools per day with signs of systemic toxicity (temperature > 37.8 °C on admission, heart rate > 90 bpm, Hb < 105 g/L, C-reactive protein > 30 mg/L). Following three days of treatment, he continues to have signs of acute severe ulcerative colitis and his blood tests also reveal acute kidney injury. The NICE guidelines recommend considering surgery for individuals who have little or no improvement within 72 hours of starting IV corticosteroids or whose symptoms worsen despite corticosteroid treatment. Although an abdominal X-ray provides useful information regarding toxic megacolon in these patients, given his lack of improvement to initial therapy, a surgical consult is the next most appropriate step.

A Continue hydrocortisone, start IV infliximab

Intravenous (IV) infliximab can be considered if there is a lack of response to medical therapy, in addition to hydrocortisone. However, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that infliximab is only used in patients in whom ciclosporin is contraindicated or clinically inappropriate.

B Proceed to flexible sigmoidoscopy

Flexible sigmoidoscopy should be completed for all patients with acute severe colitis, ideally within 24–72 hours of admission. Flexible sigmoidoscopy will give useful information regarding the severity of inflammation and will allow biopsies to be obtained. However, this patient is showing ongoing signs of toxicity and multiorgan involvement on day three. Therefore, he needs a surgical consult as a priority over further imaging at present.

D Stop hydrocortisone, start IV ciclosporin

Intravenous (IV) ciclosporin can be considered first-line as an adjunct to IV hydrocortisone in patients who do not have sufficient response to medical therapy. However, steroids should not be stopped when starting this treatment, and this patient is also showing significant signs of systemic toxicity, with a need for a surgical consult sooner rather than later. 73001

questions.question:
A 79-year-old man presents with 2 days right upper quadrant pain, rigors, a temperature of 39 °C and deranged liver function tests.

An abdominal ultrasound reports no gallstones in the common bile duct, but there are dilated intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Tumour at the ampulla of Vater
Cholangiocarcinoma at the level of the porta hepatis
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Cholangitis

The clinical picture is suggestive of ascending cholangitis. He has evidence of extrahepatic obstruction on ultrasound scanning (USS), and there is still a chance that gallstones are present in the common bile duct, despite these not having been visualised on US scanning; the sensitivity for detection of choledocholithiasis with ultrasound is 75% in the presence of dilated ducts, and 50% for non-dilated ducts. The distal common bile duct is often obscured by air-containing bowel loops.

MRCP is superior to CT for diagnosing and locating gallstones, with a sensitivity of around 93%. ERCP and sphincterotomy may be required in the acute setting if sepsis does not resolve with antibiotics. It may also prevent future recurrence, particularly if the risk of laparoscopic cholecystectomy is high.

D Pancreatic tumour

A tumour in the head of the pancreas could cause distal biliary obstruction, and subsequent ascending

cholangitis, but is likely to present more insidiously with obstructive jaundice, weight loss and dull abdominal pain. Cholangitis is an infrequent manifestation, and hence it is not the most likely explanation here.

A Cholecystitis

The ultrasound did not report evidence of cholecystitis, and the sensitivity of ultrasound for the diagnosis of cholecystitis is good (around 90%). Furthermore, this diagnosis is unlikely to explain extrahepatic duct dilatation.

C Tumour at the ampulla of Vater

A tumour at the ampulla of Vater could cause distal biliary obstruction, and ascending cholangitis, but is likely

to present more insidiously with obstructive jaundice, weight loss and dull abdominal pain. Cholangitis is an infrequent manifestation, and hence it is not the most likely explanation here.

E Cholangiocarcinoma at the level of the porta hepatis

A cholangiocarcinoma at the porta hepatis would not explain the extrahepatic duct dilatation. 2280

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease presents to the clinic with worsening abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She has undergone multiple surgical procedures over the years for fistulae and abscesses, and now takes 15 mg of prednisolone daily for her Crohn’s.

On examination, she looks tired and in pain. Her abdomen has multiple scars from previous surgical procedures and although it is soft, she complains of some tenderness.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)156 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)106 fL76–98 fL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)56 mm/hour< 10 mm/hour
Thiopurine methyl-transferase (TPMT)Activity low

Which of the following represents the most appropriate option for her?
options: Laparoscopy with a view to further bowel resection
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Infliximab

Anti-TNF therapy is an option for Crohn’s disease that is resistant to other interventions, particularly where there is fistulating disease. Patients should of course have TB excluded before therapy is commenced.

A Laparoscopy with a view to further bowel resection

Given Crohn’s has a high incidence of recurrence and affects both the large and small bowel, surgery should be avoided if possible.

B Elemental diet

Elemental diet has mixed results in Crohn’s disease, with only some studies demonstrating a positive impact on symptoms and disease activity.

C Methotrexate

Methotrexate is appropriate for patients with steroid-resistant disease who cannot take azathioprine, although infliximab is a better choice for patients like this one who have fistulating disease.

D Azathioprine

Azathioprine is not recommended in patients with low TMPT activity because of the risk of significant bone marrow suppression due to mercaptopurine toxicity.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection presents with spiking temperatures over the past two weeks, right upper quadrant pain and abnormal liver function tests. He has a low CD4 count. Ultrasound scan and computed tomography (CT) scan are normal.

Blood tests show:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)120 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White blood count (WCC)4.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 – 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)151 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.0< 1.1
Bilirubin20 µmol/L1.71 - 20.5 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)37 U/L5 - 35 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)380 U/L20 - 140 U/L
Gamma GT (GGT)189 U/L9 - 48 U/L
Albumin35 g/L35 – 55 g/L

What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)

Biliary involvement in HIV infection is commonly known as AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) cholangiopathy, and is a syndrome of biliary obstruction resulting from infection-related strictures of the biliary tract. There is a spectrum of involvement including acute acalculous cholecystitis, papillary stenosis and sclerosing cholangitis. Cholangiopathy is mostly associated with cryptosporidium parvum, but other pathogens have also been identified, including cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Microsporidium.

MRCP has developed significantly over the past few years, and is in this case a useful screening tool to confirm the underlying diagnosis before considering ERCP. In some cases progression to ERCP may be required to confirm the diagnosis for example by obtaining biopsy specimens. Symptomatic patients with papillary stenosis have responded symptomatically to endoscopic sphincterotomy. Antibiotics have not been shown to be useful. Some clinicians use ursodeoxycholic acid in patients with intrahepatic disease, with an observed improvement in liver enzymes.

C Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

In this case, given that the CT has not revealed the underlying diagnosis, MRCP is a logical next step before progressing to ERCP.

A Blood culture

This would not particularly contribute to diagnosis - imaging of the biliary tree is required to explore this patient’s symptoms pattern of liver enzyme derangement.

B Liver biopsy

Liver biopsy has little value in the diagnosis of AIDS cholangiopathy; diagnosis is informed by imaging of the biliary tree.

E CT abdomen

CT is more useful than ultrasound in identifying intrahepatic strictures, and can be effective in identifying intrahepatic masses, abdominal adenopathy, and pancreatic disease in jaundiced patients. But CT is inferior to ERCP in its ability to display the necessarily precise biliary anatomical details for the definitive diagnosis of AIDS cholangiopathy.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old man with a 12-year history of recurrent peptic ulceration presents to his General Practitioner with a further relapse.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Fasting serum gastrin480 pmol/l< 55 pmol/l
Serum gastrin following injection of secretin (2 U/kg)720 pmol/l

Which of the following is associated with the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Nephrolithiasis

This patient has Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, a rare condition in which a gastrin-secreting adenoma results in severe and recurrent gastric and duodenal ulceration. The condition may be diagnosed by detecting a raised serum gastrin level, or if there is doubt as to the diagnosis with only a mild elevation in gastrin level, the secretin test leads to a marked elevation in gastrin levels. The level of gastrin seen here is markedly elevated. Treatment is with high-dose proton pump inhibitors and, if possible, surgical resection of the adenoma. Approximately 50% of adenomas are malignant, with a 5-year survival rate of 80% for a single tumour. Zollinger–Ellison syndrome may arise as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1). Nephrolithiasis may occur in association with Zollinger–Ellison syndrome in MEN-1 due to the presence of hypercalcaemia.

D Renal cysts

Renal cysts are not a recognised complication of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome or MEN-1. Recognised risk factors for renal cysts are age, male gender, renal dysfunction and hypertension. Examples of renal cystic disease include polycystic kidney disease, medullary cystic disease and medullary sponge kidney.

A Marfanoid body habitus

This patient has Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, which may occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1). Marfanoid body habitus is associated with MEN-2.

C Medullary thyroid cancer

This patient has Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, which may occur as part of MEN-1. Medullary thyroid cancer is associated with MEN-2.

E Small bowel cancer

Small bowel cancer is not a recognised complication of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome or MEN-1. This is a complication seen in coeliac disease and Crohn’s disease.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman with no previous significant medical history presents for review.

Medication history includes the oral contraceptive pill and she smokes 15 cigarettes per day and drinks 15 units per week. She complains of vague upper abdominal pain, worse on the right-hand side.

On examination, there is a palpable non-tender mass in the right hypochondrium. Investigations reveal mild elevations in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT); alpha-fetoprotein is within the normal range. Hepatic ultrasound scan reveals a solitary mass in the left lobe of the liver, which is hypoechoic and subcapsular.

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Hepatic adenoma

This woman has a history of use of the oral contraceptive pill, with an asymptomatic liver mass. It is hypoechoic and subcapsular, appearing uniform in texture. The presence of a normal alpha-fetoprotein makes hepatocellular carcinoma unlikely; therefore, the most likely diagnosis is hepatic adenoma. Stopping the oral contraceptive pill often causes tumour regression, although complete regression is very atypical. Any tumour regression reduces risks associated with elective surgical resection; although mortality associated with resection is very rare, surgery results in significant morbidity in around 13% of patients. In patients who experience some regression after stopping the pill, there is still a risk of malignant transformation, and such patients should be monitored with alpha-fetoprotein measurement if they are unwilling or unable to undergo elective tumour resection.

D Hydatid cyst

Hydatid disease appears as a multi-loculated cyst on ultrasound scan rather than the hypoechoic mass which isn’t multi-loculated here.

B Hepatocellular carcinoma

Hepatocellular carcinoma is usually seen against a background of chronic liver disease with cirrhosis, and is associated with rapid worsening of ascites with elevation in alpha-fetoprotein.

C Liver metastasis

Liver metastases are usually characterised by more than one lesion, and the absence of other symptoms of cancer, makes this a much less likely diagnosis.

E Focal nodular hyperplasia

The echogenicity of both FNH and its scar is variable, which makes it difficult to detect on ultrasound. Some lesions are well demarcated and easily seen whereas others are isoechoic with surrounding liver. Detectable lesions characteristically will demonstrate a central scar with the displacement of peripheral vasculature on colour doppler examination, rather than the well demarcated hypoechoic lesion seen here.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old woman is referred to the clinic by her general practitioner (GP) for fatigue, lethargy, mild itching, muscle and joint pains. She has a history of hypothyroidism which is treated with 100 mcg of thyroxine daily. Her TSH has been stable for the past 5 years.

On examination, there is jaundice, with mild hepatomegaly and more than five spider naevi on the upper body.

Investigations reveal:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Bilirubin125 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)230 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)185 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Albumin28 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Hypergammaglobulinaemiapolyclonal
Anti-smooth muscle antibodiespositive
Anti-nuclear antibodypositive

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis

Autoantibodies associated with type 1 autoimmune hepatitis include anti-smooth muscle antibodies, antinuclear antibodies and anti-actin antibodies. Autoimmune hepatitis is much more common in women. Diagnosis and prognostic assessment is best informed via liver biopsy. After an initial period of high-dose prednisolone, azathioprine is often added as a steroid-sparing agent. A number of physicians employ a maintenance regime of prednisolone 10 mg and azathioprine 50 mg per day as maintenance therapy. Initial remission is possible in around 80% of patients, though relapse often occurs if therapy is withdrawn. Liver transplant is successful in patients who fail medical therapy.

B Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)

PBC is associated with an obstructive liver function test picture, and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies.

A Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, an obstructive LFT picture, and a range of positive autoantibodies which may include pANCA.

D Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis

Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis occurs predominantly in children and is associated with anti-liver kidney microsomal antibodies.

E Type 3 autoimmune hepatitis

Type 3 autoimmune hepatitis is associated with soluble liver or liver-kidney antigens. 33050

questions.question:
An 18-year-old female student is being investigated in the clinic for weight loss and diarrhoea. The symptoms started about one year ago and she has been progressively losing weight. She is in the clinic with her parents, who are extremely concerned for their daughter.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)112 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)160 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)132 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)55 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
6.0 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour (ESR)
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)83 fL76–98 fL
C-reactive protein (CRP)4.0 mg/L< 0 mg/L
Urea2.5 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Upper gastrointestinal (GI)Normal appearances with normal duodenal
endoscopybiopsies
ColonoscopyMelanosis coli

What is the most likely cause of the symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Senna abuse

Anthraquinone laxative derivatives such as senna are absorbed in the large intestine, where they lead to cellular apoptosis, resulting in brown pigmentation of the colonic mucosa, so-called melanosis coli.

B Lactulose abuse

Lactulose is an osmotic laxative which increases intraluminal/stool water, resulting in softening; it does not lead to colonic pigmentation.

C Sodium docusate abuse

Sodium docusate, like lactulose, is primarily a stool softener and does not lead to colonic mucosal cell apoptosis and melanosis coli.

D Methylcellulose abuse

Methylcellulose is a bulk-forming laxative and must be taken with large amounts of fluids to achieve its laxative effect.

E Colchicine use

Colchicine is rarely used, normally for the treatment of gout in patients where other interventions are unsuitable. It is therefore doubtful as to how this patient would have gained access to the medication. It does not cause melanosis coli.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old businessman is brought in by ambulance from the airport with sudden-onset, excruciating upper abdominal pain radiating to his back following a flight. He has had recurrent vomiting during the whole of his flight. He has a history of hiatus hernia but no history of cardiac problems. He drinks 10 units of alcohol per week. On examination, he is dyspnoeic and cyanosed. Blood pressure is equal on both arms and there is no radial– radial delay. His saturation is 88% on high-flow oxygen. Heart sounds are normal.

On chest examination, there is reduced air entry and dullness to percussion on the left side. There is marked epigastric tenderness and rigidity. His pain fails to improve with morphine or pethidine. Amylase and cardiac enzymes are within normal range.

Electrocardiography demonstrates sinus tachycardia but no other abnormalities. Chest X-ray shows a left pleural effusion.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Boerhaave’s syndrome

Repeated vomiting followed by epigastric pain and pleural effusion should lead one to consider the diagnosis of spontaneous rupture of the oesophagus, also known as Boerhaave syndrome. It is relatively uncommon but serious and potentially fatal. It is complete transmural laceration of the lower part of the oesophagus, with gastric contents entering the mediastinum and pleural cavity. If one were to perform a pleural fluid aspirate, one is likely to aspirate gastric contents. It is usually caused by vomiting against a closed glottis.

Other clinical features that may suggest the diagnosis include odynophagia and surgical emphysema in the neck. It is more common in men than women and typically present in those between 50–70 years old. Early operation after appropriate resuscitation offers the best chance of survival.

C Acute pancreatitis

A rise in amylase >3× the upper limit of normal is one of the diagnostic criteria for pancreatitis, and therefore

the normal amylase level precludes this. See AGA guidelines on management of acute pancreatitis. Reference: American Journal of Gastroenterology 108, 1400–1415 (September 2013).

A Dissecting thoracic aneurysm

Patients presenting with dissection classically have a history of hypertension. One would also expect a disparity in the blood pressure and pulse in acute dissections. Patients may also present with a neurological deficit due to involvement of the spinal and carotid arteries.

B Aspiration pneumonia

Although the recurrent vomiting and hiatus hernia would certainly be a risk factor, the persistent, excruciating pain would be uncharacteristic for an aspiration pneumonia as would such a rapid onset of a pleural effusion.

D Perforated duodenal ulcer

One would expect to see pneumoperitoneum with a perforated duodenal ulcer, and the presence of a unilateral effusion is not characteristic. 7401

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman is found to have the following blood results on routine preoperative blood tests. She presented due to yellowing of her skin following a short bout of flu, from which she has now recovered.

She has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medications. Examination reveals jaundice, but no other abnormalities.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Bilirubin36 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)108 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)20 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Urine dipstickNormal

Given the likely diagnosis, which is the best course of action?
options: Complete viral screen for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), infectious hepatitis, Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus
Ultrasound scan of the liver, including portal Doppler
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Complete full blood count

This patient has asymptomatic jaundice following a recent viral infection. Gilbert syndrome is a common cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia following fasting or physiological stress and is often diagnosed incidentally. It is characterised by mildly elevated bilirubin levels. In this patient who reveals no prior history of

jaundice, it is important to rule out haemolysis as a cause of jaundice by also checking the patient’s full blood count. If this is abnormal, a blood film, reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase level and direct antigen test may also be requested. If these tests are negative, a presumptive diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome can be made. The diagnosis can be confirmed by either an increase in bilirubin level provoked by fasting or by a slow rise in bilirubin level following administration of intravenous nicotinic acid. No treatment is necessary and the prognosis is excellent.

A Complete viral screen for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), infectious hepatitis, Epstein–Barr

virus and cytomegalovirus

Although this patient has had a recent viral illness, she has completely recovered and her liver function tests only reveal an abnormality in her bilirubin levels, pointing towards a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome, which causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Viral screening for the above viruses would be necessary if she had evidence of acute liver disease on examination or her liver function tests.

C Liver biopsy

Liver biopsy is an invasive test and is not necessary to make a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome in this patient who is otherwise well. A liver biopsy may be indicated if there is evidence of concomitant liver disease.

D No further investigations necessary

This patient likely has Gilbert syndrome which is a common cause of isolated unconjugated bilirubinaemia. However, given that this young patient reports no history of previous presentations with jaundice, it would be pertinent to rule out haemolysis (eg due to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma) as the cause of her bilirubinaemia and therefore, a full blood count of at least should be completed. If this reveals a low haemoglobin level, then further testing of reticulocyte count, blood film, lactate dehydrogenase level and direct antigen test should be completed.

E Ultrasound scan of the liver, including portal Doppler

Although ultrasound scanning is a safe and non-invasive test, it is not necessary to make a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome, especially in the absence of any evidence of liver disease on examination and normal transaminase levels on liver function testing.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man with mild haemophilia B is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic by his General Practitioner who has noted deranged liver function tests. The patient’s blood tests were checked when he moved back to the United Kingdom after having worked abroad for many years. He had attended for a routine prescription of his antihypertensive medication and statin therapy. He has not had any significant bleeding episodes for ten years and informs you his haemophilia was diagnosed when he was eight years old when he had significant bleeding after surgery for appendicitis. The haemorrhage required treatment and an admission to intensive care. He does not smoke and has never injected drugs.

On examination, he is well, with no organomegaly. He reports no symptoms of jaundice or discolouration of his urine.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)85 fL80–100 fL
Bilirubin20 µmol/L3–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)205 U/L30–150 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)25 U/L7–55 U/L
