Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)265 U/L5–35 U/L
Albumin32 g/L35–55 g/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.21.13

What further investigation is most likely to contribute towards making a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Hepatitis C ribonucleic acid

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is chronic hepatitis C infection. This patient had mild haemophilia, which was diagnosed following prolonged bleeding following an appendicectomy. It is likely that he received a blood transfusion at the time and may have been infected with hepatitis C. Blood transfusions were not routinely screened for hepatitis C before 1990–1992. Patients with chronic hepatitis C infection may remain largely asymptomatic, but within 15–25 years of infection, cirrhosis may develop. Hepatitis C antibodies and hepatitis C ribonucleic acid should be checked, with ribonucleic acid being the diagnostic test of choice (as antibodies alone will only indicate previous exposure).

A Creatine kinase levels

Creatine kinase levels may be used to identify myositis due to statin therapy. However, there is nothing in the scenario to suggest that this may be an issue, as the patient does not report any muscle pain or tenderness.

B Liver ultrasound

Liver ultrasound may indicate the degree of cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C infection; however, this is not the best test to reveal the diagnosis, as it will only indicate the degree of damage to the liver, not the cause of the damage.

C Hepatitis A antibodies

Hepatitis A is spread by the faecal–oral route and is the most common form of viral hepatitis infection worldwide. It is not spread via blood transfusions.

D Hepatitis B antibodies

Hepatitis B is an important diagnosis to rule out. It can be spread in the same ways as hepatitis C, via intravenous injection (drug use/transfusion) or via intercourse. However, blood transfusions have been screened for hepatitis B since the 1970s and this man has no other risk factors for hepatitis B spread.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old man presents with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 5/15 after being found on the floor by his neighbour. The only past medical history available is that he has chronic hepatitis C.

Medication found in his bag includes tramadol, diclofenac and furosemide. His temperature is 38.0 °C.

His BP is 100/60 mmHg, with a heart rate of 120 bpm. Heart sounds are normal. There are coarse crackles at his right lung base. His abdomen is distended, with shifting dullness. His pupils are equal and reactive and the plantar responses are flexor. He is transferred to the Intensive Care Unit and receives fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics for his chest. All his usual medications are stopped.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)134 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)101 fL76–98 fL
International normalised ratio (INR)1.6< 1.1
Urea11.0 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Bilirubin38 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)88 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)235 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Albumin32 g/L35–55 g/L
UrinalysisNo blood or protein
Computed tomography scan of theCerebral atrophy; no intracerebral
brainhaemorrhage or lesions Computed tomography scan of theFree fluid in the pelvis; cirrhotic liver abdomen Three days later, he becomes oliguric. Ultrasound scan shows no evidence of ureteric obstruction. He has become apyrexial. Repeat renal function tests reveal the following:
InvestigationResultNormal values
Sodium (Na⁺)128 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea25.0 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)300 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urinary sodium (Na⁺)8.0 mmol/L
Blood cultureNegative
Ascitic tapPolymorphic neutrophil count 30 cells/mm 3; no organisms

What is the most likely diagnosis for his worsening renal function?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Hepatorenal syndrome

This is usually a diagnosis of exclusion, after other potential causes of acute kidney disease have been ruled out. The raised white cell count and initial pyrexia are in keeping with likely chest infection, which has been treated.

Hepatorenal syndrome refers to the development of acute kidney disease in a patient who has advanced liver disease, due to cirrhosis, and who has no identifiable cause of intrinsic renal disease. It usually represents the end stage of a sequence of reductions in renal perfusion induced by increasingly severe hepatic injury. Splanchnic vasodilatation appears to play an important role in the decline in renal function in hepatic disease.

The following definition and diagnostic criteria have been proposed for hepatorenal syndrome:

(a) chronic or acute hepatic disease with advanced hepatic failure and portal hypertension (b) a plasma creatinine concentration >133 µmol/L that progresses over days to weeks (c) the absence of any other apparent cause for the renal disease, including shock, active sepsis, current nephrotoxic drugs and the absence of ultrasonographic evidence of obstruction or parenchymal renal disease. It is particularly important to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is complicated with acute kidney disease (d) a urine sodium concentration <10 meq/l (off diuretics) and protein excretion <500 mg/day (e) lack of improvement in renal function after volume expansion with 1.5 l of isotonic saline.

C Hepatitis B-related membranous glomerulonephritis

Urinalysis is negative for urine sediment containing red cells or casts, making glomerulonephritis less likely. He has also been fully fluid resuscitated and remains oliguric.

A Septicaemia

The fact that this patient is now apyrexial makes continued septicaemia very unlikely as the cause of his kidney disease.

B Drug-induced acute kidney disease

Although both diclofenac and furosemide can exacerbate renal impairment, his chronic liver disease is the much greater contributor to renal dysfunction seen here.

D Acute tubular necrosis

Acute tubular necrosis is associated with increased renal sodium excretion; urinary sodium here is 8.0 mmol/L, which is in the normal range.

questions.question:
A 66-year-old man is under investigation for recurrent fevers and arthralgia. He has had episodes of fevers over the last 4 years associated with seronegative non-destructive arthropathies. Episodes have been characterised by elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and have responded to antibiotics. Blood cultures have been persistently negative. On this admission, the patient complains of persistent diarrhoea and weight loss over the last 6 months, as well as myalgia. His wife has noticed that he has become more forgetful of late.

On examination, he is pale and thin, and auscultation reveals a systolic murmur in the aortic area. Central nervous system (CNS) examination shows signs of mild ataxia.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)115 g/L135–175 g/L
White Cell Count (WCC)10.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)300 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin10 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)16 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)21 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin29 g/L35–55 g/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)82 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)76 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Whipple’s disease

Whipple’s disease is a rare but potentially fatal condition caused by an abnormal host immune response to the intracellular organism Tropheryma whippeli. Symptoms include seronegative arthropathy (> 70%), weight loss (> 90%) and diarrhoea (> 70%). Cardiac complications including pericarditis and valvular heart disease occur in up to 30% of patients, and central nervous system (CNS) manifestations (including ocular disturbances, higher- function abnormalities and cerebellar symptoms) occur in 15%. Biochemical abnormalities include a systemic inflammatory response with anaemia and hypoalbuminaemia secondary to malabsorption.

The histological hallmarks of the disease are (1) lipid deposition in the lamina propria of intestinal villi and (2) the presence of lipid-containing macrophages with sickle-like inclusion bodies that stain with diastase-resistant Periodic acid Schiff reagent (PAS). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based detection from affected tissues and body fluids is now possible. Treatment is with protracted courses of antibiotics.

A Histoplasmosis

Although macrophage infiltration of the small bowel is associated with histoplasmosis, the clinical features seen in this case are not usually seen with histoplasmosis - a large encapsulated organism that predominantly affects the respiratory system.

C Giardiasis

This is a parasitic infection that is spread by contaminated food and water. Infection presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, usually diarrhoea and bloating, but it is not associated with any extra-intestinal symptoms, so this option is therefore incorrect.

D H. pylori infection

This condition would not account for the multitude of symptoms seen in this case. H. pylori is associated with peptic ulcer disease, anaemia and gastric malignancy, but not fevers or arthralgia as is seen in this case.

E Sickle cell crisis

Sickle cell crisis is usually associated with painful episodes with a drop in haemoglobin caused by sickling. This patient’s haemoglobin is still 115 g/L.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old premenopausal woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of epigastric pain that is occasionally retrosternal which is also worse at night. She has tried over-the-counter antacid preparations which have achieved no relief. Her weight is steady and her bowel habits are normal. Her father died from gastric malignancy aged 72. On examination, the patient is obese and her body mass index is 31 kg/m 2. Her GP has checked her haemoglobin (Hb) level, which is 137 g/L (normal range 115–155 g/L), and the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is in the normal range.

Which of the following is the best management step?
options: Check ferritin and then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy
Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and refer for endoscopy if there is no resolution within two weeks
Prescribe a PPI and review symptoms in one month
Start a PPI and perform breath test screening for Helicobacter pylori
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Prescribe a PPI and review symptoms in one month

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that in this age group, dyspepsia, in the absence of dysphagia or evidence of upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding, should be treated with lifestyle advice and proton pump inhibitor (PPI) if needed. If after one month, symptoms are not controlled, then testing for H. pylori (breath test or serology) could be carried out. Alternatively, H. pylori screening could be performed at the beginning, although there is no strong evidence as to which to do first. There needs to be a 2-week washout period of the PPI for a urea breath test to be reliable. While there are risk factors for gastric malignancy, including family history, by virtue of her age (under 55 years) and the absence of dysphagia, this patient does not satisfy the 2-week wait criterion at this point. In the event that her symptoms do not resolve after treatment, she should be referred to a Gastroenterologist, and endoscopy considered.

A Check ferritin and then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy

The Hb level is only just below the lower limit of normal and the MCV is normal. Therefore, significant iron deficiency is unlikely.

B Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and refer for endoscopy if there is no resolution within two

weeks

A 2-week trial of therapy is too short to make a decision as to the impact on symptoms so would not be

appropriate for this patient.

D Start a PPI and perform breath test screening for Helicobacter pylori

H. pylori testing should be conducted after a 2-week washout period off PPI, as use of acid suppression can make interpretation of the test unreliable.

E Upper GI endoscopy

There are no alarming symptoms such as weight loss, regurgitation of food or anaemia seen here, and the patient is under 55 years. Therefore, going straight for endoscopy is not appropriate.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with deep jaundice, drowsiness and confusion. He has been increasingly unwell for the past 3 months, and an ultrasound of his abdomen from 2 weeks earlier demonstrated a mass in the head of the pancreas, a degree of biliary obstruction and probable metastases within the liver substance itself. On examination, he is drowsy and confused, his temperature is 37.8 °C, his BP is 100/60 mmHg with a pulse of 85/min, there are several scratch marks on his skin, and he is deeply jaundiced. He is tender in the epigastrium, and you can feel a liver edge.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)101 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.2 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)102 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)105 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin280 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)485 IU/L30–130 IU/L

Which of the following is the most important intervention here?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with stenting

This patient has hepatic obstruction, as evidenced by his deep jaundice and obstructive picture on liver function testing. ERCP with stenting delivered at the same time is the preferred option here, and is likely to drive an improvement in symptoms for at least a few months.

B Percutaneous trans-hepatic cholangiography (PTC) tube

PTC is only indicated in the event that the obstruction cannot be relieved by ERCP alone.

A Oral ciprofloxacin

Ascending cholangitis is a possibility and antibiotics would be used in combination with ERCP. They are not likely to be effective used in isolation. Recent advice is also to avoid quinolone antibiotics wherever a suitable alternative is available due to the risk of debilitating side effects.

C Choledochojejunostomy

Choledochojejunostomy is a potential alternative to ERCP, although this patient’s advanced disease implies that even this procedure is not an option.

D Whipple’s procedure

Surgical resection will not be curative, carries a high operative risk and should be avoided here.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Ward with a 2-day history of fever, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, with bowel opening up to ten times per day. She has a background of ulcerative colitis and is treated with intravenous hydrocortisone and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

After 72 hours into admission, she still reports to be feeling unwell and is opening her bowels 7–8 times per day with watery, bloodstained diarrhoea. On examination, she has a temperature of 38.4 °C, a blood pressure of 105/70 mmHg and a heart rate of 90 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is generally tender, although soft, and she has active bowel sounds.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)101 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.9 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)155 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.5 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)85 mm/h1 - 20 mm/h
C-reactive protein (CRP)180 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Abdominal X-rayColon diameter 5.5 cm

What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Ciclosporin

Intravenous (IV) ciclosporin has a role in induction of remission in patients with severe or fulminant colitis. According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, it is usually offered to patients who are on steroids for 72 hours without any improvement. Therefore, it is an appropriate next step in this case but is not effective for long-term use. Ciclosporin is given as a continuous IV infusion of 2 mg/kg over 24 hours, which can be adjusted according to the concentration of the drug in the blood and the patient’s response.

B Referral to General Surgical Team

A referral would be necessary if a colectomy is indicated. A colectomy is indicated in patients with fulminant

colitis and who fail to respond to ciclosporin (due to either failure to respond or relapse) within 4–7 days and in those with toxic megacolon (diameter ≥ 6 cm or caecum > 9 cm and systemic toxicity) who do not respond to therapy within 72 hours. Surgery is also indicated if the patient experiences frequent flare-ups and whose quality of life is adversely affected by the condition.

A Azathioprine

Azathioprine is recommended in patients with corticosteroid-dependent ulcerative colitis and is an effective agent for relapse prevention. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines suggest that if aminosalicylate does not work well in preventing flare-ups, then azathioprine or mercaptopurine can be used.

D Infliximab infusion

The NICE guidelines recommend that infliximab is used in the treatment of acute exacerbations of ulcerative colitis in patients in whom ciclosporin is contraindicated or clinically inappropriate. This is not the case for this patient, and therefore, ciclosporin should be tried initially.

E Rectal mesalazine

Mesalazine (5-aminosalicylic acid) is the standard first-line therapy for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis. It is also used in the maintenance of remission and prevention of relapse of ulcerative colitis. However, it has little role in cases of fulminant ulcerative colitis or flare-ups.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man is referred for investigation of dysphagia. This had been gradually worsening over the last year, but was intermittent in nature and was for both solids and liquids. He also described the frequent regurgitation of old food several hours after eating.

Recently, he had been experiencing occasional episodes of severe retrosternal chest pain. He denied weight loss and heartburn. He had no significant past medical history and was on no regular medication. He was a non-smoker and rarely drank alcohol.

A full clinical examination was entirely normal, as was his full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests. His CXR was normal, and barium swallow is shown below:

Which one of the following investigations should be performed next?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Oesophageal manometry

The diagnosis is achalasia, where a range of investigations including endoscopy may be normal. The barium swallow, showing dilatation in the upper portion of the oesophagus with tapering at the lower end (bird beak appearance), is suggestive of achalasia and the definitive diagnostic test is oesophageal manometry, which will confirm a high oesophageal resting tone, weak or absent peristalsis and a non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter. Treatment options include endoscopic pneumatic dilation of the LOS (successful in 80% of cases), intra-sphincteric botulinum toxin injection and surgical division of the LOS (Heller’s cardiomyotomy). There is an increased risk of carcinoma of the oesophagus in patients with achalasia.

Achalasia has an incidence of 1 per 100 000 per year and is defined as reduced or absent peristalsis and failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) to relax when swallowing. It is due to the degeneration of ganglionic cells in the nerve plexi of the oesophageal wall. It can present at any age with intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, severe retrosternal chest pain and aspiration pneumonia.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acha.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acha.JPG)

D Double-contrast barium meal

A double-contrast barium meal wouldn’t add further information to that already known about this patient’s

oesophageal dysmotility, and is therefore not useful here.

B CT scan of the abdomen

Given the barium swallow points towards achalasia and endoscopy has ruled out oesophageal malignancy, the next important step is manometry. CT of the abdomen is more useful for investigation of intra-abdominal masses.

C Endoscopic ultrasound scan

Endoscopic ultrasound of the oesophagus may be of value in investigating underlying oesophageal carcinoma, but doesn’t have a role here.

E 24 hour intraluminal oesophageal pH monitoring

Intraluminal pH monitoring is most useful when oesophageal reflux is suspected, particularly when it occurs at night, but the endoscopy examination is equivocal.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of recently worsening indigestion. He also complains of fatigue, weight loss and recent night sweats.

Clinical examination shows a BP of 147/86 mmHg, pulse of 70/min and regular and a BMI of 26. He is mildly tender in the epigastrium. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals a suspicious area of mucosa in the stomach with particularly rigid folds. Biopsy reveals large numbers of lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours and abundant cytoplasm.

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALToma)

MALT is characterised by large numbers of immunocompetent cells in the lamina propria. MALTomas are B-cell lymphomas comprising large numbers of lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours and abundant cytoplasm. Higher-grade lymphomas show clusters or sheets of blast-like cells. Up to 75% of small low-grade lymphomas may regress completely after antibiotic therapy for helicobacter eradication. Where treatment fails, surgical therapy or combinations with radio- and chemotherapy may be considered. In addition, Rituxamab has recently shown success in achieving remission in this condition.

E Helicobacter infection

H pylori infection presents with lymphocytic invasion on biopsy but the abnormal lymphocyte morphology seen here is not present.

A Gastric carcinoma

Gastric carcinomas can be tubular, mucinous, poorly cohesive or unclassified in histology. A hallmark on histology is submucosal invasion.

B Gastric adenoma

Gastric adenomas are rare in Western populations, and rather than showing growth without evidence of invasion, histology normally reveals at least some evidence of carcinomatous transformation.

D Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

High grade mature B cell lymphomas in a Western population often present with symptoms of CNS lymphoma or mediastinal lymphadenopathy picked up with other symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss over a period of time. 33055

questions.question:
A 54-year-old woman has chronic autoimmune hepatitis. She is managed on prednisolone and azathioprine.

You review her in the clinic and notice that she has worsening of her jaundice with a rising bilirubin and increasing ascites.

You admit her; the nurses call you to see her urgently the following morning as she has become increasingly drowsy. Her blood pressure is 100/50 mmHg, with pyrexia of 38.2 °C.

Which investigation is most likely to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: Peritoneal tap for microscopy and culture
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Peritoneal tap for microscopy and culture

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in around 8% of cirrhotic patients with ascites, infecting organisms probably gaining access to the peritoneum via haematological spread. Most frequent infecting organisms are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and enterococci. Pain and pyrexia may frequently be absent. A raised neutrophil count alone in ascitic fluid is enough to commence treatment. Mortality is high, at up to 25%, and recurs in 70% of patients within one year. Oral quinolones may be used as prophylaxis

A Computed tomography (CT) head

CT head would be a useful investigation in confusion during which an intracranial cause is suspected or needs to be excluded. This can be considered in, for example, subdural haematomas (worsening pain and confusion), subarachnoid haemorrhage (sudden occipital severe headache) or abscess (recent sinusitis or other infection, headache and fever). In this patient there is a clear cause for confusion – acute decompensation of the liver.

B Electroencephalograpm (EEG)

EEG can demonstrate encephalopathy, but it is unlikely to be of significant aid in decision making as there is sufficient evidence of liver decompensation clinically.

C Blood culture

Blood culture should be taken in this patient to help guide antibiotic therapy, but is unlikely to be very specific in making the diagnosis. It can demonstrate bowel organisms in this setting, but may not give much help regarding the exact origin, nor would it provide an answer in a timely fashion.

D Lumbar puncture

A lumbar puncture is a useful investigation in a confused patient with fever, but the clinical picture already

suggests a clear cause of this. If he had symptoms of meningitis as well, such as photophobia or neck stiffness, then it would be a diagnostic investigation.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man who has a 20-year history of ulcerative colitis (UC) presents to the gastroenterology clinic for review. His UC is relatively quiescent, although most recently he has begun to suffer from tiredness, itching and vague right upper quadrant pain.

On examination, you can feel two fingers’-breadth hepatomegaly. His only medication is salazopyrine.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)320 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)420 U/L30 - 150 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)74 U/L7 - 55 U/L

Which of the following is the most effective therapy for his underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Liver transplantation

Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for patients with decompensated cirrhosis with a background of PSC. Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase and a positive history of ulcerative colitis make PSC a likely diagnosis. Complications of this condition include advanced-stage liver disease with hepatic decompensation. Around 70% of patients diagnosed with PSC are men, with an average age of around 40 years. Up to 90% of patients diagnosed with PSC have co-existent inflammatory bowel disease, normally ulcerative colitis. Cholangiocarcinoma is also an established complication of PSC. Indications for liver transplantation in patients with PSC do not differ from those with other forms of chronic liver disease, which primarily relate to complications of portal hypertension, chronic liver failure and impaired quality of life. Moreover, patients with PSC have specific indications for liver transplant, which include recurrent bacterial cholangitis, intractable pruritis and cholangiocarcinoma.

B Penicillamine

As described in a systemic review by Klingenberg et al., there is insufficient evidence to refute or support the use of penicillamine for patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

Reference: Klingenberg, S.L. and Chen, W. (2006). D-penicillamine for primary sclerosing cholangitis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. Jan 25(1):CD004182.

A Cholestyramine

Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant, is used to treat hyperlipidaemia and for the pruritus of biliary obstruction and chronic liver disease.

D Prednisolone

Corticosteroids, e.g. prednisolone, have not demonstrated any improvement in disease activity or outcome of PSC patients, as evident in a systemic review by Giljaca et al.

Reference: Giljaca, V., Poropat, G., Stimac, D. et al. (2010). Glucocorticosteroids for primary sclerosing cholangitis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. Jan 20(1):CD004036

E Azathioprine

Many immunosuppressive agents are used in the management of patients with PSC, However, there no substantial evidence for its role in prognosis of patients with PSC is noted. A review study by Goode et al. mentioned controversial evidence underlying the usage of immunosuppressive therapy and other prospective agents that may bring new hope regarding the treatment of PSC in the 21st century.

Reference: Goode, E.C. and Rushbrook, S.M. (2016). A review of the medical treatment of primary sclerosing cholangitis in the 21st century. Therapeutic Advances in Chronic Disease, 7(1), 68–85. http://doi.org/10.1177/2040622315605821

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with a 5-month history of tiredness. He has no previous medical history and takes no medication. There is no history of weight loss or fever. He eats a regular healthy diet and has no urinary or bowel symptoms. His examination is unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)115 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)300 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)70 fL80 - 100 fL
Mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH)20 pg27 - 33 pg
Ferritin10 µg/L24 - 355 µg/L (male)
Vitamin B 12500 ng/L160 - 760 ng/L
Folate9 µg/L2.0 - 11.0 µg/L Urinalysis: negative.

Which investigation should be performed next?
options: Urgent referral to Colorectal Services under 2-week wait
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Faecal occult blood testing

Faecal occult blood testing is appropriate in this patient. Indications for faecal occult blood testing include:

An abdominal mass Change in bowel habit Iron-deficiency anaemia ≥40 years and over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain ≥50 years with rectal bleeding and either:

Abdominal pain Weight loss.

≥Aged 50 years with any of the following unexplained symptoms:

Rectal bleeding Abdominal pain Weight loss.

≥60 years with any anaemia.

As this patient is 50 years old and has iron deficiency anaemia, a faecal occult blood sample is recommended. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) as the primary method of testing. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies and urinalysis would also be appropriate investigations here.

A Capsule endoscopy

This investigation is usually reserved for patients who have a normal OGD and colonoscopy but remain anaemic despite iron replacement therapy. This investigation is then performed to rule out a small bowel cause for their anaemia such as Crohn’s disease or angiodysplasia. It is not a first-line investigation.

C Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD)

In all men, post-menopausal women and women aged over 50 years, mandatory investigations for iron deficiency anaemia include an OGD. However, more simple non-invasive investigations, such as a faecal occult blood sample, would be considered first.

D Outpatient colonoscopy

This would be indicated, particularly to exclude malignancy as a cause for this patient’s anaemia. However, it would not be the next test performed as it is an invasive procedure.

E Urgent referral to Colorectal Services under 2-week wait

Urgent referral under the 2-week wait is not appropriate here. Criteria for a 2-week wait referral for colorectal cancer investigation include:

patients aged ≥ 40 years with weight loss and abdominal pain patients aged ≥ 50 years with unexplained rectal bleeding patients aged ≥ 60 years with iron deficiency anaemia or change in bowel habit positive faecal occult blood anal or rectal mass on examination abdominal mass on examination patients aged < 50 years with rectal bleeding and any:

abdominal pain change in bowel habit weight loss iron-deficiency anaemia.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old businessman presents with a 12-month history of intermittent lower back and right knee pain and diarrhoea. He has previously undergone investigations for diarrhoea when a gastroscopy and colonoscopy performed 8 months ago revealed a small area of non-specific inflammation in the ascending colon, but investigations were otherwise normal. He has lost approximately 3 kg in weight over the last 18 months. He takes no regular medication, drinks occasional alcohol and smokes 10 cigarettes per day.

Cardiovascular and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Examination of his spine reveals tenderness over the sacroiliac joints but no restriction in movement. He has a small right knee effusion.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)120 g/L135–175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)108 fL76–98 fL
White cell count (WCC)5.6 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)206 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)38 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea5.3 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)84 µmol/L50–120 mol/l
Albumin40 g/L35–55 g/L
Bilirubin12 µmol/L2–17 mol/l

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Whipple’s disease

Whipple’s disease is caused by infection with Tropheryma whippelii. The organism can be identified by PAS staining of a jejunal biopsy. It is an uncommon condition classically affecting men aged 40–60 years. Gastrointestinal symptoms of diarrhoea, malabsorption and steatorrhoea are often preceded by arthropathy. In the past, various antibiotic regimens (including penicillins) were used on an empirical basis. Tetracycline treatment seems to be associated with a high frequency of relapse, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg orally twice daily) or long-term ampicillin given for around a year is now recommended.

A Chronic pancreatitis

Chronic pancreatitis is a syndrome involving progressive inflammatory changes in the pancreas that result in permanent structural damage, which can lead to impairment of exocrine and endocrine function. Chronic pancreatitis may be asymptomatic over long periods of time, can present with a fibrotic mass or there may be symptoms of pancreatic insufficiency without pain. The serum amylase and lipase concentrations tend to be normal in patients with chronic pancreatitis, but are almost always elevated with acute disease. Morphologically, chronic pancreatitis is a patchy focal disease characterised by a mononuclear infiltrate and fibrosis. There are no joint symptoms associated with chronic pancreatitis.

B Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is a common and underdiagnosed condition, which may present at any age. It is a hypersensitivity to gluten found in wheat, rye and barley. The gliadin fraction of the protein provokes an inflammatory response causing subtotal or total villous atrophy of the small bowel, resulting in malabsorption. It classically presents with a history of diarrhoea, weight loss, oral ulceration, lethargy and anaemia (folate, B 12 or iron-deficient). There is an association with dermatitis herpetiformis, a very pruritic polymorphic skin rash, and an increased risk of developing gastrointestinal malignancy. Treatment is by maintaining a strict diet avoiding foods containing wheat, rye, oats or barley. The clinical picture in this scenario is not consistent with Coeliac disease.

D Increased plasma renin activity

Patients with renin-secreting tumours are typically young (average age 22 years) and have severe hypertension and hypokalaemia. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) appears to be the diagnostic procedure of choice, since false-negative results occur with arteriography or renal vein renin sampling. Surgical removal of the tumour cures the disease. The clinical picture in this scenario is not consistent with increased plasma renin levels.

E Ulcerative colitis

Ulcerative colitis is characterised by recurring episodes of inflammation limited to the mucosal layer of the colon. It commonly involves the rectum and may extend in a proximal and continuous fashion to involve other parts of the colon. Patients with ulcerative colitis usually present with diarrhoea, which may be associated with blood. Bowel movements are frequent and small in volume as a result of rectal inflammation. Associated symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, urgency, tenesmus and incontinence. Patients with mainly distal disease may have constipation accompanied by frequent discharge of blood and mucus. The endoscopic findings in patients with ulcerative colitis include loss of vascular markings due to engorgement of the mucosa, giving it an erythematous appearance. In addition, granularity of the mucosa, petechiae, exudates, oedema, erosions, touch friability and spontaneous bleeding may be present. More severe cases may be associated with macro-ulcerations, profuse bleeding and copious exudates. The endoscopic findings in this scenario are not consistent with ulcerative colitis. 9508

questions.question:
An 82-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department in the early hours of the morning after vomiting blood. Her blood pressure is 125/85 mmHg, with a pulse of 89/min, you arrange routine bloods.

Around 30 min after arrival, she has a further small (100 ml) haematemesis. Her daughter is briefly questioned and reports that her mother has been previously well apart from mild indigestion and occasional angina.

She has not been taking any medication, has no history of gastrointestinal (GI) or liver disease and does not drink alcohol.

She is taken into the resuscitation room and her initial assessment is outlined below.

InvestigationResultNormal values
Bilirubin10 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)21 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Albumin40 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)80 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)300 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Prothrombin time (PT)12 s11 - 14 s
Pulse125 bpm
Blood pressure80/40 mmHg
Respiratory rate38/min

Which of the following would you instigate immediately?
options: High dose intravenous (IV) proton pump inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C 0.9% normal saline via peripheral cannula

The initial step in the management of upper GI haemorrhage is the assessment of hemodynamic state. A systolic blood pressure of 80mmHg identifies the patient as ‘High risk’ with severe acute bleeding. 0.9% saline via peripheral cannula is given immediately to stabilize the patient, making it the best answer. Urgent GI endoscopy is indicated as soon as possible in this patient after adequate resuscitation as there is increased risk of death due to bleeding in this patient in view of his age, blood pressure reading and history of ischemic heart disease.

A Triple lumen central line placement

Triple lumen Central line is desirable in conditions of significant cardiac overload, but it should not interfere with rapid volume resuscitation via large bore peripheral cannula.

B O negative (uncrossed) transfusion

Patients with evidence of hemodynamic compromised state are given IV fluids and cross-matched for 2-4 units of red blood cells. However, it is rarely required to administer type specific or O-negative transfusion. Blood loss seen in this patient should be replaced with crystalloid initially, followed by typed and cross-matched blood. Unmatched blood should only be used in patients with uncontrolled blood loss who are unresponsive to other fluid resuscitation.

D High dose intravenous (IV) proton pump inhibitor

High dose IV proton pump inhibitors have been shown to be of benefit in upper GI haemorrhage but only to prevent re-bleeding, and do not form an integral part of initial resuscitation attempts.

E IV Terlipressin

According to British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage, it is important to exclude variceal haemorrhage due to liver disease in any patient with significant hematemesis. Normal liver function tests and lack of history makes ‘oesophageal varices’ highly unlikely. Thus IV terlipressin is not recommended in this case. Teripressin is preferred in reducing bleeding, as it reduces blood flow in splanchnic circulation and decreases portal blood pressure.

questions.question:
A 51-year-old Chinese man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic with hepatitis B. He is teetotal.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Hepatitis B surface antigenPositiveNegative
Hepatitis B e antigenNegativeNegative
Hepatitis B virus (HBV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) level2100 copies/mlNegative
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)96 U/L5–30 IU/L Similar results were observed when these tests are repeated three months later and the liver biopsy shows early cirrhosis.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Close monitoring of liver function test
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Start pegylated interferon

The patient has e antigen-negative (eAg) chronic hepatitis B. The eAg negativity indicates there is no active viral replication; however, raised alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels and high viral titres indicate chronic active infection, which is confirmed on biopsy, thereby necessitating treatment. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines now recommend treatment in patients who meet the following criteria:

adults aged > 30 years with Hepatitis B virus (HBV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) > 2000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (> 30 IU/ml in men; > 19 IU/ml in women) on two consecutive tests, three months apart

adults aged < 30 years with HBV DNA > 2000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (> 30 IU/ml in men; > 19 IU/ml in women) on two consecutive tests, three months apart, if there is evidence of necro-inflammation or fibrosis on liver biopsy or a transient elastography score > 6 kPa adults who have HBV DNA > 20 000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (> 30 IU/ml in men; > 19 IU/ml in women) on two consecutive tests conducted three months apart, regardless of age or the extent of liver disease. patients without a liver biopsy with a transient elastography score > 11 kPa.

The NICE guidelines recommend first-line treatment with pegylated interferon alfa-2a in patients with compensated liver disease for 48 weeks. Entecavir and tenofovir are offered as second-line treatments where pegylated interferon therapy has failed or is not tolerated.

D Start pegylated interferon and ribavirin

This is offered as first-line therapy for patients with hepatitis C. However, NICE has recently recommended new antivirals for hepatitis C, eg sofosbuvir–velpatasvir (Epclusa®), and patients are being selected based on clinical need. Therefore, patients may elect to defer treatment with interferon–ribavirin due to its side-effect profile and opt to wait for the newer, better-tolerated antivirals.

A Close monitoring of liver function test

The patient has chronic hepatitis B with histological evidence of early cirrhosis, making treatment imperative to avoid progression to further fibrosis and to reduce hepatocellular carcinoma risk.

B Repeat biopsy in two years

Having established that the patient has early cirrhosis, it is clear that he requires treatment. Indications for a further biopsy would be in cases of suspected hepatocellular carcinoma or failure to respond to treatment and therefore exclude an alternative diagnosis. Transient elastography (FibroScan), as an assessment of liver stiffness and as a surrogate marker of cirrhosis, has reduced the number of biopsies performed before commencing antiviral therapy.

E Start lamivudine

Lamivudine is only indicated as an adjunct in patients who are hepatitis B e antigen-positive and with compensated liver disease and who, despite 96 weeks of tenofovir, still have detectable hepatitis B DNA or in patients who are likely to be immunocompromised for six months with hepatitis B DNA < 2000 IU/ml.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old pre-menopausal woman presented to her general practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of epigastric pain, occasionally retrosternal and worse at night. She had tried over-the-counter antacid preparations but had achieved no relief. Her weight was steady and bowel habit normal. There was no history of gastric malignancy in the family. Examination was unremarkable except for obesity. Full blood count is normal.

Which of the following describes the next best management step?
options: Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and review symptoms in one month
Start a PPI and perform a Carbon 13 urea breath test. If this is positive, prescribe pylori eradication therapy
Check repeat haemoglobin in three months. If low, then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy.
Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on a proton pump inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and review symptoms in one month

NICE guidelines state in this age group that dyspepsia, in the absence of alarm symptoms, should be treated with lifestyle advice and PPI if needed. In the event that symptoms of indigestion have not been relieved, H. pylori testing or upper GI endoscopy can then be considered.

D Check repeat haemoglobin in three months. If low, then refer for upper gastrointestinal (GI)

endoscopy.

This is the appropriate course of action where there are alarm features, these including weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass.

B Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy

A routine endoscopy would be considered where symptoms don’t improve after 1 month of empirical PPI

treatment.

C Start a PPI and perform a Carbon 13 urea breath test. If this is positive, prescribe pylori eradication

therapy

Urea breath testing for H. pylori should ideally be conducted off PPI for a period of at least 2 weeks.

E Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on a proton

pump inhibitor

This time period is too short to assess response to PPI therapy. At least four weeks of therapy to assess response is required. 8536

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male patient presents with non-bloody diarrhoea with mucus and 1-stone weight loss over six weeks. He has had no recent travel except to France for a holiday one year ago. All his family and friends are well but his uncle has diarrhoea for which he has to take tablets.

On examination, he looks unwell, his BMI is 21, BP is 110/70 mmHg, heart rate is 75/min and regular. His abdomen is soft but there is mild tenderness. You suspect inflammatory bowel disease and perform a sigmoidoscopy and biopsy.

Which one of the following findings would most favour a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis over Crohn’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Crypt abscesses

Ulcerative colitis is inflammation confined to the mucosa and lamina propria with crypt abscesses. The mucosal appearance is characterized by erosions, mucopus, and edema with a diffused involvement of large intestine

D Non-caseating granulomas

Non-caseating granuloma are present in less than 25 % of patients but highly suggestive of crohn’s disease.

B Ileitis

One third of crohn’s disease cases involve the small intestine (especially the terminal ileum) causing ileitis.

C Skip lesions

Skip lesions are seen characteristically in crohn’s disease, which are areas of normal appearing mucosa adjacent to inflamed mucosa.

E Large joint arthritis

Arthritis of large joints is associated with crohn’s disease, along with other conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis, conjunctivitis, episcleritis, sacroilitis.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic after presenting to his General Practitioner with a 1- year history of tiredness. He has no previous medical history and takes no regular medication. He denies weight loss or a change in bowel habits. He has a varied diet, including red meat. There is nothing to find on examination. Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)115 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.0 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)300 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)70 fL80 - 100 fL
Mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH)20 pg27 - 33 pg
Ferritin10 µg/L24 - 355 µg/L (male)
Vitamin B 12500 ng/L160 - 760 ng/L
Folate9 µg/L2.0 - 11.0 µg/L

Which of the following investigations should be performed next?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Urinalysis

In the developed world, iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) has a prevalence of 2–5% among adult men and post- menopausal women. The British Society of Gastroenterology published guidelines on the investigation of such patients. For the investigation of IDA, urinalysis for blood is recommended, as an estimated 1% of patients with IDA will have renal tract malignancy caused by haematuria and haemosiderin deposition in the tumour. This is a non-invasive test and, therefore, should be performed next on this patient. A faecal occult blood test is also indicated.

C Colonoscopy

This would be indicated, particularly to exclude malignancy as a cause for this patient’s anaemia. However, it would not be the next test that is performed, as it is an invasive procedure.

B Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy

In all men, post-menopausal women and women aged over 50 years, mandatory investigations for IDA include an oesophageal-gastro-duodenoscopy, looking for a source of occult bleeding. However, this would not be the next test you would perform.

D Iron studies

Iron studies in this patient would reveal a low iron level and high total iron binding capacity. This does nothing but confirm the iron deficiency anaemia we know exists. Iron studies might be useful in cases where iron deficiency is suspected but ferritin is high due to a presumed inflammatory response or in iron overload.

E Capsule endoscopy

This investigation is usually reserved for patients who have a normal OGD and colonoscopy but remain anaemic despite iron replacement therapy. This investigation is then performed to rule out a small bowel cause for their anaemia such as Crohn’s disease or angiodysplasia.

questions.question:
A 59-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an acute upper GI bleed. He admits to having had symptoms of indigestion for the past 6 months, he smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks 30 units of alcohol per week. Most recently he has been taking ibuprofen for a back injury.

On examination, is blood pressure (BP) is 110/70 mmHg, with a pulse of 90/min; on moving from lying to sitting, his systolic falls to 90 mmHg and his pulse increases to 105/min. He is acutely tender in the epigastrium and vomits up a mix of fresh and altered blood after the consultation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin87 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets152 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine110 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urea18.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Albumin38 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)24 IU/L5–30 IU/L Large bleeding DU, Upper GI endoscopy injected during the procedure

Which of the following further interventions has been shown to positively impact on prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C IV omeprazole

IV omeprazole has been proven in a number of meta-analyses to impact positively on mortality when used in addition to optimal endoscopic therapy. The aim of IV PPI therapy is to increase the pH in the stomach to promote coagulation. Oral PPI has also been shown to reduce the length of hospital stay and re-bleeding rates.

B Oral lactulose

Lactulose is used to reduce absorption and production of ammonia from a blood meal in patients with liver failure who have had a significant GI bleed.

A Oral propranolol

Oral propranolol is used as a chronic treatment in patients with proven portal hypertension and varices.

D Oral famotidine

Oral H2 receptor antagonists have not been shown to reduce the risk of ulcer re-bleeding.

E IV terlipressin

Terlipressin is an acute treatment that has a role in the management of variceal bleeding. This patient has risk factors and history suggestive of peptic ulcer disease, and a bleeding duodenal ulcer is found on upper GI endoscopy.

Leontiadis GI, Sreedharan A, Dorward S, et al. Systematic reviews of the clinical effectiveness and cost- effectiveness of proton pump inhibitors in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Health Technol Assess. Dec 2007;11(51):iii-iv, 1-164.

questions.question:
You are asked to review a 65-year-old retired politician in the Coronary Care Unit who was admitted 6 days ago with a non ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).

On admission, he was haemodynamically stable and apyrexial. He developed atrial fibrillation 24 h after admission and was commenced on intravenous digoxin.

On questioning, he complains of severe abdominal pain, which is initially dull in nature but has now become sharp and radiates to his back. This pain is precipitated by meals and he finds it worse after food. He has never had similar symptoms previously and denies any chest pain. His drug chart shows that he is currently on aspirin, clopidogrel, digoxin, low molecular weight heparin, atorvastatin, omeprazole and regular salbutamol inhalers.

He was diagnosed with non-insulin-dependent diabetes 6 years ago, and had an inferior myocardial infarction 2 years after that. There is a strong family history of ischaemic heart disease. He is also hypertensive and has mild chronic obstructive airway disease. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks a glass of brandy in the evening.

On examination, he looks pale and unwell. He has xanthelasma. His heart rate is 120 beats/min and regular and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. His temperature is 37.5 °C and saturation is 98% on 2 l oxygen. The jugular venous pressure is not visible and there is a soft systolic murmur at the apex. He has a left carotid bruit. There are sparse bibasal crackles on chest examination. His abdomen is tender in the epigastric and umbilical area. There is no palpable aortic aneurysm or ascites. Scanty bowel sounds are audible.

Investigations are as below:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)220 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)93 fL80 - 100 fL
International normalized ratio (INR) 1.3< 1.1
Sodium (Na⁺)141 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.3 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea14.0 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)147 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)15 mmol/L22 - 29 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)34 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Liver function testsNormal
Amylase380 U/L23 - 85 U/L
ElectrocardiogramSinus tachycardia and Q waves on inferior leads
Chest and abdominal radiographsNormal

Which of the following is likely to be the most useful next investigation?
options: CT scan of the abdomen with angiography
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E CT scan of the abdomen with angiography

CT scan of the abdomen with angiography. The combination of acute abdominal pain 15-30 min post-meal, relative hypotension (note normal hypertensive) and acidosis all point towards acute mesenteric ischaemia. The condition is often associated with modest elevations in amylase. He is diabetic, a long-term smoker and has had a cardiac event in the past. All these favour atherosclerosis, making the diagnosis of intestinal ischaemia more likely in this situation, although other differential diagnosis includes acute or chronic pancreatitis. Carcinoma of the pancreas normally has a more insidious onset. Increased intestinal motility after a meal exacerbates ischaemia, causing pain. Mesenteric ischaemia is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion. In this situation a computed tomography (CT) scan will help exclude necrosis of the pancreas, and mesenteric angiography would help validate the clinical suspicion of mesenteric ischaemia. The patient will probably need a laparotomy, which will be high risk in view of recent coronary event, but mortality is extremely high without surgery. An arterial blood gas will no doubt show a metabolic acidosis, and amylase can be normal in chronic pancreatitis.

A Blood cultures

Blood cultures may reveal evidence of bowel pathogens, but they won’t reveal the underlying cause of this patient’s acute presentation.

B Urgent digoxin level

Given there is tachycardia, and no signs of digoxin toxicity such as yellow vision, nausea or vomiting, digoxin toxicity is very unlikely.

C Creatine kinase

There are no specific pointers towards a further myocardial infarction or towards rhabdomyolysis.

D Re-check troponin

The presentation with abdominal pain and hypotension is much more consistent with a primary abdominal cause rather than an acute myocardial infarction.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of intermittent jaundice and right upper quadrant pain.

She drinks minimal alcohol and is a non-smoker. She had an emergency surgery many years ago when she presented with diarrhoea and abdominal pain.

On examination, she is mildly icteric. There is no lymphadenopathy. There is a visible scar on the abdomen.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Bilirubin101 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)54 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)370 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyl transferase (γGT)240 IU/L5–30 IU/L

What is the most likely operation she has had in the past?
options: Left lobectomy of the liver for carcinoid tumour
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Ileal resection for Crohn’s disease

Her predominantly cholestatic liver function tests and abdominal pain would be consistent with biliary calculi/choledocolithiasis. Ileal resection reduces the reabsorption of bile salts and as a result, a reduction in the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts. This, in turn increases the risk of cholesterol stone formation.

C Right hemicolectomy for caecal carcinoma

Although part of the ileum may be resected in a right hemicolectomy (and thus lead to bile salt malabsorption), this is not guaranteed whereas ileal resection for Crohn’s disease is much more likely to lead to this side effect.

A Partial gastrectomy for gastric ulcer

This is associated with an increased frequency of iron deficiency anaemia and B 12 deficiency (due to the reduced acidic environment required to convert Fe3+ to the more absorbable Fe2+ and the reduction in parietal cells to produce intrinsic factor).

D Left lobectomy of the liver for carcinoid tumour

Left liver lobectomy is not associated with the formation of gallstones. Indeed, depending on the position of the tumour the gall bladder may need to be resected as well.

E Jejunal resection for gastrointestinal lymphoma

Depending on the length resected, small bowel resection may result in short bowel syndrome characterised by malabsorption, maldigestion and malnutrition and frequently diarrhoea. However, it is not associated with the formation of gallstones.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her husband, complaining of upper abdominal and lower chest pain radiating to the back. As part of their fortieth wedding anniversary celebrations, they had been out for a large meal, at which they had consumed more alcohol than they were normally used to. On returning home, she had become nauseated and had vomited three times, and developed sudden-onset upper abdominal and lower chest pain and, subsequently shortness of breath.

On examination, she is tachycardic with a heart rate of 105 bpm, and tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations of 94% on air, and has a temperature of 37.8 °C. On abdominal examination, there is firmness in the upper abdomen.

A CXR is completed and is shown below:

By Jto410 (In my work as a radiologist) [GFDL (http://www.gnu.org/copyleft/fdl.html) or CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia Commons

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Boerhaave syndrome

Boerhaave syndrome is defined as a spontaneous (as opposed to an iatrogenic) oesophageal rupture. It is classically associated with violent vomiting and is more common in men than in women. It most commonly occurs in the distal oesophagus and typically affects the left posterior wall. Unlike in Mallory–Weiss syndrome (in which a partial-thickness tear occurs), haematemesis is uncommon in Boerhaave syndrome. Instead, the classic presentation is vomiting, followed by sudden onset of severe retrosternal chest pain/upper abdominal pain. Other symptoms may include shortness of breath, odynophagia and pleuritic pain.

Clinical findings include surgical emphysema, pleural effusions (normally left-sided, as this is where the perforation tends to be) and – depending upon the interval between onset and presentation – features of mediastinitis.

A CXR may be normal early in the disease process but can demonstrate pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax,

subcutaneous emphysema and pleural effusions as the condition progresses. The X-ray shows streaky linear opacities tracking down the mediastinum, which indicates subcutaneous emphysemam and, therefore, pneumomediastinum.

CT scans may confirm the diagnosis and demonstrate any associated collections. In contrast, the pattern of contrast extravasation on a water-soluble contrast swallow helps to define the anatomy and extent of the leak. Definitive management of the condition is surgical.

E Spontaneous pneumothorax

The radiological findings make a spontaneous pneumothorax very unlikely to be the unifying diagnosis. Severe coughing and vomiting can precipitate a spontaneous pneumothorax. However, the history and clinical features are more suggestive of Boerhaave syndrome.

A Aspiration pneumonitis

Although vomiting, particularly while intoxicated or with a reduced GCS score, may predispose patients to aspiration pneumonitis, the presence of severe lower chest and abdominal pain makes pneumonitis less likely. The CXR findings show a pneumomediastinum, more likely to be secondary to oesophageal rupture from

vomiting.

C Mallory–Weiss tear

A Mallory–Weiss tear is unlikely here, given the lack of haematemesis and the systemic response following the

vomiting.

D Perforated peptic ulcer

A perforated peptic ulcer could explain the vomiting and abdominal discomfort but would not explain the CXR

findings.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old woman is referred to the Cardiology Clinic with a heart murmur and symptoms of flushing, especially when she drinks alcohol. She has a history of atrial fibrillation and thyroid disease.

An echocardiogram and ultrasound scan are arranged, but she misses her appointments and defaults to follow- up.

Nine months later, she re-presents to the Emergency Department with widespread pigmentation on her face and neck, confusion and diarrhoea.

What is the cause for her new symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Pellagra

Pellagra is characterised by the ‘4Ds’, which are dementia, diarrhoea, dermatitis and death. The rash is photosensitive and normally affects the face, neck and forearm. It is rare and can be either primary or secondary. Primary causes include niacin or tryptophan (precursor of niacin) deficiency. Secondary causes include carcinoid syndrome, which is what this woman has. Patients with carcinoid get pellagra as the tumour cells convert tryptophan to serotonin, thereby reducing endogenous niacin production. It can also present in patients with anorexia nervosa, chronic alcoholism, gastrointestinal tuberculosis and human immunodeficiency virus. In carcinoid syndrome, patients develop right-sided valvular disease and, if she has attended for her echocardiogram, the possible findings are tricuspid incompetence or pulmonary stenosis.

C Cerebral abscess

A cerebral abscess is a focal collection within the brain parenchyma. It can occur either through direct spread

from the ears, sinuses or oropharynx, or by haematogenous spread. It presents with headache, changes in mental state and fever. The absence of high fever and headache, and the presence of diarrhoea and rash, makes this a less likely diagnosis.

A Cerebral systemic lupus erythematosus

SLE is an idiopathic chronic inflammatory disease which is characterised by the presence of antinuclear antibodies. Presentation is varied as SLE can affect virtually any organ. In some patients the presentation can be neuropsychiatric, causing a broad range of neurological deficits which could explain this patient’s confusion. However, the skin involvement in SLE is usually in the form of a butterfly rash or discoid lesions, rather than the type of pigmentation this patient has, which is why this is a less likely diagnosis. In addition, SLE is not a good explanation for diarrhoea.

B Cerebral tuberculosis

TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which can cause infection in almost any organ. In 1% of TB cases the presentation is with tuberculous meningitis. This presents with a subacute febrile illness preceded by an insidious headache and malaise, then characterised by meningismus, vomiting and confusion. It can proceed to coma as well. It is of much higher risk in the presence of HIV. Whilst this could be an explanation for her confusion, the absence of meningism and headache makes this a less likely diagnosis, which also could not explain her rash.

D Amiodarone toxicity

Amiodarone is an anti-arrhythmic drug which can cause multiple side effects. In the lungs it can cause interstitial pneumonitis, in the thyroid it can cause both hyper- and hypothyroidism, and it also causes AV block, photosensitivity rash and gastrointestinal upset. Whilst it could explain many of the patient’s symptoms, including a rash which could be photosensitive in nature, it would not explain the confusion or the previous murmur.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to Outpatients after noticing the whites of her eyes changing colour. She is 36 weeks’ pregnant with her first child. She feels well in herself and has no relevant past medical history other than a transient episode of jaundice in her late teens, and takes no medication. There is no history of recent travel. Clinical examination reveals icteric sclerae and excoriations on the upper arms.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Bilirubin150 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)150 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)600 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Albumin40 g/L35–55 g/L
UrinalysisBilirubin +++
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)350 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Prothrombin time (PT)17 s10.6–14.9 s

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets)
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Cholestasis of pregnancy

Cholestasis of pregnancy is by far the most likely diagnosis. This condition is caused by a bile acid transporter defect and usually manifests in the last trimester. It is not associated with significant constitutional symptoms for the mother, although the risk of stillbirth and postpartum haemorrhage is slightly increased. Milder episodes may have occurred earlier in life associated with hormonal contraception, and it recurs in subsequent pregnancies. Prothrombin time may be prolonged in any cholestatic process due to deficiency of vitamin K. Pre-eclampsia, HELLP syndrome and acute fatty liver of pregnancy form a spectrum of disease known as toxaemias of pregnancy. All are associated with constitutional symptoms and are potentially life-threatening.

A Pre-eclampsia

Pre-eclampsia is defined as pregnancy-induced hypertension with proteinuria. There can also be oedema, but this is not essential for a diagnosis. It can become life-threatening and any organ can be affected. Blood pressure would by greater than 160/100 mmHg and proteinuria should be greater than 0.3 g/24 h. Eclampsia is evidenced by convulsions following features of pre-eclampsia. The patient may present with severe headache, new oedema, RUQ tenderness or visual disturbances, and examination can show oedema, clonus and papilloedema. Pre-eclampsia is associated with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) in 20% of cases, but jaundice is unusual in all but severe cases and proteinuria would be expected.

B HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets)

The vast majority of cases occur with pre-eclampsia and this has similar clinical features, but with the addition of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets. The absence of a low platelet count excludes HELP.

D Hepatitis E

Hepatitis E is an enterically spread RNA virus, the epidemic form of which has a high (10–20%) mortality in pregnant women in developing countries. It is especially common in India, but in the absence of any travel history this is a very unlikely diagnosis.

E Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

This is a rare condition which tends to occur late in pregnancy and is associated with first pregnancy and pre- eclampsia. It is associated with nausea, vomiting, fever, headache and pruritis and can present with jaundice on examination. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is associated with abnormalities of synthetic function, and therefore serum albumin would be expected to be low. The absence of clinical symptoms as well makes this unlikely.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of feeling unwell and very lethargic. He is a known hypertensive. His wife tells you he has been rather stressed at work recently and is drinking fairly heavily.

As a child, he was found to have an abnormality in the structure of his heart though she is not sure what this is, but she does know that he has had problems with palpitations.

In Accident and Emergency, he has two generalised tonic-clonic seizures, which are treated with intravenous lorazepam.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)134 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)122 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils8.4 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.58 ×10⁹/L
Bilirubin44 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Cholesterol6.0 mmol/L< 5.2 mmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)647 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)110 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyl-transferase (γGT)540 IU/L5–30 IU/L
C-reactive Protein (CRP)84 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Total Protein50 g/L60–80 g/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.4< 1.0
Albumin28 g/L35–55 g/L

Which of the following drugs is the best choice for the long-term treatment of his seizures?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Lamotrigine

The most important intervention is for this patient to stop drinking, although this should take place under cover of a reducing course of benzodiazepines. Lamotrigine is an appropriate first-line intervention for seizures: it has the advantage of not being a CYP450 enzyme inducer or inhibitor, and has data suggesting it may reduce long- term alcohol dependence.

A Sodium valproate

Sodium valproate should not be used in patients with hepatic dysfunction, because it is a CYP450 inhibitor. Additionally, MHRA advice (due to the risk of impaired fertility in men and teratogenicity in women) suggests that no patient under the age of 55 should be commenced on valproate unless two consultants agree that there is no suitable alternative treatment.

C Gabapentin

Gabapentin is a normal adjunctive therapy for patients with persistent seizures despite starting a first-line agent; as such, it’s not the appropriate choice here.

D Vigabatrin

Vigabatrin is associated with peripheral visual field defects in up to 1/3 of users. It is also associated with suicidal ideation, and is therefore not an ideal option in a patient with alcoholism.

E Carbamazepine

Carbamazepine is a potent CYP450 enzyme inducer, and it may also be associated with AV conduction defects and is therefore not ideal in a patient with congenital heart disease.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old premenopausal woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of epigastric pain that is occasionally retrosternal and worse at night. She has tried over-the-counter antacid preparations and esomeprazole which have achieved no relief. Her weight is steady and her bowel habits are normal. There is no history of gastric malignancy in the family. The examination is unremarkable, except for the fact that the patient is obese. The full blood count is normal.

Which of the following describes the next best management step?
options: Arrange upper GI endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on an alternative proton pump inhibitor (PPI)
Check repeat haemoglobin level in three months; if low, refer for upper GI endoscopy
Start an alternative PPI and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test; if positive, prescribe Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy
Stop esomeprazole and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test after two weeks
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Stop esomeprazole and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test after two weeks

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that in this age group, dyspepsia, in the absence of alarm symptoms, should be treated with lifestyle advice and a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) if needed. In the event that symptoms of indigestion have not been relieved, H. pylori testing or upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy can then be considered. However, PPI therapy needs to have been stopped for two weeks before H. pylori testing, due to the risk of a false-negative result.

D Start an alternative PPI and perform a carbon-13 urea breath test; if positive, prescribe Helicobacter

pylori eradication therapy

Urea breath testing for H. pylori should ideally be conducted off PPI therapy for a period of at least two weeks.

A Arrange upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy

A routine endoscopy would be considered where symptoms do not improve after one month of empirical proton

pump inhibitor (PPI) treatment.

B Arrange upper GI endoscopy if symptoms do not settle in two weeks on an alternative proton pump

inhibitor (PPI)

Patients with dyspepsia without any alarm features should ideally be tested for H. pylori infection before more invasive endoscopy is considered.

C Check repeat haemoglobin level in three months; if low, refer for upper GI endoscopy

This is the appropriate course of action where there are alarm features, including weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass. 72962

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening abdominal distension, severe epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. She was previously fit and well with no significant past medical history and the only medication she took was the oral contraceptive pill. There was no relevant family history. She smoked 10 cigarettes per day and drank approximately 12 units of alcohol per week. On examination, she was unwell, drowsy and deeply jaundiced. She was apyrexial. Her heart sounds were normal, her chest was clear to auscultation and she had peripheral oedema. Her abdomen was distended with shifting dullness and tender hepatomegaly. There were no focal neurological signs.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)132 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)82 fL76–98 fL
Urea7.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Bilirubin120 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)410 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)900 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyl-transferase (γGT)850 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Albumin29 g/L35–55 g/L
Prothrombin time (PT)30 s10.6–14.9 s Ascitic fluid analysis reveals the following:
InvestigationResult
Protein17 g/L
Neutrophils80 cells/mm 3
Gram stainNo organisms seen
Amylase100 IU/L

Which investigation should be performed next?
options: Colour flow Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Colour flow Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature

The diagnosis is Budd–Chiari syndrome. Doppler ultrasound will show obliteration of the hepatic veins and abnormalities of the direction of blood flow in the remainder of the hepatic vasculature. Budd-Chiari syndrome is defined as the obstruction of venous outflow from the liver caused by hepatic vein occlusion. The most common cause is thrombosis, usually in association with a hypercoagulable state, in conditions such as primary polycythaemia, thombophilias and leukaemia. There is also an association with the oral contraceptive pill. Other causes include malignancy (especially hepatocellular, renal and adrenal), radiotherapy, trauma and congenital venous webs. The cause is unknown in one-third of cases. It can present either acutely or chronically. In the acute from, there is abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, ascites, tender hepatomegaly and sometimes fulminant hepatic failure. The chronic form presents more insidiously, with signs of cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Ascitic fluid analysis will show a high serum ascitic albumin gradient (SAAG= serum albumin – ascitic fluid albumin) and is classified as a transudate.. An enlarged caudate lobe may be seen on ultrasound/computed tomography (CT)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the liver. Liver biopsy usually shows centrilobular congestion with fibrosis. Management includes treating the underlying cause, portocaval shunts and TIPSS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunt). Treatment with streptokinase and subsequent anticoagulation may be attempted if the thrombus is known to be of recent onset. Liver transplantation is the only option in the acute presentation, which has a very poor prognosis, with two-thirds of patients dead within 1 year.

A Serum alpha-fetoprotein

A rising alpha-fetoprotein may be seen in hepatocellular carcinoma, known to be associated with Budd-Chiari

syndrome, but isn’t specific for the condition itself.

C Liver biopsy

Liver biopsy usually shows centrilobular congestion with fibrosis which is related to pressure and flow changes within the liver, but this isn’t the next investigation here.

D Anti-mitochondrial antibodies

Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive in primary biliary cholangitis, a disease of insidious onset, which usually presents with tiredness, lethargy and itching, rather than the acute deterioration seen here.

E Serum caeruloplasmin

This is an investigation for Wilson’s disease, which presents with abnormal transaminases either picked up incidentally or associated with neuropsychiatric features, rather than the acute deterioration seen here.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with a history of abdominal pain and distension for the past 7 days.

On examination, she is found to have jaundice, a smooth, 5 cm hepatomegaly and ascites. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease and she does not take any regular medication.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)150 g/L115–155 g/L
White Cell Count (WCC)11.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.7 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)200 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urea20 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
