Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT)50 s23.0–35.0 s
Prothrombin Test (PT)13 s10.6–14.9 s

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Budd–Chiari syndrome

The prolonged APTT in the presence of a normal PT is suggestive of lupus anticoagulant, which would be consistent with anti-phospholipid syndrome, well recognised as a cause of Budd–Chiari syndrome. Budd-Chiari syndrome commonly presents with a triad of abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and ascites. It is a rare condition caused by occlusion to the hepatic vein. Treatment is with anticoagulation, surgery or a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure.

C Glomerulonephritis

This would not explain the hepatomegaly and jaundice.

A Alcoholic liver disease

Although this could account for her presentation, there is no mention of excessive alcohol intake in the history and her presentation is far more typical of Budd-Chiari syndrome.

B Right heart failure

Although this might cause an engorged liver and ascites, it would not explain her clotting abnormalities.

E Metastatic liver disease

You would not expect to feel a smooth liver in this case, and the ascitic fluid tap is more likely to be exudative in malignancy rather than transudative.

questions.question: Which of the following should be the next step?
options: Colonoscopy and removal of the object
Laparotomy and removal of the object
Monitor with weekly X-rays to ensure passage through the GI tract
Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy and removal of the object
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy and removal of the object

While most ingested foreign objects will pass through the GI tract without complication, there are certain instances where intervention is required.

The presence of large objects that are unlikely to negotiate the duodenum, sharp objects, batteries and multiple magnets are indications for intervention. After four hours, these swallowed foreign bodies are still located proximally, which suggests that they cannot pass through the pyloric sphincter to the duodenum. Furthermore, the close contact of the two objects is suspicious for magnet ingestion. Urgent endoscopic intervention is required to remove these objects.

(Of note, narcotic packages should probably not be removed endoscopically, because of the risk of accidental rupture.)

C Laparotomy and removal of the object

This is not the optimal course of action for this situation. Currently the object is easily accessible via endoscopy, given its proximal location.

A Colonoscopy and removal of the object

Colonoscopy is usually not indicated, as once the foreign object has passed distally, it is likely to pass naturally with a bowel motion. Furthermore, colonoscopy would only be indicated for a more distally located foreign body, which is not seen here.

B Gastrointestinal stimulation with metoclopramide

Because of where the object appears to be lodged, advising metoclopramide or other GI stimulants runs the risk of significant pain and potentially even oesophageal rupture.

D Monitor with weekly X-rays to ensure passage through the GI tract

Where endoscopic removal is not possible or is contraindicated, an alternative strategy is for daily X-rays to monitor the progress of more distal objects, and for surgery to be considered for objects that do not move for 72 hours and/or people in whom symptoms develop. This would be the alternative strategy if the patient was deemed to have capacity and refused endoscopy. 73452

questions.question:
A 44-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of shortness of breath and tiredness. She recently started oral steroids prescribed by her General Practitioner for an intensely itchy, vesicular rash on the elbows, knees, buttocks and back. She also gives a history of mild diarrhoea and abdominal bloating and has lost a stone in weight. Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)56 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)90 fL80 - 100 fL
White cell count (WCC)5.8 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)387 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Red cell distribution width (RDW)22 %11.8 - 14.5 %
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.4 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea4.4 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)99 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Albumin3.2 g/dl3.4 - 5.4 g/dl
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.0 mmol/L2.2 - 2.7 mmol/L
Bilirubin25 µmol/L1 - 22 µmol/L

Which of the following is most likely to be contributing to her anaemia?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Iron deficiency due to malabsorption

The constellation of anaemia, weight loss, diarrhoea and bloating – together with a pruritic rash on the extensor surfaces – is highly suggestive of this patient having coeliac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis.

Coeliac disease may present in various ways, but iron deficiency anaemia is not an infrequent presentation. In contrast, folate deficiency may also occur in the condition; B₁₂ deficiency is less common, as this vitamin is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Hypocalcaemia may also occur due to malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D. Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely pruritic, vesicular rash that typically affects the elbows, scalp and extensor surfaces of the forearms and buttocks. It is more common in men and may occur at any age, although it tends to present in young adulthood. It is normally – if not exclusively – associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy.

Treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis includes strict adherence to a gluten-free diet. Dapsone may be effective in controlling the rash but is often associated with mild, dose-related haemolytic anaemia. Haemolysis can, however, be dramatic in people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Monitoring of liver function tests and a full blood count is advised, as dapsone may also rarely cause liver dysfunction and aplastic anaemia. Drug treatment can often be withdrawn after a period of adherence to a gluten-free diet.

A Anaemia of chronic disease

Anaemia of chronic disease is associated with normochromic normocytic anaemia but would only be entertained as a diagnosis once other causes of anaemia, including iron deficiency, have been ruled out.

B Autoimmune haemolysis

The clinical presentation here is much more consistent with coeliac disease, which is not associated with haemolysis. Although dapsone, occasionally prescribed for dermatitis herpetiformis, may lead to haemolysis, this is not seen with corticosteroids.

C Bone marrow failure

Bone marrow failure is unlikely in the context of an isolated anaemia. It would be more likely to be bone marrow failure if there were associated thrombocytopenia and leukopenia.

E Pernicious anaemia

Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune disorder characterised by atrophic gastritis and a reduction of parietal cells in the gastric mucosa, leading to vitamin B₁₂ malabsorption. The MCV here is inconsistent with isolated B₁₂ deficiency. The MCV of 90, together with increased RDW and symptoms of coeliac disease, is more consistent with a mixed picture of iron and B₁₂ vitamin deficiencies. 73451

questions.question:
A 46-year-old man is admitted from the clinic with dysphagia and weight loss. Over the last few months, he has found that it has been progressively harder to swallow solids. He was able to swallow them but he had to regurgitate them about 30 minutes later.

Over the last few weeks, he has been having increasing difficulty with fluids. He has previously been in good health and never smoked. He drinks half a bottle of wine at weekends and the only other history of note has been long-term dyspepsia for which he uses antacids.

On examination, there is nothing to find except some mild tenderness on palpation in the epigastric area.

Barium swallow – oesophagus appears dilated and the distal oesophagus is narrowed. Oesophageal manometry – incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter in response to swallowing with high resting pressure. Absent oesophageal peristalsis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Achalasia

Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder characterised by failure of a hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter to relax and the absence of normal oesophageal peristalsis. Oesophageal manometry will demonstrate findings as for our patient. An OGD should be carried out to make sure there is no cancer.

The goal of therapy for achalasia is to relieve symptoms by eliminating the outflow resistance caused by the hypertensive and non-relaxing sphincter. This can be accomplished by mechanical disruption of the muscle fibres of the lower oesophageal sphincter (e.g. pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy or per-oral endoscopic

myotomy) or by pharmacological reduction of oesophageal sphincter pressure (e.g. injection of botulinum toxin, oral nitrates or calcium channel blockers).

C Plummer–Vinson syndrome

Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a triad of iron deficiency anaemia, dysphagia and a cervical oesophageal web. It is more common in women, and may be associated with glossitis, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, splenomegaly, an enlarged thyroid and symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia. Oesophageal webs characteristically cause intermittent solid food dysphagia. These typically arise from the anterior wall, or are circumferential, and are best seen on barium swallow as they are more easily missed on endoscopy due to their proximal nature. The barium swallow report for this patient is not consistent with an oesophageal web.

B Oesophageal cancer

The dysphagia is usually for solids, with the possibility of difficulty swallowing liquids in advanced disease. Barium swallow would show obstruction by the tumour, rather than the characteristic ‘bird’s beak’ appearance of achalasia, as described in this case.

D Oesophageal candidiasis

Oesophageal candidiasis is more likely to cause retrosternal odynophagia rather than a progressive dysphagia. Patients usually have a history of immunosuppression, of which there is no suggestion in this case. In severe cases, barium swallow may reveal an irregular, ‘shaggy’ appearance to the oesophagus due to pseudo- membrane formation.

E Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

This patient has reported dyspepsia, suggesting possible gastro-oesophgeal reflux. While barium swallow studies could reveal obstruction from a peptic stricture in the context of long-standing gastro-oesophageal reflux, the oesophageal dilation and abnormal manometry findings would not be present in simple gastro- oesophageal reflux disease. 6872

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman with a history of ulcerative colitis comes to the Emergency Department with an exacerbation. She is opening her bowels some ten times per day with bloody diarrhoea. She tells you that she stopped taking oral mesalazine some eight weeks ago after she found out she is pregnant with her first child. She is now 16 weeks pregnant. On examination, her BP is 105/70 mmHg and his heart rate 88 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft but generally tender. She has active bowel sounds.

Investigations;

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)98 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)387 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)75 mm/1 sthour0–10 mm in the 1 sthour
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin31 g/L35–55 g/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her exacerbation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Oral Mesalazine and oral Prednisolone

While no randomised controlled trials of 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) compounds exist specifically in pregnant women, they are generally thought to be safe, with animal studies revealing no evidence of teratogenicity. As such, it is most appropriate to restart oral mesalazine and to add oral prednisolone to gain control of the exacerbation.

A Azathioprine and Prednisolone

Research suggests that azathioprine is less effective than mesalazine in controlling symptoms, although it is also an appropriate option from the point of view of safety for use in pregnancy.

B Mycophenolate mofetil

Mycophenolate mofetil use during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk for malformations and first- trimester pregnancy loss. The most frequent malformations include external ear and other facial malformations such as cleft palate and lip. As we know that there are safer options in this case, mycophenolate mofetil should be avoided.

D Prednisolone

Prednisolone would be a reasonable option to control the exacerbation, but it should be done in conjunction with restarting mesalazine.

E Rectal Mesalazine and Predsol enemas

The generalised abdominal tenderness raises the possibility of more than just rectal disease. For this reason, rectal mesalazine and prednisolone are unlikely to be effective.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old sales assistant undergoes upper endoscopy for symptoms of dyspepsia. The OGD demonstrates a duodenal lesion and biopsies have returned showing a MALT lymphoma.

What would be the best initial therapeutic strategy?
options: Test and treat for Helicobacter pylori
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Test and treat for Helicobacter pylori

A MALT lymphoma is a B-cell tumour caused by an immune response to chronic H. pylori (HP) infection. The

first therapeutic strategy in treating a GI MALT lymphoma is to eradicate HP with a regimen of standard antibiotics and PPI, which leads to remission in 75% of cases. HP eradication regimens are usually given to all patients, due to the possibility of negative HP results. Patients should undergo a Carbon-13 urea breath test (UBT) approximately ≥6 weeks after eradication therapy and ≥2 weeks after PPI withdrawal, to confirm eradication.

The carbon-13 UBT is based on the detection of the products created when urea is split by the organism. Patients are asked to drink urea (usually with a beverage) labelled with a carbon isotope (carbon-13 or -14). After a certain duration, the concentration of the labelled carbon is measured on the breath. The concentration is high only when urease is present in the stomach. Because the human stomach does not produce urease, such a reaction is possible only with HP infection. Problems include negative results due to infection with coccoid forms of HP that do not produce as much urease; and intake of antibiotics, bismuth, histamine-2 (H2) blockers, or proton pump inhibitors.

In the minority of patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, irradiation and systemic oncological therapies should be considered, depending on the stage of disease.

A Duodenal stent insertion

There is no suggestion from the history that the patient is suffering from symptoms of upper gastrointestinal tract or gastric outlet obstruction.

B Radiotherapy

In patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, radiotherapy with curative intent might be the preferred option for localised-stage disease. However, this is not an initial treatment strategy for this patient.

C Chemotherapy

In patients who do not achieve lymphoma regression following antibiotic therapy, chemo-immunotherapy with cyclophosphamide or chlorambucil may play a role in management, but this would not be an initial treatment strategy for this patient.

D Laparoscopic resection

Endoscopic mucosal resection and resectional surgery are rarely needed. In such instances, this would follow failure of initial medical therapies.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic alcoholism presents to the clinic with increased abdominal swelling. She has noticed increasing abdominal girth over the past 4-6 months.

On examination, there are signs of chronic liver disease, including spider naevi and ascites, and she also has jaundiced sclerae. Her BP is 100/65 mmHg.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)105 g/L135 - 175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)107 fL80 - 100 fL
White cell count (WCC)5.6 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)202 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)85 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
CA-12565 u/ml< 35 u/ml

What is the most likely cause for the increased CA-125?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Cirrhosis

The patient has clinical features of chronic liver disease and the alcohol history makes cirrhosis the most likely option. Cirrhosis with ascites is a well recognised cause of a false positive CA125.

C Colonic carcinoma

Colon cancer can produce a falsely positive CA-125. However, this patient clearly has signs of chronic liver disease.

A Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B infection is not strongly associated with an elevated CA-125.

B Ovarian carcinoma

A patient presenting with ascites and a raised CA-125 raises the suspicion of ovarian cancer, however, there is

a clear alcohol history and the patient has features of chronic liver disease. Although CA-125 is often used to screen for ovarian cancer there are multiple conditions that also result in an elevated CA-125 (including cirrhosis and ascites, other intra-abdominal cancers, endometriosis, PID, fibroids, pancreatitis and heart failure amongst others).

If ovarian cancer is suspected, NICE recommend using the “Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI)”, which combines transvaginal US, menopausal status and CA-125 level to assess the risk. All women with a score >250 should be referred for specialist assessment.

In women where there is a family history of ovarian carcinoma, genetic screening for BRCA1/2 is recommended as the preferred method for assessing future ovarian carcinoma risk.

D Hepatocellular carcinoma

HCC is not associated with a rise in CA-125 (although it may be elevated in a patient with HCC as HCC occurs as a consequence of cirrhosis). Alfa-fetoprotein can be elevated in HCC.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old woman who has undergone multiple small bowel resections comes to the clinic for review. She is finding it virtually impossible to maintain her weight and suffers from chronic diarrhoea. On examination, her blood pressure is 103/80 mmHg; her pulse is 80 bpm and regular. She has a healed laparotomy scar on her abdomen. Her body mass index is 19. She was tried with total parenteral nutrition but unable to be weaned from it.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)87 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)162 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)85 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)11 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Albumin22 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)39 U/L7–55 U/L
Bilirubin12 µmol/L1–22 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most effective next intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Teduglutide

The answer is Teduglutide.

Teduglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 2 agonist, which promotes small bowel mucosal growth; therefore, it is of value in the treatment of short bowel syndrome caused by multiple resections for Crohn’s disease. Six months after commencing therapy, patients with short bowel syndrome requiring total parenteral nutrition (TPN) top-ups achieved a reduction in their TPN requirements between 20 and 100%.

A Codeine phosphate

Codeine phosphate is incorrect. Although codeine phosphate may slow gastrointestinal transit and have an impact on the symptoms of diarrhoea, it is not likely to have a significant impact on the symptoms of malabsorption.

B Liraglutide

Liraglutide is incorrect. Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide 1 agonist used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes; it has no significant impact on small intestinal mucosal growth.

C Loperamide hydrochloride

Loperamide hydrochloride is incorrect. Like codeine phosphate, loperamide hydrochloride may improve the symptoms of diarrhoea, but it is not likely to improve the symptoms associated with malabsorption.

E Vildagliptin

Vildagliptin is incorrect. Vildagliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old man presented with an attack of acute upper abdominal pain associated with vomiting.

On examination, he had epigastric tenderness and guarding. Serum amylase was 1300 IU/L. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, fluids and analgesia. His pain settled and he made a good recovery and was discharged from hospital several days later.

Eight weeks later, he was readmitted with malaise and persistent abdominal pain.

On examination, he had low-grade pyrexia and there was a tender mass palpable in the upper abdomen. His heart rate is 96 bpm and his blood pressure is 124/81 mmHg.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)112 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)390 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)82 fL76–98 fL
C-reactive protein (CRP)200 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea4.8 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Corrected Calcium (Ca²⁺)2.50 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
Bilirubin22 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)160 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)78 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)42 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Amylase1000 U/L< 200 U/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Pancreatic pseudocyst

Pancreatic pseudocysts are an uncommon complication of acute pancreatitis, and are localised collections of pancreatic fluid and debris, usually in the lesser sac. They are initially contained within a fragile wall of granulation tissue which eventually forms a fibrous capsule. They cannot be diagnosed until more than 6 weeks after the acute attack, and may present with abdominal pain or a mass, fever and persistently raised amylase and liver function tests. Small pseudocysts usually resolve on their own, but those that are greater than 6 cm in diameter seldom disappear spontaneously and may lead to complications such as haemorrhage and infection. They are usually managed by endoscopic or percutanous drainage or surgical intervention.

B Pyogenic liver abscess

Liver abscesses mostly occur following peritonitis due to leaking of bowel content with spread to the liver by portal circulation. Alternatively, there can be direct spread from the biliary system or haematogenous seeding from systemic infection. Liver abcesses commonly cause fever and abdominal pain, whilst patients can also have anorexia, vomiting and weight loss. The low-grade, as opposed to a high-grade, fever, as well as the very delayed timing, makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

C Chronic pancreatitis

Chronic pancreatitis occurs with progressive inflammatory changes causing permanent structural damage, which results in impaired exocrine and endocrine function. It can present as chronic epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting which radiates to the back, or with pancreatic insufficiency causing malabsorption and steatorrhea. The acute abdominal signs and elevated amylase make this a less likely differential.

D Recurrent attack of acute pancreatitis

Recurrent acute pancreatitis can occur, and in some patients this becomes a regular problem necessitating surgery if very severe. The presence of a tender and palpable mass makes this a less likely diagnosis.

E Pancreatic carcinoma

Pancreatic carcinoma is a cause of a painless epigastric mass and progressively worsening jaundice. The presence of pain and tenderness reduces the likelihood of this diagnosis, as does the absence of jaundice. 6743

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with a history of type I diabetes presents with a 3-month history of nausea, early satiety, bloating and intermittent vomiting, particularly after meals. She reports poor glycaemic control and frequently experiences hypoglycaemic episodes after eating. Physical examination is unremarkable. She has tried antacids and proton pump inhibitors, with no improvement in her symptoms. Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L135–175 g/L
Platelets (PLT)300 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Fasting blood glucose8.0 mmol/L4.0–6.0 mmol/L
HbA1c9.5%Less than 7%
Creatinine (Cr)85 µmol/L60–120 µmol/L

What is the most appropriate diagnostic test to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Gastric emptying scintigraphy

Gastric emptying scintigraphy is the gold standard for diagnosing gastroparesis, as it quantitatively assesses the rate of gastric emptying. In gastroparesis, delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction is a key feature, especially in patients with a history of diabetes.

A Abdominal ultrasound

While abdominal ultrasound can be helpful in ruling out other causes of abdominal pain, such as gallstones or biliary pathology, it does not assess gastric emptying function. This patient’s symptoms and history are suggestive of delayed gastric emptying, making gastric emptying scintigraphy more appropriate.

C Upper GI endoscopy

While an endoscopy can help to identify structural abnormalities, it cannot evaluate gastric emptying. Endoscopy may be helpful to rule out other causes of this patient's symptoms if gastroparesis is not confirmed, but it is not the primary diagnostic tool for delayed gastric emptying.

D CT of the abdomen

A CT scan is useful for evaluating intra-abdominal pathology but does not provide information on gastric

motility. It may help to exclude other causes but is not diagnostic for gastroparesis.

E Hydrogen breath test

The hydrogen breath test is used to diagnose small intestinal bacterial overgrowth or carbohydrate malabsorption disorders, which can cause bloating and discomfort but would not confirm gastroparesis. 74428

questions.question:
A 27-year-old office worker presents with a 3-year history of epigastric pain, especially 30 min after eating. This is associated with nausea and belching. She also describes constipation with occasional explosive diarrhoea. The stools are normally hard with mucus and she needs to strain with every motion.

Abdominal pain is relieved after defecation but abdominal bloating persists. She wakes up an hour earlier each morning to finish her breakfast in order to prevent vomiting. She has missed work on a few occasions and feels that her weight has fluctuated.

Past medical history includes scarlet fever. She is not on any regular medications except intermittent laxatives over the counter. Abdominal examination is normal. Rectal examination reveals an anal fissure.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)180 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)87 fL76–98 fL
International normalised ratio (INR)1.0< 1.1
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)1.1 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea3.7 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)70 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin39 g/L35–55 g/L
Liver function tests (LFTs)Normal
Anti-endomysial antibodyNegative
Thyroid function tests (TFTs)Normal
GastroscopyNormal
Flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsyNormal
Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound scanNormal

What is the most likely diagnosis to account for her symptoms?
options: Overlap irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Overlap irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia

This lady has signs of irritable bowel syndrome, especially in light of all the normal investigation results. It is the result of complex interactions between psychosocial factors, disordered bowel motility and altered intestinal sensations. This disorder is commonly associated with functional dyspepsia and patients are more likely to get chronic fatigue syndrome and globus hystericus.

Diagnostic criteria have been developed, most notably the ‘Rome criteria’. These include symptoms of abdominal pain relieved by defecation that is associated with a change in stool frequency and consistency, abdominal bloating and passing mucus per rectum.

B Diarrhoea pre-dominant irritable bowel syndrome

Although she does report occasional diarrhoea, her more predominant symptom is constipation.

C Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction

The classical symptoms of Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction are of recurrent biliary-type epigastric / right upper quadrant pain, which last from 30 minutes to several hours, and is not relieved by bowel movements. It is not typically associated with diarrhoea, or a change in stool consistency. For diagnosis, the patient must have biliary pain, and imaging must reveal the absence of bile duct stones or other structural abnormalities, and elevated liver enzymes or dilated bile duct, but not both.

D Malabsorption sydrome and non-ulcer dyspepsia

There is no supporting evidence in the history of a malabsorption syndrome: no sustained weight loss, albumin is normal, and coeliac antibodies are negative.

E Globus hystericus

Globus sensation is a functional oesophageal disorder characterized by a sensation of a lump, retained food bolus, or tightness in the throat that is not due to an underlying structural lesion, gastroesophageal reflux disease, mucosal abnormality, or an esophageal motility disorder. This is not the presentation of this patient.

questions.question:
A 59-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She was referred by her General Practitioner with cramping abdominal pain and frequent episodes of diarrhoea. On further questioning, she denies indigestion. There is no significant past medical history, apart from hypertension which is controlled with bendroflumethiazide. She drinks two bottles of wine per week. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/72 mmHg and a heart rate of 75 bpm and regular. She has pale conjunctivae. There are no abnormal findings, and her body mass index is 24 kg/m 2.

Investigations:

InvestigationsResultsNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)91 g/L115–155 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)78 fL76–98 fL
Ferritin18 µg/L10–120 µg/L
White cell count (WCC)8.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine85 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Albumin30 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)44 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Amylase50 U/L70–300 U/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Tissue transglutaminase

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend coeliac screening for any patient who presents with iron deficiency anaemia before beginning specific investigations. This is because of the recognition that underlying coeliac disease may present without the classical symptoms of abdominal bloating and diarrhoea. In this case, the low albumin level hints at chronic malabsorption, which may be due to an underlying small bowel disease. Following coeliac antibody testing, the patient should be referred for both upper and lower gastrointestinal investigations, with colonoscopy being a more definitive option (when preparation is adequate), compared to barium enema.

A Ultrasound abdomen

An abdominal ultrasound scan would be an appropriate first-line investigation in patients with deranged liver function tests or abdominal pain. In this case, the patient importantly has no symptoms to suggest this and there are no data indicating significantly deranged liver function tests.

B Colonoscopy

Colonoscopy is an important investigation to consider. However, importantly, in this case, there are no red flag symptoms (eg weight loss or change in bowel habit). Therefore, it would be reasonable to screen the patient for coeliac disease before referring them for a colonoscopy. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines state that all patients over the age of 60 with unexplained iron deficiency anaemia should be referred for a colonoscopy on the 2-week wait rule.

C Faecal elastase

Faecal elastase is a test of the exocrine function of the pancreas, particularly for patients with chronic pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis is commonly caused by alcohol excess and symptoms include abdominal pain and steatorrhoea. Amylase levels are often elevated, but not always. However, chronic pancreatitis does not explain this patient’s anaemia and the lack of a history of acute pancreatitis makes the diagnosis even less likely.

E Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

This would be an investigation that could be considered if the patient had a normal colonoscopy and a normal coeliac screen.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old former intravenous drug abuser presents to the Hepatology Clinic for review. He has just completed a 48-week course of Peg-interferon alpha-2a for hepatitis B infection. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. His abdomen is soft, with no obvious stigmata of liver disease.

On review in the clinic, his results are as follows:

InvestigationResult
HBsAgPositive
HBeAgPositive
Anti-HBc IgGPositive
Anti-HBs IgGNegative
Anti-HCV IgGNegative
HCV RNANegative
InvestigationResult Normal value
Albumin27 g/L 35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)122 U/L 7–55 U/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)148 U/L 30–150 U/L
Bilirubin24 µmol/L 1–22 µmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Switch to tenofovir

This patient still shows signs of hepatitis B infection, given positive HBsAg and HBeAg. A positive anti-HBc IgG suggests chronic infectivity. Management of hepatitis B and C has been revolutionised over recent years by the introduction of novel antiviral agents. In this situation, tenofovir is a logical next step and is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor which inhibits hepatitis B deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) replication.

A Continue interferon

Given that interferon has failed to achieve clearance of hepatitis B, alternative therapy is required.

C Switch to lamivudine

Lamivudine is less effective, compared to modern agents such as entecavir or tenofovir. It does, however, carry a lower acquisition cost, compared to more modern agents.

D Reassurance and stop treatment

This patient still shows signs of active infection with positive HBsAg and HBeAg. Therefore, additional treatment is needed.

E Switch to ribavirin

Ribavirin is used in combination with interferon for the treatment of hepatitis C. However, the combination is less effective than more modern agents, such as boceprevir, and has therefore been largely superseded. 70041

questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. She undergoes emergency laparotomy, which is normal.

On further questioning, she reveals a family history of an aunt who has a light-sensitive rash and a diagnosis of porphyria.

On examination, she is hypertensive, with generalised rebound tenderness. She responds to analgesia and once she is stabilised a porphyrin screen is sent.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Sodium (Na⁺)125 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.0 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Glucose5.0 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L
Full blood count (FBC)Normal
CT abdomenNormal
Urinary porphobilinogen (PBG)300 µmol/dl0 - 18.0 µmol/dl
Faecal porphyrinsNormal (co-proporphyrins and protoporphyrins)
Plasma porphyrinsMarkedly increased

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Acute intermittent porphyria

Attacks of acute porphyria are often mistaken for surgical abdomens. Family histories may be misleading, as porphyria may be misdiagnosed or may not be manifest in other family members. Acute intermittent porphyria is correct as it fits the clinical symptoms of gastrointestinal upset with abdominal pain and cramp with nausea and vomiting. Urinary porphyrins are raised in all three acute porphyrias (acute intermittent porphyria, hereditary co-proporpyria and variegate porphyria), so these can often be impossible to distinguish clinically. Faecal porphyrins can be useful to differentiate the conditions, because they are elevated in coproporphyria and variegate porphyria.

B Variegate porphyria

Variegate porphyria is an autosomal dominant disease caused by a mutation of protoporphyrinogen oxide. It is characterised by symptoms of neurovisceral crises similar to those in a patient with AIP, but is also associated with a classic photosensitive skin disorder which this patient did not have.

C Hereditary coproporphyria

Similarly, hereditary co-proporphyria is also incorrect as it is associated with a blistering skin rash, particularly in sun-exposed areas.

D Porphyria cutanea tarda

Although it is the most common of all porphyrias, it is purely a skin disease, resulting from a deficiency of the enzyme uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

E Lead poisoning

This does not cause increase in urinary porphyrins. Lead poisoning predominantly affects the nervous system, with symptoms such as delirium, tremor and convulsions.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old truck driver has been referred by his general practitioner (GP) to the rapid access upper gastrointestinal (GI) clinic with a 10-day history of intermittent epigastric pain and nausea.

He has been prescribed a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) which he started taking 4 days ago with some relief. He has taken regular co-codamol for years for chronic back pain but otherwise has no previous medical history. His weight is stable and clinical examination is unremarkable.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)147 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.6 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)212 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)86 fL76–98 fL

Which is the most appropriate next step in management according to available evidence?
options: Refer for routine upper GI endscopy and give symptomatic antacids in first instance
Add metoclopramide 10 mg tds and review in 2 weeks
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Continue proton pump inhibitor

This gentleman is <55 years old without ‘alarm’ features – weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia – and does not take non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). He is not anaemic and has no epigastric mass on examination. As he has gained some relief from the PPI it’s therefore appropriate to continue the medication.

A Urgent upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy

Alarm features that prompt urgent referral for endoscopy include weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, anaemia and the presence of an epigastric mass on physical examination.

B pylori eradication therapy

H. pylori testing is useful, particularly where there is a limited response to PPI, although a 2-week wash-out should be accomplished if possible before breath testing is instituted.

D Refer for routine upper GI endscopy and give symptomatic antacids in first instance

Before referral for routine endoscopy, a trial of PPI and/or H pylori breath testing should first take place.

E Add metoclopramide 10 mg tds and review in 2 weeks

Although metoclopramide is a pro-kinetic and may improve nausea, its use is now discouraged because of dopamine antagonist-related adverse effects of therapy.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with an upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. He is a non-smoker and drinks only occasional wine. On further questioning, he admits to problems with indigestion over the past few months, for which he has tried over-the-counter Ranitidine tablets, and increasing diarrhoea.

Upper GI endoscopy reveals multiple small gastric ulcers and helicobacter testing is negative. He is willing to have a short period off Ranitidine to be properly investigated.

Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation in this case?
options: Fasting gastrin on three different days
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Fasting gastrin on three different days

There is a suspicion that this patient may have Zollinger–Ellison syndrome as a result of a gastrinoma. The best initial screen is a fasting gastrin level on three separate days, as the secretion of gastrin is pulsatile. Three samples in the normal range make a gastrinoma unlikely. This is usually followed by basal acid output estimation and a secretin stimulation test. After this, patients usually move on to imaging studies. In the absence of metastases, surgical resection is advised. Octreotide, interferon and chemotherapy may be useful in non-surgically resectable lesions.

D Secretin stimulation test

Like basal acid output estimation, secretin stimulation test is an investigation which follows the three gastrin measurements.

A Single fasting gastrin level

Gastrin has a short half-life and release is cyclical, hence re-measuring on 3 separate days is recommended.

C Basal acid output estimation

Basal acid output estimation is a subsequent test after elevated gastrin has been established.

E Protein meal test

An arginine stimulation test is used in the evaluation of growth hormone deficiency.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman is referred to the Hepatology Clinic with liver failure. She drinks no alcohol but over the past few months has suffered from increasing tiredness, upper abdominal discomfort, nausea, anorexia and itching. Most recently, she has noticed markedly increased bruising if she takes a knock on something.

On examination, her blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg. You notice signs of chronic liver disease including scratch marks on her skin, spider naevi and evidence of mild jaundice. She also has extensive bruising on her limbs. Hepatomegaly is also present.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)105 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.5 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)110 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)134 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Prothrombin time (PT)27.3 s10.6–14.9 s
Albumin22 g/L35–55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)765 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin100 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Anti-soluble liver antigen antibody+
Gamma-globulinsIncreased
Liver biopsyHepatic cirrhosis

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Autoimmune hepatitis Type 3

This patient has an autoantibody pattern consistent with autoimmune hepatitis type 3, and features of cirrhosis which are said to occur in around 75% of patients with the condition. It is commonest in those of the 30–50- year group, the vast majority being women. The prolonged PT is likely to be as the result of severe hepatic dysfunction. Corticosteroids achieve remission in around 2/3 of patients, although the relapse rate is as high as 80% after steroid withdrawal. Azathioprine is the main steroid-sparing agent used in the treatment of the condition.

A comparison between subtypes of autoimmune hepatitis is listed below:

Clinical Features Type 1 Type 2 Type 3

Anti-LKM ASMA Soluble liver-kidney P-450 IID6 antigen Diagnostic autoantibodies ANA Synthetic core motif peptides 254- Cytokeratins 8 and 18 Anti-actin 271

Paediatric (2-14y) Age 10y - elderly Adults (30-50y) Rare in adults

Women (%) 78 89 90

Concurrent immune disease 41 34 58 %

Gamma globulin elevation +++ + ++

Low IgA No Occasional No

B8, DR3, HLA association B14, DR3, C4AQO Uncertain DR4

Steroid response ++ ++ +++

Progression to cirrhosis 45 82 75

A Wilson’s disease

Wilson’s disease presents at an earlier age and is usually associated with an asymptomatic rise in transaminases, psychiatric symptoms or a movement disorder.

B Haemochromatosis

Haemochromatosis presents later in women because of the natural blood loss afforded by the regular menstrual cycle. It also presents with other features such as diabetes and chondrocalcinosis, which aren’t seen here.

C Autoimmune hepatitis Type 1

This is associated with anti-smooth muscle antibodies rather than the soluble liver–kidney antigen antibodies seen here.

D Primary biliary cholangitis

Primary biliary cholangitis presents with itching and lethargy and is associated with an obstructive picture on liver function testing.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old alcoholic is admitted after an upper GI haemorrhage. An endoscopy is performed soon after admission with variceal banding, but you are asked to see him the following morning as he is drowsy and confused.

On examination, his BP is 100/60 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular and his temperature is 36.5°C. He is mildly tender in the epigastrium and there is evidence of ascites. He is very drowsy and appears confused when you wake him from sleep. PR reveals melaena.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)91 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)131 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)128 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.1 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)122 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)17 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Albumin23 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)231 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Glucose5.9 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L

Which of the following is most likely to reveal the cause of his confusion?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Serum ammonia

The fact that the increased confusion has occurred following the upper GI bleed is suggestive that blood ingestion has led to increased ammonia production by the bacteria within the GI tract. Strategies to reduce bacterial ammonia production include use of rifaximin and lactulose.

B Ascitic tap

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is potentially one of the differential diagnoses in a case of confusion in a patient with decompensated alcoholic liver disease; in the current situation, however, the onset of confusion soon after the GI bleed points towards the blood ingestion and ammonia production as the likeliest cause.

C Blood cultures

Sepsis is a potential cause of confusion, but in this scenario there is no evidence for it, either from the physical examination/observations or from the blood results.

D CT head

A subdural haematoma could be another cause for confusion, but in our case there is no history of fall or head

injury.

E Lumbar puncture

Neither the history nor the blood results support the diagnosis of meningitis/encephalitis.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic complaining of long periods of constipation interspersed with short episodes of diarrhoea. She has not lost any weight over the past year and continues to eat a varied diet.

On examination, her BP is 122/82, her heart rate is 67 and regular and her BMI is 22.5 kg/m 2. Full blood count and viscosity are normal. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is unremarkable.

What is the next most appropriate management step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Soluble fibre supplementation

Normal clinical examination, stable weight and normal routine bloods make a sinister diagnosis unlikely. Irritable bowel syndrome is, therefore, the most likely cause of her symptoms. Psyllium or ispahula supplementation is of value in patients like this who have predominant constipation symptoms.

A Colonoscopy

Given the normal findings so far, there is little value in progressing to colonoscopy in this patient. Committing her to further investigation will only serve to increase anxiety.

B Barium enema

Like colonoscopy, progressing to barium enema would be considered over-investigation in this situation.

C Lactose-free diet

A lactose-free diet may be effective in reducing bloating associated with irritable bowel syndrome, but has

limited impact on constipation.

E Wheat-free diet

There is no evidence this patient has coeliac disease. Some patients with bloating benefit from reducing their wheat intake, although greater benefit is usually found from lactose exclusion.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old man presents complaining of diarrhoea for the past 2 days. It is watery and he has opened his bowels three times already today. He feels concerned as he thinks there was a small amount of blood mixed in with the stool on the most recent occasion. He does not feel too unwell and has been drinking plenty of fluids.

He has not eaten anything unusual or been travelling abroad in the last 6 months. He had an infected boil on his back, for which he received flucloxicillin 2 weeks ago for one week in total. No one else in the household feels unwell.

He has no past medical history and takes no medications. BP is 105/80 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing.

What would be the most appropriate next management step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Oral rehydration salts

NICE suggest that acute diarrhoea should be assessed for cause and the severity of dehydration should be established. The Table below is based on NICE guidelines to help divide the different features.

Mild dehydration Moderate dehydration Severe dehydration

Lassitude Apathy/tiredness Profound apathy

Anorexia/nausea Dizziness Weakness

Light-headedness Muscle cramps Confusion

Postural hypotension Pinched face Shock

Dry tongue or sunken eyes Tachycarida

Reduced skin elasticity Peripheral vasoconstriction

Postural hypotension Hypotension

Tachycardia Oliguria or anuria

Oliguria As his only feature dehydration is postural hypotension he can be managed for mild dehydration with oral rehydration.

C Loperamide

Whilst infection has not been proven, it is suspected, especially as there is an element of PR bleeding. Loperamide should be avoided if infective diarrhoea is suspected.

A Oral antibiotics

According to guidance, antibiotics should be reserved for when a patient has a positive stool culture or is extremely unwell. This patient is very stable. He has noticed a small amount of blood on passing stool so it is definitely worth sending a stool culture. His short course of flucloxicillin is very unlikely to have precipitated Clostridium difficile infection in an otherwise healthy young man.

B IV antibiotics

As with the previous option there is no indication to treat with antibiotics, IV or oral, unless there is a specific pathogen identified or there is evidence of severe infection. This patient is well and no samples suggesting infection have yet been returned.

D Sigmoidoscopy

Endoscopic examination would be necessary if inflammatory bowel disease was suspected to be the underlying cause. There is not very much in the history or examination to support such a suspicion; absence of fever, chronic history, abdominal pain and systemic features. Should such features develop or his diarrhoea not settle then this could be a reasonable choice.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old teacher presents to his General Practitioner with bloating, abdominal pain and weight loss. He also reports diarrhoea, which is very difficult to flush away and tends to float on the toilet pan.

On examination, his blood pressure is 115/72 mmHg and he looks pale. His BMI is 21 kg/m 2 and his abdomen is soft and non-tender. Results of blood tests show iron deficiency anaemia and an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level; his albumin level is low at 30 g/L.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following associated complications will have the best response to treatment?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Osteopenia

The symptoms and iron deficiency anaemia in this scenario are suggestive of coeliac disease. Coeliac disease can be associated with deranged liver function tests. Serological tests for coeliac disease include immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies to tissue transglutaminase (TTG) (preferred and most widely available), anti-endomysial antibodies and gliadin antigen. The ‘gold standard’ for diagnosis remains a duodenal or jejunal biopsy. There are many recognised complications of untreated or undertreated coeliac disease in adults including depression, anxiety and eating disorders like nutritional deficiencies and anaemia due to malabsorption, reduced bone mineral density, hyposplenism malignancy and dermatitis herpetiformis. Some renal diseases, including IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy and chronic kidney disease, are associated with coeliac disease; however, this does not include renal cystic disease.

A Dermatitis herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin manifestation of active coeliac disease. Episodes can recur, even on a strict gluten-free diet, making it inappropriate here. In recurrence, treatment with dapsone, in conjunction with a gluten-free diet, may be helpful.

B Infection with encapsulated organisms

Hyposplenism and splenic atrophy are closely associated with the development of other complications and autoimmune diseases in patients with coeliac disease. This increases patients’ risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria and sepsis. Studies have shown that treatment with a gluten-free diet can reverse functional hyposplenism, but not splenic atrophy, making it inappropriate for this patient.

D Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

People with coeliac disease are at increased risk of cancer, including an estimated 2- to 4-fold risk of non- Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Increased risk of malignancy in coeliac disease has been shown to normalise following a few years of a gluten-free diet. As this risk takes longer to normalise, compared to osteopenia, it is not appropriate here.

E Small bowel cancer

Those with coeliac disease are at increased risk of cancer, including an estimated 30-fold risk of small bowel cancer. As the increased risk of malignancy in coeliac has been shown to normalise after a few years of a gluten-free diet, compared to osteopenia, this risk takes longer to normalise and is not appropriate here. 2277

questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of shortness of breath and cough. There is a long past medical history of indigestion, worse when she lies flat on the bed, with occasional acid regurgitation. She may even wake at night occasionally with acid in her mouth and paroxysms of coughing.

On examination, her body mass index (BMI) is 31, she is pyrexial with a temperature of 39 °C, there is an area of bronchial breathing over the right lung and a suggestion of increased shadowing on the chest X-ray at the right base.

Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause for this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD)

This woman has a long history of indigestion, particularly worse when lying flat, and acid regurgitation, complicated by a chronic nocturnal cough. It is likely that an episode of regurgitation has led to right-sided lower respiratory tract infection. She is obese, which may well contribute to her symptoms. Other predisposing factors which increase the likelihood of GORD include smoking; hiatus hernia; medications which relax the lower oesophageal sphincter such as calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers; pregnancy; and foods such as chocolate and peppermint. Weight reduction would be the mainstay of management in this case, with the addition of proton pump inhibitors.

D Benign oesophageal stricture

Benign oesophageal stricture leads to regurgitation of food, often a mix of both solid and liquid meals, rather than the progressive dysphagia seen with oesophageal Ca.

A Bronchiectasis

Bronchiectasis is associated with longer-term shortness of breath and recurrent episodes of lower respiratory tract infection.

B Exacerbation of asthma

Given the long history of water brash and associated coughing, reflux is the more likely primary cause of her symptoms, and the CXR changes, rather than asthma alone.

C Oesophageal carcinoma

The long history of indigestion without progression to dysphagia and lack of weight loss doesn’t fit with a diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman has been referred to the clinic by her GP who suspects she may have irritable bowel syndrome. She suffers intermittent bouts of diarrhoea, problems with bloating, and flatulence. On further questioning, it transpires that she has been feeling a little tired over the past few months.

On examination, her BP is 125/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. She looks a little pale, her BMI is 22. Abdominal examination is unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin105 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.4 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets201 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine110 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Small bowel biopsyvillous atrophy, increased epithelial lymphocytes

Which of the following represents the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Gluten free diet

This patient has symptoms consistent with coeliac disease. She is also anaemic, which likely reflects iron deficiency from malabsorption. Her small bowel biopsy shows increased intraepithelial lymphocytes and villous atrophy, which is characteristic of the condition. As such the most appropriate therapy is a trial of gluten free diet.

Coeliac disease is caused by an immune response to gluten exposure causing a small bowel enteropathy in patients with a genetic predisposition. It is associate with HLA-DR3 + DQ2. Diagnosis is made on the basis of serology (IgA for endomysial or tissue transglutaminase (EMA/TTG) and duodenal biopsy. NB there is an association with IgA deficiency. In these cases patients should be tested for IgG to tissue transglutaminase. (TG2). The histological findings are not pathognomic and may also be seen in other disorders, such as immune deficiency, AI enteropathy, tropical sprue, Whipple’s disease and microscopic colitis amongst others so combination with positive serology is key to the diagnosis.

B Lactose free diet

Lactose avoidance may be of value in patients with symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome, particularly those of an ethnic origin where congenital lactase deficiency is increased. An increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes may be seen in cow’s milk hypersensitivity, but not villous atrophy.

A Metronidazole

Metronidazole would be used to treat giardiasis, a protozoal infection that can cause chronic diarrhoea with bloating and malabsorption. However, there is no history of travel and although one can see an increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes, villous atrophy is not typical.

D Doxycycline

Treatment with a tetracycline would be indicated in Whipple’s disease, which is a differential for the finding of villous atrophy on small bowel biopsy. However, one would also see PAS positive macrophages on histology.

E Prednisolone

Corticosteroids may be of value in Crohn’s, but are not used in the management of coeliac disease. Histology in small bowel Crohn’s might yield cryptitis or crypt abscesses in addition to intraepithelial lymphocytes.

questions.question:
A 79-year-old man was referred by his GP with a 4 month history of dysphagia. He was unable to pinpoint the site of his symptoms accurately but noted that his dysphagia worsened as he ate. At times he would regurgitate food during his meals, which would temporarily relieve his symptoms.

According to his GP, who had weighed him, he had lost 1 kg in weight over the past 2 months. His medications include Bendroflumethiazide for hypertension, and Ranitidine, which he takes intermittently for symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.

A barium swallow is shown below;

What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Pharyngeal pouch

The barium swallow shows a pharyngeal pouch (or Zenker’s diverticulum). These occur predominantly in elderly men (male: female of 5: 1), and are rare before the age of 40 years. The aetiology is unclear, although they may be related to poor relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter. An association with gastro- oesophageal reflux disease has also been noted.

Pharyngeal pouches commonly cause dysphagia, regurgitation and aspiration, and are a rare cause of halitosis. If large, they may cause a mass in the neck that gurgles on palpation (Boyce’s sign). Regurgitation of the contents of the pouch may temporarily ease dysphagia until the pouch refills with food and fluid.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is risky, since the pouches are thin-walled and easy to perforate; this is the reason why a barium swallow may be the preferable first-line investigation in elderly patients with dysphagia. Treatment is surgical, with either an open or endoscopic approach.

C Benign oesophageal stricture

This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Barium studies in those with benign oesophageal strictures typically produce a smooth, tapering narrowing of the oesophagus.

A Schatzki ring

This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Schatzki rings are benign narrowings in the distal oesophagus.

B Achalasia

This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Barium swallow in people with achalasia is associated with a very tight tapering at the gastro-oesophageal junction, generating a so-called ‘bird’s beak’ or ‘rat’s tail’ appearance, together with a dilated oesophagus.

E Post-cricoid web

This would give a very different appearance on barium swallow to those of a pharyngeal pouch. Post-cricoid webs occur near the upper oesophageal sphincter and may occur in association with iron-deficiency anaemia (Patterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome).

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has peripheral calcinosis, sclerodactyly and multiple telangiectasia, particularly marked on her face. Her main complaint over the past few months has been of increasing indigestion. She occasionally has acid coming up in her throat.

Which of the following is the most useful next step in managing the patient’s gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Oesophageal manometry

Patients with systemic sclerosis, the likely diagnosis here, given the presence of peripheral calcinosis, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia, suffer from oesophageal dysmotility because of a sclerotic process affecting the smooth muscle. Lower oesophageal pressure is commonly decreased in systemic sclerosis and can be measured using manometry. Prokinetic agents such as domperidone may be useful in relieving symptoms.

Esophageal dysmotility can present as dysphagia or a sensation of food being stuck in the throat. In patients with persistent symptoms despite twice-daily PPI therapy, we suggest a trial of prokinetic drugs (eg, metoclopramide, cisapride, domperidone, prucalopride) to relieve these symptoms. These drugs act by increasing esophageal sphincter pressure, improving peristalsis, and enhancing gastric emptying. Other very common disorder is GERD which require medical attention.

D Trial of omeprazole

Although proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole may improve symptoms from oesophageal dysmotility in systemic sclerosis, prokinetic agents and calcium channel antagonists are likely to be more effective.

A Breath testing

Small bowel bacterial overgrowth is seen in patients with systemic sclerosis and can be diagnosed with hydrogen breath testing. Usual symptoms of bacterial overgrowth include abdominal bloating, eructation and anorexia, not the symptoms reported here.

B Helicobacter pylori testing

Although H. pylori is a recognised cause of epigastric pain and indigestion, the symptoms of waterbrash described here are more suggestive of oesophageal dysmotility.

E Upper GI endoscopy

Although upper GI endoscopy may reveal the presence of oesophagitis, it will not shed light on any underlying dysmotility as a result of systemic sclerosis. 72465

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with a long history of Crohn’s disease presents with increased lethargy, weight loss and diarrhoea over a period of several months.

She had undergone a very extensive small bowel resection an unknown length of time ago and has recently returned from a period of work in Thailand. While abroad, she was admitted with an episode of renal pain due to kidney stones.

On examination, she has a midline scar and is thin with a BMI of 18.5. Her BP is 125/72 mmHg.

Investigations reveal:

Investigation Result Normal values

Features suggestive of megaloblastic Blood count and film anaemia

Prothrombin time (PT) 21.2 s 11 - 14 s

Albumin 28 g/L 35 - 55 g/L

Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺) 2.05 mmol/L 2.2 - 2/7 mmol/L

C-reactive protein (CRP) 15 mg/L < 10 mg/L

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 17 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h (ESR)

Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Short bowel syndrome

In patients who have removal of more than one-half of the small intestine, malabsorption syndrome may result. It may occur in patients with Crohn’s disease or those with ischaemic bowel who have undergone significant bowel resection. Patients present with diarrhoea and steatorrhoea, weight loss, anaemia, osteoporosis/osteomalacia, electrolyte disturbances and hypovolaemia. In patients with more than 100 cm of jejunum, oral intake is still possible. Diarrhoea may reduce with lactose exclusion or with a course of metronidazole to eradicate bacterial overgrowth. In patients with less than 100 cm of jejunum, total parenteral nutrition is recommended as the only way to maintain adequate nutritional intake.

A Active Crohn’s disease

Active Crohn’s disease is unlikely given that both the CRP and ESR are only just above the upper limit of the normal range.

C Coeliac disease

Although coeliac disease can co-exist with Crohn’s disease, it is unlikely, and would not lead to increased risk of renal stones. Oxalate renal stones are a recognised consequence of short bowel syndrome.

D Tropical sprue

Tropical sprue presents with symptoms similar to those of coeliac disease, but is infective in origin and particularly occurs in patients who have spent time in the Caribbean.

E Ulcerative colitis

Ulcerative colitis is associated with bloody diarrhoea and is not associated with the oxalate renal stones seen here.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old South Asian woman is referred to the Hepatology Clinic with progressive tiredness and lethargy, coupled with abnormal liver function tests. She has a history of hypertension, for which she takes Bendroflumethiazide, and she received a blood transfusion in 1989 after the birth of her last child in India but is otherwise well. On examination, her blood pressure is 115/85 mmHg; pulse is 70 bpm and regular. There is no organomegaly on palpation of the abdomen, although there is mild ascites. Her body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/m 2. She appears mildly jaundiced.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)114 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.9 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)101 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)81 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)181 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)278 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin45 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Glucose6.2 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Prothrombin time (PT)19.2 s10.6–14.9 s

Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Hepatitis C serology

The blood transfusion in 1989 occurred before widespread screening for Hepatitis C was introduced to blood banks in the 1990–1992 timeframe. As such, presentations with chronic liver disease are consistent with chronic active hepatitis due to hepatitis C. Quantification of hepatitis C RNA and genotyping are important to determining prognosis. Non-invasive imaging including ultrasound and fibroscan, coupled with liver biopsy can be used to assess the extent of fibrosis. The key to successful management of hepatitis C-related liver disease is identification and eradication of chronic carriage before fibrosis and cirrhosis is established.

A Autoimmune profile

Although an autoimmune profile would be helpful to pick up potential diagnoses, the blood transfusion is significant. Therefore, hepatitis C serology is more useful in terms of the next investigation.

B Caeruloplasmin

This patient has evidence of chronic liver disease; however, there are no symptoms or signs suggestive of Wilson’s disease. Patients often present by their mid-30s and although patients can be non-specifically unwell, they will often have psychiatric symptoms, such as depression and personality change, at some point prior to diagnosis.

C Ferritin

This patient has evidence of chronic liver disease; however, there are no symptoms or signs that would suggest haemochromatosis as a diagnosis. In addition to deranged liver function, these patients often present with skin hyperpigmentation (‘bronze skin’) along with joint pains and symptoms related to a possible diagnosis of diabetes mellitus.

D Hepatitis B serology

She is started on intravenous (iv) fluids and ranitidine. Six hours later, her vomiting persists and she becomes confused. She is a non-smoker and does not drink any alcohol.

On examination, she is afebrile. Her blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg and she is tachycardic. Cardiovascular and chest examinations are normal. Her abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant but there is no rebound or rigidity. There are no focal neurological signs.
